items.title: Auscultation for pre-exercise screening in the horse.
items.abstract: Objective To describe the highlights of cardiac auscultation of the equine athlete in the context of pre-exercise screening for cardiac adverse event prevention. Animals Horses. Methods Tutorial description. Results Description of the highlights of cardiac auscultation of the equine athlete in the context of pre-exercise screening for cardiac adverse event and exercise-associated sudden death prevention. Clinical relevance Cardiac adverse events and exercise-associated deaths are problems that affect horses' health, riders' safety, and the public perception of welfare during equestrian sports. Screening before participation in sports has helped decrease the incidence of sudden death in humans. We believe auscultation may be a high-yield, low-cost strategy to improve equine welfare and a key component of a prevention program for exercise-associated sudden death in equine athletes. What we describe here highlights that an irregularly irregular rhythm is atrial fibrillation until proven otherwise and is the main target of pre-exercise auscultation. Concerning murmurs are the second target; multiple examples of audio, video, and electrocardiograms are shown.

items.title: Antibiotic overuse and mortality in patients hospitalised for COVID-19: a global cohort study.
items.abstract: Background Global antibiotic use during the COVID-19 pandemic and its impact remain unclear. This study analysed antibiotic use, bacterial co-infections, and the association between antibiotic use and in-hospital mortality among patients hospitalised for COVID-19, using a WHO database. Methods We conducted a multicountry cohort study using anonymised patient-level data from The WHO Global Clinical Platform for COVID-19. Data were collected across 64 countries in all six WHO regions between January, 2020, and October, 2023. The study included hospitalised patients of all ages with suspected or confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection. We obtained patient-level data from standardised WHO case report forms completed prospectively or retrospectively and from harmonised national registries, research studies, and hospital databases. Patients without a suspected or confirmed COVID-19 diagnosis or missing information on hospital admission date, antibiotic use, or outcome were excluded from the analysis. Patients were followed up from hospital admission until death, discharge, transfer, or 28 days, whichever occurred first. Follow-up data were collected at hospital discharge or death by the treating facility and entered into the platform. The primary outcome was 28-day in-hospital mortality, and we analysed this outcome using Cox proportional hazards models with a shared frailty term to account for country-level clustering. Findings The median age of the study population was 61·9 years (±21·7), with 198 223 women and 251 990 men with data available on antibiotic use. Of the 592 898 patients enrolled, 451 291 (76·1%) had data on antibiotic use and were included in the descriptive analysis; 122 854 had complete data on empirical treatment type, of whom 47 359 (38·5%) were included in the regression analysis. Among the 451 291 patients with data on antibiotic use, 341 125 (75·6%) received antibiotics, more frequently in severe to critical cases than in mild to moderate cases (80·5% vs 71·6%). Prescribing was highest in the Eastern Mediterranean (83·0%) and African (82·7%) regions and lowest in the Western Pacific region (32·8%), declining in the European region and region of the Americas but increasing in the African region between 2020 and 2022. Treatment was predominantly empirical and involved Watch antibiotics of the WHO Access, Watch, and Reserve classification. Clinically suspected co-infections were reported in 47 050 (7·9%) of the 592 898 patients; among those with positive cultures, 1815 (42·8%) of 4237 had multidrug-resistant bacteria. In the unadjusted analyses, empirical antibiotic use was associated with higher mortality across severity strata. After adjustment for age, sex, comorbidities, and disease severity, empirical antibiotic use remained associated with increased mortality in mild to moderate cases (adjusted hazard ratio 1·80, 95% CI 1·36-2·38) and severe to critical cases (1·16, 1·08-1·24). Interpretation Despite clinically suspected co-infections being reported in only 47 050 (7·9%) of the 592 898 enrolled patients, 341 125 (75·6%) of the 451 291 patients with data on antibiotic use received antibiotic therapy, predominantly broad-spectrum agents. As antibiotic use was not associated with improved clinical outcomes and is known to increase antimicrobial resistance, it should be rationalised through strengthened antimicrobial stewardship and behavioural interventions, particularly during respiratory viral epidemics. Funding None.

items.title: Cholera rapid diagnostic test performance at the host-microbe interface: a prospective longitudinal study in Bangladesh.
items.abstract: Background Effective cholera outbreak response requires accurate bedside rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) because of poor laboratory access. Formative studies suggest that cholera diagnostics have multiple vulnerabilities, including target degradation by virulent bacteriophage (phage) specific to Vibrio cholerae and antibiotics. Our study objectives were to evaluate the performance of RDTs as a function of these antimicrobials to improve deployment and guide future diagnostic development. Methods In this prospective longitudinal study, participants were enrolled at seven hospitals across Bangladesh from March 13, 2018, to April 9, 2019. Inclusion criteria were participants aged 2 months or older with uncomplicated diarrhoeal disease. Exclusion criteria were the presence of severe comorbidity or the absence of participant or guardian consent or assent. Stool samples were analysed using culture, quantitative PCR (qPCR), and mass spectrometry. The primary outcome was RDT performance (eg, sensitivity and specificity) as a function of phage detection. Exploratory outcomes were the effects of antibiotics and disease severity on RDT performance. Findings 2574 participants were enrolled, and for 2078 samples, all assays were completed for analysis of the primary outcome. 394 samples without RDT data and 102 samples without qPCR data were excluded. Using the current gold standard of culture or qPCR positivity for V cholerae, we found that phage detection had no effect on RDT performance. When the diagnostic criteria were expanded to include phage detection, RDT sensitivity decreased from 0·46 (95% CI 0·41-0·51) to 0·38 (0·34-0·43), and the odds of RDT positivity among patients with cholera decreased with phage exposure (odds ratio 0·428; 95% CI 0·296-0·613). Antibiotics were detected in more than 80% of samples using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, limiting assessment of their effects on RDT performance. Among patients with moderate and severe dehydration, large increases in sensitivity and specificity were observed. We estimated that restricting RDT use to patients with severe dehydration and no reported antibiotic exposure increased sensitivity by 50% compared with unrestricted RDT use. If the presence of phage is considered a diagnostic proxy for V cholerae infection, then RDTs might not detect an additional 17% of cholera cases. Interpretation Cholera RDTs have limitations that require consideration during global deployments. Inclusion of phage detection in diagnostic criteria might improve case detection, although this requires further research in diverse settings. The implications of these findings likely extend to other diseases in which diagnostics share similar vulnerabilities. Funding Wellcome Trust (DFID grant), NIH, and Thrasher Research Fund.

items.title: Biomarker tests for invasive Candida infection in critically ill patients in the UK (A-Stop): a multicentre diagnostic test accuracy study.
items.abstract: Background The current practice of empirical antifungal treatment for suspected invasive Candida infection in the intensive care unit (ICU) leads to overtreatment. Biomarkers might better target treatment; however, their diagnostic accuracy in this patient group is uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate whether a biomarker or a combination of biomarkers has sufficiently high negative predictive value (NPV) to enable early cessation of empirical antifungal treatment in patients in ICUs. Methods In this prospective, multicentre, diagnostic test accuracy study, we recruited patients who had been started on empirical antifungal treatment for suspected candidiasis and had blood cultures drawn within 24 h of starting treatment from 43 UK ICUs. We tested a research blood sample, collected within 24 h of the standard-of-care care blood culture (ie, within 48 h of starting empirical antifungal treatment), with three DNA detection tests (Fungiplex, T2Candida, and CandID) and one (1,3)-β-D-glucan test (Fungitell). We assessed the accuracy of these tests against an international consensus definition of proven invasive Candida infection and a constructed reference standard for proven or probable infection. The primary outcome was NPV for exclusion of proven Candida infection; we also reported sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios. Findings Among 4005 patients screened, 1251 were enrolled. A total of 1225 participants, recruited between April, 2018 and Feb, 2023, were evaluable, among whom 54 (4·4%) had proven invasive Candida infection. The median duration of antifungal treatment was 9 days (IQR 5-15), and survival at 28 days was 76·8%. The index tests had similar NPVs: 96·6% (95·3-97·6) for Fungiplex, 97·1% (94·7-98·6) for T2Candida, 96·7% (95·4-97·8) for CandID, and 97·2% (95·5-98·4) for Fungitell; however, sensitivity varied widely among the tests, from 27·5% to 68·6%. The optimal test combination was Fungitell and CandID, which had an NPV of 97·5% (95·7-98·7) and a sensitivity of 75·0%. Combining these biomarkers with standard-of-care blood culture testing further increased the NPV to 98·6% (97·0-99·4), with a sensitivity of 85·1%. Interpretation No single biomarker had sufficiently high sensitivity to justify stopping empirical antifungal treatment. Combining Fungitell and CandID with standard-of-care blood culture testing could provide a sufficiently high NPV to allow early cessation of empirical antifungal treatment in this patient group, thereby reducing overtreatment, although this gain in sensitivity is accompanied by a reduction in specificity. Randomised trials are needed to confirm the clinical and cost-effectiveness of this diagnostic strategy before it is adopted in practice. items.title: Perioperative chemotherapy and stereotactic body radiotherapy versus perioperative chemotherapy alone in patients with high-risk, localised pancreatic cancer (MASTERPLAN): an open-label, phase 2, multicentre, randomised trial of the Australasian Gastro-Intestinal Trials Group.
items.abstract: Background Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) has poor outcomes and high rates of locoregional recurrence. MASTERPLAN evaluated whether stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) reduced locoregional recurrence in patients with high-risk, localised PDAC. Methods MASTERPLAN was an open-label, randomised, phase 2 trial conducted across 14 hospitals in Australia and New Zealand. Eligible participants were aged 18 years or older with an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 0-1, and had previously untreated localised PDAC with at least one high-risk feature, including tumour size more than 4 cm, extrapancreatic extension, node-positive disease, borderline resectable disease, or locally advanced disease. Participants were randomly assigned (2:1) using the method of minimisation to investigator-choice chemotherapy, with or without SBRT, stratified by participant cohort (potentially operable vs inoperable), planned chemotherapy regimen, randomisation before or within the first 28 days of chemotherapy, and institution. Chemotherapy consisted of mFOLFIRINOX (day 1 oxaliplatin 85 mg/m 2 , irinotecan 150 mg/m 2 , leucovorin 50 mg, and fluorouracil 2400 mg/m 2 over 46 h every 14 days for six cycles; all intravenous) or gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel (gemcitabine 1000 mg/m 2 and nab-paclitaxel 125 mg/m 2 on days 1, 8, and 15 every 28 days for three cycles; both intravenous). SBRT was delivered as 40 Gy in five fractions, with two to four fractions delivered per week, with real-time radiotherapy quality assurance. Surgical resection was considered following induction therapy, followed by a planned further 12 weeks of adjuvant chemotherapy with either mFOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine plus capecitabine (28-day cycles of 1000 mg/m 2 intravenous gemcitabine administered on days 1, 8, and 15 with 830 mg/m 2 oral capecitabine twice daily administered on days 1-21). Participants deemed not suitable for surgery continued the same chemotherapy for an additional 12 weeks with reassessment for surgical suitability permitted, for a total planned duration of chemotherapy of 24 weeks. The primary endpoint was 12-month locoregional recurrence in the intention-to-treat population, with safety endpoints analysed by treatment received. The trial planned to recruit 120 patients but due to slow accrual closed to recruitment early on Jan 6, 2025. Trial closure and database lock occurred on July 21, 2026. This trial was registered with the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trial Registry (ACTRN12619000409178) and ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT04089150), and is complete. Findings Between Feb 26, 2020, and Jan 6, 2025, 74 participants (43 [58%] male, 31 [42%] female) were randomly assigned to chemotherapy and SBRT (n=49) or chemotherapy alone (n=25). After a median follow-up of 3·2 years (IQR 1·9-4·3), 12-month locoregional recurrence was 20·2% (95% CI 9·9-33·1) in the SBRT group and 52·0% (30·3-69·9) in the chemotherapy alone group (subdistribution hazard ratio 0·44 [95% CI 0·22-0·88]; p=0·022). Grade 3 or higher adverse events occurred in 33 (70%) of 47 participants in the SBRT group and 16 (64%) of 25 participants in the chemotherapy alone group (p=0·27), with one (4%) treatment-related death secondary to biliary tract infection in the chemotherapy alone group. The most common grade 3-4 adverse events were diarrhoea (seven [15%] in the SBRT group vs five [20%] in the chemotherapy alone group), and thromboembolic events (three [6%]) vs one [4%]). Overall grade 3 or higher serious adverse events occurred in 30 (64%) of 47 participants in the SBRT group, and 14 (56%) of 25 participants in the chemotherapy alone group (p=0·24). There were two serious adverse events attributable to SBRT; grade 2 small bowel obstruction and grade 3 pancreatitis. Interpretation In patients with high-risk, localised PDAC, the addition of SBRT to chemotherapy was associated with significantly reduced locoregional recurrence without a significant increase in toxicity and warrants further investigation in larger studies. Funding Medical Research Future Fund, Australasian Gastro-Intestinal Trials Group, National Health and Medical Research Council Clinical Trials Centre (University of Sydney), and Gut Cancer Foundation, New Zealand.

items.title: Online continuing education for the Indian Health Service: Public health intervention wheel update.
items.abstract: Background Following the work-priority disruption caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, the supervisor of the Four Corners Regional Health Center of the Indian Health Service requested an update of the Public Health Intervention Wheel for public health staff across 11 healthcare facilities. The Wheel explains what public health nurses do in their practice. Purpose Nursing leaders chose a staff development project to help public health nursing staff shift their focus to address health priorities and health disparities among Native American communities. Methods Public health nursing staff completed five synchronous online sessions on the revised Public Health Intervention Wheel. The online sessions included PowerPoint presentations, discussion, and group reports. Participants reported that the Public Health Intervention Wheel applied to and explained their practice. A survey revealed that 93% to 97% of participants strongly agreed or agreed that the learning objectives were met and the learning strategies were effective. Discussion The online education format provided convenient access for participants over a large geographic area. Both the benefits and challenges of the online synchronous education sessions were identified. Conclusion The integration of the Wheel into staff orientation and departmental initiatives will contribute to a comprehensive scope of public health nursing practice in Native American communities.

items.title: Differences in reporting child abuse by mothers and young adults.
items.abstract: Background Measuring violence against children (VAC) requires understanding competing sources of bias, with evidence suggesting caregivers underreport abuse. Objective This study examined differences in reported child abuse by respondent using longitudinal data and identified factors influencing maternal reporting. Participants and settings Using data from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC), we analyzed mothers' cumulative prospective reports of physical and psychological abuse experienced by their children, alongside young adults' retrospective self-reports. Methods Difference between prevalence of abuse by respondents was estimated using McNemar's test for paired proportions. Concordance between respondents was assessed using Cohen's kappa and Prevalence-Adjusted Bias-Adjusted Kappa (PABAK). Multivariable logistic regressions identified maternal characteristics associated with reporting. Results Physical and psychological child prevalence was 6.23% (95% CI 5.51-7.02), and 11.77% (95% CI 10.80-12.81) among young adults, with significant differences by respondent (p Conclusion While reports from mothers and children showed limited concordance, there was no consistent evidence that mothers systematically underreported abuse when identical questions were used. However, mothers' reporting varied by the child's sex and maternal characteristics. This work underscores the importance of considering identity and social norms in VAC measurement, by triangulating data from multiple respondents to improve accuracy in prevalence estimates.

items.title: The association between green space and mental health, physical activity, and sedentary behaviour in rural populations: A systematic review.
items.abstract: Objective To review evidence on associations between green space with mental health and physical activity in rural populations. Methods We searched PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, and SPORTDiscus databases for studies published through August 2024. Eligible studies examined the relationships between green space with depression, anxiety, depression anxiety, physical activity or sedentary behaviour. Studies in care facilities or virtual green space exposure were excluded. Methodological quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute Tools. Due to heterogeneity, we conducted narrative syntheses. Results Of 4,441 records identified, 25 met inclusion criteria, most (80%) of which were cross-sectional studies. Evidence on green space and mental health outcomes was mixed. However, beneficial associations were observed for private green spaces, including gardening and high-quality spaces. Associations between green space and physical activity were inconsistent, but accessibility and quality were positively associated with moderate-to-vigorous physical activity. Conclusions Private and high-quality green space may improve mental health and physical activity in rural populations, although overall evidence remains heterogeneous and limited. Implications for public health Public health interventions and policies should prioritise improving green space access, quality, and support backyard gardening or similar initiatives. Longitudinal and qualitative research is needed to advance understanding and guide context-specific rural health strategies.

items.title: Housing improvements and the health of older Pacific people in Aotearoa New Zealand.
items.abstract: Objective This study aimed to explore associations between housing remediation programmes and health among older Pacific people in Aotearoa New Zealand. Methods Interviews were conducted with clients and staff involved in Pacific Healthy Homes, a housing improvement programme for Pacific adults aged ≥45 years. Quantitative analyses used a pre-post design and examined 5-year health outcomes among Pacific adults aged ≥45 years who participated in the Healthy Housing Initiative (HHI), a child-focused programme. Results Pacific Healthy Homes participants reported that repairs, heating and insulation improved warmth and well-being. However, disrepair and inaccessibility challenges persisted in some homes. Trusted relationships with staff and home visits were central to participants' positive experiences. Quantitative analysis showed that HHI participation was associated with lower all-cause hospitalisation rates among households of older Pacific people (incidence rate ratio [IRR]: 0.82, confidence interval [CI]: 0.80-0.85), but not among older adults themselves (IRR: 1.04, CI: 0.97-1.11). Pharmaceutical dispensing increased for both individuals (IRR: 1.14, CI: 1.10-1.18) and households (IRR: 1.08, CI: 1.06-1.10), potentially reflecting increased engagement with health services. Conclusions Housing improvement programmes combining remediation and relationship-based support may contribute to improved well-being among older Pacific peoples. Implications for public health Public health strategies should address housing quality, repair, and accessibility needs to maximise benefits.

items.title: Long-term communication and swallowing disability in adults with persistent critical illness following COVID-19: A mixed-methods observational study.
items.abstract: Objectives To describe the lived experience of communication and swallowing disability in adults with persistent critical illness following COVID-19. Methods A mixed-methods study. Semi-structured interviews were conducted alongside patient-reported communication and swallowing outcome measures. Setting Participants were recruited from a registry-embedded COVID-Recovery study. All patients were eligible if they were ≥ 18 years, positive PCR for SARS-CoV-2 and had persistent critical illness. This was defined as admission to ICU for >10 consecutive days with invasive mechanical ventilation for at least 24 h. Main outcome measures Semi-structured interviews were used to explore communication and swallowing disability. Additional patient-reported outcomes were assessed with the Dysphagia Severity Rating Scale and the La Trobe Communication Questionnaire. General function outcomes were evaluated with the WHODAS 2.0, EQ-5D-5L, HADS, MoCA-Blind, IADL and IES-6. Findings Of the 113 participants followed up, 29/113 (26%) reported communication or swallowing disability, and of these 17/29 (59%) consented to semi-structured interviews. From the 16 participants who answered questions about communication function 100% self-reported difficulty in ≥1 communication domain, including expressive language 13/16 (81%), voice 13/16 (81%), receptive language 9/16 (56%) and speech 5/16 (31%). Although all participants were consuming an oral diet and most with nil texture restrictions (13/17,76%), many reported ongoing swallowing concerns regarding safety and efficiency. Impacts of these new disabilities were beyond physical function and impacted on their activities and participation. Recovery was unclear, prolonged and compounded by judgement from others. Participants navigated their own recovery journey and whilst some were well supported, others described critical healthcare gaps. Conclusions We identified approximately one quarter of people admitted to ICU for COVID-19 related critical illness with a length of stay of 10 days or more report ongoing communication and swallowing disability at 6 months. The impacts continued well beyond hospital discharge and highlight a need to specifically address swallowing and communication in recovery pathways. Implications for clinical practice Specific assessment of communication and swallowing function is essential for individuals who experience persistent critical illness.

items.title: Mapping perinatal health interventions for improving perinatal outcomes in Australia: A scoping review.
items.abstract: Objectives To synthesise existing evidence on perinatal health interventions implemented in Australia to improve perinatal outcomes. Study design Scoping review. Methods The scoping review followed Arksey and O'Malley's methodological framework, refined by the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI), and was reported in accordance with the PRISMA extension for scoping reviews checklist. A systematic search was undertaken in PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and CINAHL for literature published from 01 January 2000 to 30 September 2025, supplemented by grey literature. Structured programs, models of care, and policy initiatives aimed at improving perinatal health outcomes in Australia were included and synthesised narratively. Results Of the 3649 records identified from five databases and grey literature, 59 studies were included. Observational cohort designs were the most common (18; 30.5%). Most studies (31; 52.5%) were conducted in New South Wales, Victoria, and Queensland, and a few (8; 13.6%) in remote settings. Midwifery continuity-of-care models were the most frequent interventions (16; 27.1%), followed by clinical and biomedical risk-targeted interventions (15; 25.4%). Preterm birth (12; 20.3%) was the most reported outcome. In 52.5% of studies, authors reported improvements in maternal and neonatal outcomes. Only (23; 39%) studies were specifically targeted at Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women. Implementation and sustainability plans were reported in (30: 50.8%) studies. Conclusions Continuity models of care and risk-targeted interventions were associated with improved perinatal outcomes. However, most evidence comes from metropolitan settings; evidence from remote areas, where the burden is greatest, remains uncertain. Equitable progress will require culturally appropriate and community-led models of care in regions of greatest need.

items.title: Antiviral activity of tannic acid against porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus and transcriptomic identification of TNFAIP3 as a candidate proviral host factor.
items.abstract: Porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus (PRRSV) causes enormous economic losses to the global swine industry. Given the extensive viral diversity and the limited heterologous cross-protection of current vaccines, antiviral strategies with broad activity against diverse PRRSV strains are urgently needed. This study investigated the anti-PRRSV activity of tannic acid (TA), a plant-derived polyphenol. TA potently inhibited PRRSV replication in both MARC-145 cells (half-maximal inhibitory concentration [IC 50 ] = 5.34 μM; selectivity index [SI] = 12.59) and primary porcine alveolar macrophages (IC 50 = 4.22 μM; SI = 42.65) and exhibited broad activity against multiple lineages of PRRSV-2. Mode-of-action assays revealed that TA primarily exerts virucidal and post-entry inhibitory effects. RNA sequencing-based transcriptomic analysis of TA-treated, PRRSV-infected cells identified differentially expressed genes significantly enriched in the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), tumor necrosis factor (TNF), and interleukin-17 (IL-17) signaling pathways. Among five candidate genes selected for small interfering RNA (siRNA)-mediated functional validation, knockdown of TNF alpha-induced protein 3 (TNFAIP3, also known as A20) most significantly suppressed PRRSV replication. PRRSV infection markedly upregulated TNFAIP3 expression, and TA reversed this upregulation in a dose-dependent manner. TNFAIP3 silencing reduced viral RNA levels, nucleocapsid (N) protein expression, and infectious titers, with the most pronounced effect during early infection. Collectively, the findings identify TA as a potent anti-PRRSV polyphenol and reveal TNFAIP3 as a candidate proviral host factor that is upregulated during PRRSV infection, providing insights into virus-host interactions and potential targets for host-directed antiviral strategies.

items.title: In silico conservation and HLA-binding profiles of HMPV F and G protein epitopes: implications for universal vaccine development.
items.abstract: Background Human metapneumovirus (HMPV) is a significant cause of respiratory infection, yet no licensed vaccine exists. Variability across viral subgroups, particularly in the attachment (G) protein, can complicate universal design. We assessed the immunogenetic regions in the fusion (F) and G proteins to identify stable vaccine targets. Methods We analyzed N = 324 Pittsburgh and N = 655 global HMPV genomes (2017-2022) for genome diversity per viral subgroup. Previously identified epitope sequences were obtained from the Immune Epitope DataBase (IEDB) for F and G proteins and sequence similarity was determined. Using NetMHCpan-4.1, we identified and computed inferred human leukocyte antigen (HLA) binding affinities for 15 epitope variants (1 or 2 substitutions) against universally common human alleles. Results The F protein was highly conserved across all subgroups (>96% amino acid sequence identity). In the G protein, we identified a conserved epitope cluster (G3-G7) where epitope G7 was present in 91% of A2 genomes. Functional modeling of the G-protein epitope variants revealed that the majority of HLA alleles maintained or gained binding affinity, a subset exhibited diminished binding (escape), suggesting these regions are subject to ongoing antigenic drift. B-genotypes showed fewer retained binders and were notably underrepresented in the current epitope databases. Conclusion The conserved F protein remains an optimal target for neutralization, while the G3-G7 cluster provides a robust secondary target for T-cell mediated immunity. A bivalent vaccine strategy could pair the stable F protein with these high-frequency G-protein epitopes to elicit an immune response. This approach addresses the A2 subgroup, and incorporating B-genotypes through ongoing surveillance and epitope mapping will be essential to achieve comprehensive, multi-antigen coverage across circulating HMPV strains.

items.title: Prenatal PFOS impairs offspring cognition via HDAC and translational repression.
items.abstract: Perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS) is a persistent environmental pollutant widely detected in human cord blood and breast milk, raising concerns about its neurodevelopmental toxicity. While epidemiological and animal studies have linked prenatal PFOS exposure to cognitive deficits, the molecular mechanisms-particularly those involving translational regulation-remain unclear. The present study tested whether prenatal PFOS exposure induces hippocampal-dependent cognitive deficits through histone deacetylase (HDAC) overactivation and eukaryotic initiation factor 2α (eIF2α)-mediated translational repression. Pregnant Wistar rats received vehicle or PFOS (0.5 or 2 mg/kg/day) from gestation day 1-21. Offspring cognitive function was assessed using the Morris water maze on postnatal day 28; hippocampal tissue was collected for histopathology, apoptosis, HDAC activity, and expression of phosphorylated PKR-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (p-PERK), phosphorylated eIF2α (p-eIF2α), activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP), small ubiquitin-like modifier 1/2 (SUMO1/2), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and protein phosphatase 1 (PP1). Maternal PFOS exposure impaired learning and memory, reduced normal neuron density, and increased neuronal apoptosis. PFOS elevated HDAC activity and activated the PERK-eIF2α-ATF4-CHOP integrated stress response (ISR) pathway, while reduced protein levels of SUMO1/2, BDNF, and PP1-despite elevated mRNA levels, suggesting translational repression. To test whether HDAC overactivation directly contributes to these changes, we pretreated PC12 cells with trichostatin A (TSA), a pan-HDAC inhibitor. TSA partially reversed PFOS-induced apoptosis, suppressed HDAC overactivation, attenuated ISR activation, and restored SUMO1/2, BDNF, and PP1 expression. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that prenatal PFOS exposure causes hippocampal-dependent cognitive deficits through HDAC overactivation and eIF2α-mediated translational repression, shifting the focus from transcriptional to translational control and identifying HDACs as a potential target in PFOS developmental neurotoxicity.

items.title: Q fever in Spain: Epidemiology and demographic characteristics of hospitalized patients (2016-2023).
items.abstract: Background Q fever, caused by Coxiella burnetii, is a zoonosis with significant public health implications. This study described the epidemiology, demographic and clinical characteristics, clinical and hospitalization burdens, and geographical distribution of hospitalized Q fever patients in Spain from 2016 to 2023. Methods We conducted a nationwide, retrospective study using a nationwide registry between 2016 and 2023. We analyzed temporal trends, demographic data, comorbidities, complications, and mortality. Results We identified 3358 hospitalizations for Q fever, representing an overall hospitalization rate of 0.89 per 100,000 population. The median patient age was 56 years, and the cohort was predominantly male (72%). The median hospital length of stay was 9 days (IQR 6-15). The overall mortality rate was 2.4%. The most common complication was pneumonia (32%). The highest hospitalization rates in the Canary Islands, and La Rioja. Conclusion The risk of hospitalization increases with age and the presence of predisposing conditions. The marked regional heterogeneity and high frequency of complications such as pneumonia underscore the need for enhanced surveillance and a strengthened One Health approach to control this zoonosis.

items.title: Selective attenuation of wastewater resistomes and residual ARG-MGE co-occurrence in semi-arid lagoon-treated effluents.
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs), mobile genetic elements (MGEs), and clinically relevant bacterial taxa are environmental-health concerns in wastewater-impacted ecosystems. However, the capacity of lagoon systems to attenuate these AMR-related signals before effluent discharge or reuse remains insufficiently characterized in semi-arid regions. Shotgun metagenomics was applied to 34 influent and treated-effluent samples collected approximately weekly during January-March 2025 from two Moroccan lagoon systems: Settat (urban, n = 18) and Ouled Said (rural, n = 16). TPM-normalized taxonomic, resistome, and mobilome profiles were analyzed using diversity metrics, PERMANOVA, differential-abundance testing, and correlation networks. Lagoon treatment produced site-dependent microbial restructuring, with a marked shift in Ouled Said (Aitchison PERMANOVA, R 2 = 0.376, p = 0.002) but a weaker, non-significant shift in Settat (R 2 = 0.125, p = 0.054). ESKAPE-associated bacteria declined from approximately 38% to 32% of CARD-annotated taxa but remained detectable in effluents. The resistome was broadly attenuated, but last-resort antibiotic resistance genes (LR-ARGs) responded unevenly: most mcr variants decreased by 82.4-89.9%, with significant reductions for several variants, whereas bla VIM-1 and tet(X) showed limited or non-significant reductions. The mobilome declined, although transposases and insertion sequences remained prominent. Network analysis indicated denser residual statistical ARG-MGE-taxa co-occurrence after treatment, without implying increased genetic mobility or HGT. Overall, the systems acted as selective, context-dependent barriers, reducing AMR-related burdens while retaining clinically relevant residual signals. The contrasting site responses indicate that treatment performance should not be assumed to be uniform across lagoon systems and support targeted effluent surveillance for safer discharge and reuse.

items.title: Substate variation in US Cannabis policy: Local opt-outs and drive times to legal retailers.
items.abstract: Background In most U.S. states with legalized adult-use cannabis (AUC) sales, local jurisdictions can prohibit retail dispensaries within their borders ("opt-out" policies). Yet analyses quantifying AUC legalization's effects typically focus on binary state policy indicators, ignoring local opt-out policies' potential effects on retailer locations and the consequences thereof. Methods Compiling novel data on local opt-out ordinances and dispensary locations across five states-California, Illinois, New Jersey, New York, and Washington-we matched these to U.S. Census population counts to estimate the share of each state's population residing in opted-out jurisdictions. Using geospatial methods to assess drive times from jurisdiction centroids to the nearest dispensary, ordinary least squares regressions then estimate associations between opt-out status and drive times to the nearest dispensary within each state, adjusting for geographic and transportation covariates. Results Opt-out coverage varied substantially across states, ranging from 1.5% of the population in New York to about 55% in New Jersey. Opt-out laws were associated with longer drive times in California (+5.5 min; 20% of that state's average minimum drive time to a legal dispensary) and Washington (+8.9 min; 42% of that state's average minimum drive time), where county-level opt-outs policies and geography limited opportunities for retailers to locate just outside of opted-out jurisdictions. Adjusted associations were largely non-significant in Illinois, New Jersey, and New York. Conclusions Both the degree to which localities opt-out of retail AUC sales and those policies' relationship with drive time to the nearest cannabis dispensaries vary across states. Critically, this variation is not explained by the percent of the population covered by opt-out policies but appears more common where opt-outs create genuine geographic barriers to retailer entry along the borders of opted out jurisdictions. Findings underscore the potential for mismeasurement in evaluations of cannabis legalization that rely on binary state-level exposures and highlight the need for more careful consideration of local policies' effects.

items.title: Fear-Specific Technophobia as a Mediator Between Daily Technical Support and Instrumental Versus Hedonic Technology Use in Later Life: Cross-Sectional Survey Study.
items.abstract: Background Population aging and rapid digitalization have intensified concerns about older adults' digital participation. Although access disparities have narrowed, older adults continue to differ from younger groups in how they use digital technologies, with their use skewed toward instrumental rather than hedonic purposes. Technophobia is a salient psychological barrier; yet, its distinct fear dimensions and their links to different forms of technology use remain insufficiently differentiated. Daily technical support (DTS) may provide an important sociotechnical context for understanding these relationships. Objective This study aimed to test how DTS promotes older adults' instrumental and hedonic technology use by reducing multidimensional technophobia (fear of inconvenience, fear of personal failure, and human-machine ambiguity) and whether these mechanisms differ by gender. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among Chinese adults aged ≥55 years recruited via online platforms and offline communities in Nanjing (June-October 2024). A total of 212 valid responses were included (mean age 66.96, SD 6.96, range 55-86 years; 142/212, 68.4% women). Measures assessed day-to-day technical support, 3 dimensions of technophobia, instrumental versus hedonic technology use, and demographic variables. We used partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with 5000 bootstrap resamples to test direct, indirect, and moderated mediation effects, reporting 95% bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) CI. Results DTS significantly reduced fear of inconvenience (β=-0.455, 95% BCa CI -0.632 to -0.229; P P =.12) or human-machine ambiguity ( P =.26). Fear of inconvenience and human-machine ambiguity negatively predicted instrumental use (IU; β=-0.215, 95% BCa CI -0.410 to -0.009; P =.05 and β=-0.211, 95% BCa CI -0.389 to -0.001; P =.04). DTS had a positive direct effect on IU (β=0.104, 95% BCa CI 0.009 to 0.203; P =.04) but not on hedonic use (HU; β=0.075; P =.11). The indirect effect of DTS on IU through fear of inconvenience was significant (β=0.097, 95% BCa CI 0.020-0.204). Gender moderated the effect of DTS on fear of inconvenience (β=0.287, 95% BCa CI 0.052-0.518; P =.02), and such conditional indirect effect was significant for men (β=0.098, 95% BCa CI 0.001-0.219) but not for women (β=0.036, 95% BCa CI -0.002 to 0.116). Conclusions DTS was associated with greater instrumental technology use among older adults through lower fear of inconvenience, with a stronger indirect association among men, whereas no comparable pathway emerged for HU. This suggests that gender may shape how older adults benefit psychologically from technical support rather than reflect general differences in support needs. Interventions should move beyond one-size-fits-all approaches by providing targeted, task-oriented support that addresses older adults' specific technological fears and practical barriers.

items.title: Virtual Reality for Delirium Prevention in Intensive Care Unit Nurses and Mechanically Ventilated Patients: Descriptive Qualitative Study.
items.abstract: Background Patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) who are on mechanical ventilation are at high risk of developing delirium. Virtual reality (VR) technology, as an emerging intervention method, shows promising application prospects in delirium prevention, but its specific experience in clinical practice still requires in-depth exploration. Objective This study aims to explore the real experiences of ICU nurses and mechanically ventilated patients in participating in VR delirium prevention, with the aim of providing practical evidence for the optimization and application of this technology in clinical practice. Methods A descriptive qualitative research design was adopted. From March to June 2025, using purposive sampling, participants were selected from the internal medicine, surgery, central, and respiratory ICU departments of a tertiary hospital in Zhengzhou. A total of 73 patients on mechanical ventilation were screened. Among them, 49 were excluded due to not meeting the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) or Barthel Index (BI) score criteria, 5 had delirium at the time of enrollment, 1 was excluded due to visual impairment, and 2 voluntarily withdrew during the study. Finally, 16 patients on mechanical ventilation and 16 nurses were included for semistructured interviews. Data analysis was conducted using the inductive content analysis method. Results Through the analysis of the interview data, a total of 3 main themes and 14 subthemes were extracted. In terms of perceived benefits, patients experienced an immersive environment and a sense of empowerment driven by tasks, while nurses felt the convenience of resource integration, the intimacy of the nurse-patient relationship, and a sense of professional significance. In terms of perceived challenges, patients faced difficulties with the interaction interface and physical and mental obstacles, while nurses encountered difficulties in communication assessment and responsibility definition. In terms of perceived needs, patients expected personalized content design and continuity of nursing services, while nurses suggested differentiated content adjustment, comprehensive functional integration, and standardized safety management. Conclusions The participants expressed a positive attitude towards the prevention of delirium based on VR and reported various perceived benefits, challenges, and needs. Future research should prioritize content personalization, functional integration, and safety management. Meanwhile, it is necessary to recognize the limitations of this technology in specific target populations. For those who do not meet the inclusion criteria, adaptive alternative intervention measures should be developed to promote the precise and sustainable application of VR-based delirium prevention.

items.title: Restoring Landscapes: A Structured Dataset of Forest Restoration Projects and Initiatives in Spain
items.abstract: ABSTRACT This dataset provides the first centralized compilation of forest restoration and adaptation projects in Spain, developed within the REFORADAPT project supported by the Biodiversity Foundation of the Spanish Ministry for Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge. The initiative responds to the growing policy momentum around ecosystem restoration and the need for structured, harmonized information to inform planning and decision‐making. Data were collected through a dual approach: a systematic review of European Union and national funding databases (including LIFE, INTERREG, and SUDOE) using forest restoration‐related keywords, complemented by contributions from expert networks and partner organizations. This allowed the identification of both large‐scale projects and small‐scale, community‐led initiatives often absent from official sources. Projects were screened based on titles and abstracts, and relevant metadata were standardized using an Excel template with custom variables on restoration types, goals, and degradation causes. The resulting dataset includes 382 initiatives implemented fully or partially in Spain. Ecological restoration aimed at conserving species and habitats is the most frequently assigned restoration type, representing 18% of all classified entries. In parallel, biodiversity conservation is the most frequently identified goal, occurring in 60% of the projects. Wildfires are the most frequently addressed degradation driver, accounting for 25% of all recorded occurrences. The EU LIFE programme is the most common funding source, present in 28% of the projects. This structured and comprehensive resource offers insights into the diversity, scope, and distribution of restoration efforts across Spain. items.title: Coupled responses of aboveground and belowground net primary productivity stability to nitrogen deposition in grasslands
items.abstract: Abstract The temporal stability of plant net primary productivity (NPP), defined as the ratio of temporal mean productivity to its standard deviation, is crucial for sustaining ecosystem services. Yet, little is known about whether the effects of nitrogen deposition on aboveground NPP (ANPP) stability are coupled with corresponding changes in belowground systems. Here we conducted a global meta-analysis based on 542 multi-year observations from 111 studies to assess the impacts of nitrogen deposition on the stability of ANPP and belowground NPP (BNPP). Nitrogen addition significantly decreased the stability of both ANPP and BNPP in a synchronized manner, reflecting a coupled response resulting from the allocation trade-off between mean ANPP and BNPP and their synchronized increase in variability. Further analysis showed that the declines in both ANPP and BNPP stability were associated with decreased plant species richness under nitrogen addition. Moreover, the negative responses intensified with longer treatment durations and higher nitrogen addition intensity. These findings highlight the importance of considering above- and below-ground interactions in future ecosystem management strategies under global change scenarios.

items.title: Phylogeny of Poaceae tribe Andropogoneae in Australia as a contribution to biological control research on gamba grass ( Andropogon gayanus )
items.abstract: Andropogon gayanus (gamba grass, Poaceae) is a large, tropical grass native to Africa, but introduced as a pasture plant across the tropics worldwide. It is considered invasive in northern Australia, and a research program into the potential of biological control of the species has recently been initiated. Because biological control agents are more likely to pose risks to non-target species closely related to the target weed than to distantly related species, risk management and experimental design in weed biological control require information on the evolutionary relationships of the target weed. Here, we inferred target sequence capture phylogenies of Poaceae tribe Andropogoneae with a focus on Australian lineages of the tribe, combining newly generated and previously published data. Our results place some lineages treated as incertae sedis in the most recent classification of Andropogoneae, including Australian endemics. Clausospicula extensa was retrieved as sister to Chrysopogon, and Spathia neurosa was nested in Dichanthium, but the position of Pseudopogonatherum was inconsistent across our analyses. Our analyses imply that subtribes Apludinae and Anthistiriinae as currently recognised may be non-monophyletic. Only 2 of 25 replicate specimen pairs of the same species failed to group together, confirming a high degree of reproducibility despite differences in bioinformatic approaches between our study and that used for previously published data. The revised phylogeny presented here supports the development of risk assessment plans for biological control and provides additional resources for broader Andropogoneae phylogeny.

items.title: From black plates to backyard animals: Chigger communities associated with wild and domestic hosts and the environment in a rural village setting
items.abstract: Chigger mites (larval Trombiculidae) are obligate ectoparasites, some species transmit Orientia tsutsugamushi , the causative agent of scrub typhus. Despite their public health significance in rural Southeast Asia, relationships between chiggers infesting wildlife, domestic animals and those present in the surrounding environment remain poorly characterised. We hypothesised that agricultural–forest ecotones would support higher chigger occurrence and that murid rodents would be the principal maintenance hosts of chigger communities. We conducted ecological observations of chigger communities associated with backyard chickens (n = 117), free-roaming dogs (n = 22), murid rodents (n = 96), insectivorous bats (n = 24) and environmental black-plate samples (n = 150) within a scrub typhus-endemic rural village in Nan Province, northern Thailand. Host-chigger associations were characterized using bipartite and unipartite network analyses. Twenty-one chigger species were identified, including four previously known to harbour O. tsutsugamushi: Ascoschoengastia indica, Leptotrombidium imphalum, Eutrombicula wichmanni and Walchia kritochaeta. Unfed questing chiggers occurred within the central residential area rather than being restricted to peripheral agricultural-forest interfaces as hypothesised. Murid rodents contributed the greatest chigger diversity, while backyard chickens exhibited unexpectedly high infestation prevalence (54.7%) and mean abundance. Environmental chigger detection rate was 11.3%. Eutrombicula wichmanni was recorded on free-roaming dogs, representing the first documented chigger infestation on dogs in Thailand, and a complete mitogenome was obtained from environmentally collected adults. Network analysis identified distinct rodent- and domestic animal-associated chigger communities, with the environmental chiggers linking both groups, whereas bat-associated chiggers were clearly isolated. These findings reveal complex chigger community structures with distinct ecological partitioning, highlighting the importance of domestic animals, particularly backyard chickens and free-roaming dogs (in addition to rodents) as critical components of peri-domestic transmission cycles. Future studies integrating host-chigger ecology with rickettsial pathogen screening would inform targeted disease surveillance and control programmes in rural endemic communities.

items.title: Biodiversity is a key motivation for European urban green space planning and management
items.abstract: Abstract Many urban green spaces are ecologically degraded. Yet, when designed and managed using ecologically motivated practices, green spaces can support biodiversity. However, many municipalities have not yet adopted strategies to enhance biodiversity. To better understand the importance assigned to biodiversity in public urban green spaces, we interviewed 574 municipalities across 18 European countries. Using a standardized questionnaire, we examined the underlying motivations, management goals and the measures municipalities used to support the public acceptance of biodiverse green spaces. Most municipalities (85%) reported biodiversity as a key motivation in green space planning and management. Many provided staff training (82%) and took action to increase public acceptance (75%) of biodiversity-promoting management. The reported perceptions of municipalities’ ecological condition were mostly positive, but 19% reported declines in the last decade. Differences between municipalities could be linked to regional and structural factors such as the sealed surface of the municipality, highlighting the need for locally adaptable policies for urban biodiversity.

items.title: Morphological variation of the conus arteriosus in Chondrichthyes: Implications for ecology and evolution
items.abstract: Cartilaginous fish have diverse morphological traits that are essential for understanding their evolutionary history and ecological adaptations. However, the conus arteriosus and its valves, key components of the heart and blood circulation, have been underexplored in phylogenetic and ecomorphological contexts. Here, we (1) characterize the morphological diversity and distribution of conal valves across Chondrichthyes, (2) evaluate the phylogenetic signal of valve characters and their potential usefulness for understanding evolutionary relationships, and (3) test whether variation in valve morphology is associated with lifestyle and locomotor demands. Our results show that the number of valves, as well as their distribution along the conus arteriosus, is generally consistent with the pattern observed in previous studies of two to seven rows of valves, with predominantly three series. Novel findings include a higher number of valve rows (up to six) than previously found in sharks and the first detailed descriptions for the orders Torpediniformes and Squatiniformes. Our results indicate that conal morphology is weakly correlated with phylogeny, but is strongly associated with locomotor demands and lifestyle.

items.title: Strengthening Institutional Governance to Counteract Urban-Driven Carbon Emissions in Central Europe: Insights from Economies in the Black Triangle Industrial Zone
items.abstract: Urban expansion and industrial concentration in Central Europe’s historic Black Triangle zone-encompassing Germany, Poland, and the Czech Republic-continue to drive elevated carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions, posing significant challenges to regional climate goals and the downstream ecological stability of the Baltic and North Sea basins. Rapid employment-based urban migration expands built environments, alters land-use patterns, and intensifies energy demand across industrial corridors. This research empirically examines the dynamic long-run impacts of institutional governance, urban migration, and fossil energy consumption on CO2 emissions in three economies across the Black Triangle Industrial zone of Central Europe over the period 1998:Q4 to 2021:Q4. Utilizing the Pooled Mean Group (PMG) estimator within a Panel Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) framework, the long-run empirical results reveal that: (i) strengthening institutional quality significantly abates CO2 emissions, whereas (ii) both fossil fuel consumption and urban migration exert a statistically significant positive effect on long-run carbon emissions. These insights underscore that robust institutional governance is essential to decoupling urban economic growth from environmental degradation. To achieve UN Agenda 2030 targets and mitigate transboundary environmental impacts-including marine resource degradation and eutrophication in connected Central and Northern European catchments-policy interventions must prioritize institutional capacity building, accelerated investments in renewable energy alternatives, and the deployment of smart, green technology-driven transport systems leveraging artificial intelligence and the Internet of Things (IoT).

items.title: Integrating Ecological Fiqh into Transformative Pesantren Education
items.abstract: Environmental crises challenge Islamic educational institutions to translate religious ethics into sustained ecological practice. This study examines how ecological fiqh operates as a pedagogical and institutional mechanism in pesantren education and identifies the conditions that shape its integration. A qualitative multiple-case design was used across ten pesantren in Sumatra and Java. The study analyzed evidence from semi-structured interviews, participatory observations, and curriculum and institutional documents thematically and compared it across cases. Five themes were identified: institutionalization of ecological responsibility, curriculum and pedagogy, internalization of ecological fiqh, institutional capacity and constraints, and resource stewardship. Integration was strongest where Islamic ecological reasoning was connected to experiential learning, repeated routines, student participation, leadership, and material support; where these conditions were weak, practices remained fragmented or extracurricular. Practically, the findings indicate that leaders and educators should align curriculum, teacher development, student responsibilities, and resource-management routines. The study's originality lies in proposing a provisional normative-pedagogical-institutional chain that explains how religious ethics can move from normative meaning to learning, habitual enactment, and environmental stewardship.

items.title: System noise temperature measurements of a 19-element phased array feed
items.abstract: Abstract We present multi-epoch system noise temperature measurements of a 19-element hexagonal room-temperature phased array feed (PAF) using a modified Y-factor method. A Python-based pipeline with iterative channel calibration and maxSNR beamforming is developed to do data reduction, and a covariance-based decomposition scheme is proposed to extract mutual coupling noise temperature \(T_\mathrm{mc}\). Long-term observations from March to June 2026 capture temporal receiver noise drift \textbf{mainly} induced by LNA temperature variations. Within the 1.37–1.47 GHz operating band, the measured beam-equivalent system noise temperature of the PAF is $\sim$73–89 K. \textbf{ The measured \(T_\mathrm{mc}\) baseline ranges from $\sim$2 K to $\sim$8 K, while under thermal loading, the resonant peak of \(T_\mathrm{mc}\) can increase to more than 20 K. The baseline of \(T_\mathrm{mc}\) is consistent with the S-parameter measurements, which show the \(T_{\rm mc}\) of the full array ranges less than 10.7 K. } \textbf{ The baseline fluctuation of \(T_\mathrm{mc}\) most likely arises from the superposition of thermal and non-thermal components of the spatial electromagnetic fields. } A detachable stainless steel shield is deployed to quantify sidelobe spillover noise, and comparative tests show unshielded environmental interference increases receiver noise temperature by over 60 K. The proposed measurements and data processing framework provides a practical reference for noise performance characterization of ground-based radio telescope PAF prototypes.

items.title: A review of error analysis and compensation methods in white-light interferometric surface topography measurement
items.abstract: Surface topography directly affects the functionality and performance of workpieces, while its high-accuracy and repeatable measurement is essential for quality control and precision manufacturing. White-light interferometry, benefiting from the unique advantages of broadband low-coherence light sources, enables high-accuracy measurement while effectively avoiding phase ambiguity and related issues, and therefore plays an important role in surface metrology. However, various error sources in practical measurements can cause deviations from ideal measurement conditions, directly affecting the accuracy and reliability of surface topography reconstruction. Therefore, an in-depth investigation of error mechanisms and the development of effective compensation strategies are essential for ensuring the measurement reliability of white-light interferometry and promoting its application in broader engineering scenarios. This review systematically examines error processing in white-light interferometry. The fundamental principles of white-light interferometry are first described based on an interferometric signal model. The potential error sources and their physical mechanisms are then analyzed in detail, covering environmental vibration, sample characteristics, the batwing effect, and algorithmic errors. Research progress over the past two decades in suppressing these errors is systematically classified and summarized. Based on these developments, future trends in white-light interferometry are further discussed. This review aims to provide a systematic theoretical reference and technical guidance for error analysis and performance improvement in white-light interferometry.

items.title: Non-Axisymmetric Pillar Structures due to Embedded Stars in AGN Accretion Discs
items.abstract: Abstract Gravitationally unstable outer regions of AGN discs may host in situ formation of massive stars whose heating produces localized vertical “pillars” on the disc surface, in the same region that emits the broad lines. Here we investigate the reverberation-mapping signatures that such pillars would produce. We compute velocity–delay maps Ψ(λ, τ), time-evolving emission-line spectra, and continuum reverberation lag spectra for these structures. We model each pillar as a 2D Gaussian perturbation to the disc height under lamp-post irradiation and weight the line response with Cloudy photoionization grids covering the major BLR lines. We show Hα, Mg ii, and C iv as representative examples. A single pillar produces a localized hotspot in Ψ and a clear “S-wave” pattern in the time-evolving spectrum that persists, though diluted, for N ∼ 100 pillars. Emission-line fluxes are suppressed in shadows behind the pillars, but when normalized by Hβ (or by the local continuum) the line-to-Hβ ratios move in opposite directions: Mg ii/Hβ rises while C iv/Hβ drops. This contrast distinguishes pillars from purely kinematic features that would modulate all lines by similar factors. Across scans of the pillar shape and lamp-post height, the pillar models produce an optical continuum reverberation lag spectrum of the observed magnitude. The once-per-orbit modulation grows with sin i from foreshortening, and at sufficiently high inclination the pillar’s body geometrically self-occults its lamp-facing inner slope, adding a sharper near/far contrast. These signatures provide observational diagnostics for detecting in situ star formation in AGN discs through velocity-resolved reverberation mapping campaigns.

items.title: Composition-controlled cutoff-resonance coupling and polarization-selective wave propagation in a four-component magnetized plasma
items.abstract: Abstract This study deals with the propagation of circularly polarized electromagnetic waves in magnetized multicomponent plasmas composed of electrons, deuterium positive ions (D+), hydrogen negative ions (H−), and oxygen negative ions (O−). Based on the cold-fluid approach combined with Maxwell’s equations, the dielectric functions of right-hand circularly polarized (RCP) and left-hand circularly polarized (LCP) waves are obtained analytically. The numerical values of the cutoff frequencies, the reflection, transmission, and absorption coefficients for a finite multicomponent plasma slab are found using electromagnetic boundary conditions. Due to the presence of two kinds of negative ions, three cutoff frequencies of the RCP waves and the propagation and stop bands related to the negative-ion and electron cyclotron resonances are found. In turn, the LCP wave has only one cutoff-controlled propagation boundary. The effects of negative-ion concentrations of hydrogen and oxygen, magnetic field strength, slab thickness, and frequency are studied. Increase in the concentration of the H− ions leads to a shift in cutoff frequencies, changes in the widths of propagation and stop bands, decrease in the gap between the RCP and LCP cutoffs, and improvement of the low-frequency transparency when both RCP and LCP modes are propagating. A remarkable effect is a tendency of the second RCP cutoff towards the H− cyclotron resonance that results in the cutoff-resonance coincidence with an enhancement in absorption of the light negative ions. The cutoff-resonance proximity produces enhanced electromagnetic absorption associated with the resonant response of the light negative-ion population, indicating enhanced wave-ion coupling. The results provide a fluid-level basis for controlling frequency-selective electromagnetic energy deposition in multicomponent plasmas and show how negative-ion composition can tune polarization-dependent propagation and electromagnetic power deposition in the present model. It can be used in plasma diagnostics, ionospheric wave propagation, plasma electromagnetic filters, tunable polarization devices, and ion-selective heating.

items.title: Exploring the potential of Low Gain Avalanche Detectors for low-energy ion spectrometry
items.abstract: Low Gain Avalanche Detectors (LGADs) have emerged as key sensors for High Energy Physics and related applications due to their excellent time resolution and enhanced signal-to-noise ratio. However, their use in low-energy ion spectrometry has generally been limited by gain suppression effects, arising from the high ionization densities produced by such ions within the multiplication layer, which leads to a reduction of the gain and a non-linear detector response with ion energy. In this work, we investigate an alternative detection configuration aimed at mitigating this effect by shifting the region of highest ionization density away from the gain layer. Alpha spectrometry measurements in the energy range 3-9 MeV were performed by irradiating the detector from both the frontside (multiplication layer side) and the backside of the devices. Additionally, potential gain suppression effects when the detected particles are photons were evaluated using an X-ray tube operated at 40 kV, with irradiation from both the front and back sides. The results show that backside irradiation leads to a higher and more uniform gain and a linear relationship between generated charge and alpha particle energy. In particular, a gain of 3-4 is obtained for backside irradiation, while a nearly constant gain of ≈ 2 is achieved for frontside irradiation. In addition, the achieved energy resolution (1%–2%) is comparable to that of standard PiN detectors fabricated under the same conditions. Finally, the gain response to X-rays was found to be very similar to that observed for alpha particles, suggesting that no gain suppression is observed in the studied LGADs for backside irradiation. These findings demonstrate the potential of LGADs for low-energy ion spectrometry, particularly in applications where low deposited energy makes enhanced signal-to-noise ratio a critical advantage.

items.title: Magnetic Field and Electromotive Force of Faraday’s Unipolar Generator
items.abstract: The comparison between the theoretical and experimental results derived from the consideration of a Faraday’s homopolar generator experiment is the topic developed in this work. The theoretical results are based on measurements of the magnetic field and on high-precision measurements of the induced electromotive force (EMF). These magnetic field measurements are confirmed by the theoretical estimations of magnetic field according to the geometric dimensions and the effective magnetic surface-charge density of the magnet used in the experiment. The derivation of these theoretical results is based on Faraday’s view on the one hand and on the special relativity on the other, considering three different cases, namely the case in which the magnet is immobilized and the conductive disk rotates which gives the same results regardless of the theoretical basis used, the case in which the magnet and the conductive disk corotate and the case in which the conductive disk is immobilized and the magnet rotates. Comparing the theoretical results, a discrepancy was found between Faraday’s view and the special relativity. Precise measurements of EMF confirmed Faraday’s view in both cases under consideration. When the magnet and the conductive disk corotate, the theoretical result of Faraday’s view is 20.0 ± mV, the relativistic theoretical result is 16 mV and the measurement result is 19.86 ± 0.02 mV, whereas when the conductive disk is immobilized and the magnet rotates, the theoretical result of Faraday’s view is zero, the relativistic theoretical result is −4 mV, and the measurement result is practically zero.

items.title: Mapping the Evolving Landscape of Ransomware Research: A Bibliometric Analysis for Cybersecurity Advancements
items.abstract: Ransomware is a critical cybersecurity threat that disrupts healthcare, finance, and government by encrypting data and demanding ransom. Although narrative and systematic reviews have examined ransomware from technical, sector-specific, and legal perspectives, quantitative bibliometric mapping remains scarce, and existing studies cover shorter periods and fewer analytical techniques. This study addresses that gap through a bibliometric analysis of 1,386 ransomware-related publications indexed in Scopus from 2007 to 2024, using Scopus, BiblioMagika, VOSviewer, Publish or Perish, and Bibliometrix. It examines publication trends, leading authors, institutions, countries, thematic clusters, and collaboration patterns. Results show a sharp rise in output since 2017, though only seven researchers have published ten or more papers on the topic. Keyword and thematic-map patterns point to early detection techniques, deep learning, data breach analysis, convolutional neural networks, feature selection, machine learning, and artificial intelligence as areas of growing activity, consistent with a shift toward proactive and intelligent defense mechanisms. By mapping the intellectual structure and evolution of ransomware research, this study offers insights for cybersecurity professionals, academics, and policymakers seeking to understand current trends, anticipate future challenges, and design more effective mitigation strategies.

items.title: Evaluating machine-learning models for multiclass classification of LIGO gravitational-wave glitches
items.abstract: Abstract Gravitational-wave detectors are affected by short-duration non-Gaussian noise transients, or glitches, which can obscure astrophysical signals and complicate downstream analyses. We present a systematic benchmark of XGBoost and nine deep tabular architectures for 24-class glitch classification using structured metadata from the Gravity Spy O3 catalogue. The original comparison evaluates predictive performance, random-seed robustness, computational cost, data-scaling behavior, and model-native feature-attribution rankings. We additionally reconstruct a duplicate-aware cohort of 437,753 events and evaluate representative tree-based, fully connected, and attention-based models under frozen grouped-random and chronological protocols. XGBoost achieves the highest grouped-random mean weighted F1 among the three audited representative models, reaching 0.8297 ± 0.0002 with the original nine features. Chronological testing is materially more difficult for all three architectures, and removing absolute timestamp variables does not eliminate the random-to-chronological performance gap; the effects of timestamp removal are also model dependent. Targeted ablations show substantial reliance on signal-strength descriptors and quality factor, whereas restoring bandwidth to the timestamp-free representation produces only modest, architecture- and split-dependent changes. Model-native TreeSHAP and Integrated Gradients rankings exhibit partially aligned but heterogeneous feature orderings. A common permutation-importance analysis supports interpreting this agreement as a protocol-dependent comparative diagnostic rather than as evidence of explanation equivalence or causal feature importance. Controlled operational measurements further show that XGBoost provides the strongest grouped-random predictive performance, while the custom multilayer perceptron has the smallest reconstructed deployment bundle and the lowest measured single-event CPU latency. These results show that random-split performance can overestimate temporal generalization and that model selection depends on the relative importance of predictive performance, deployment footprint, latency, temporal robustness, and interpretability stability.

items.title: The ALMA REBELS Survey: The [C ii ] Luminosity Function of UV-Selected Galaxies at z ∼ 7
items.abstract: Abstract Luminosity functions (LF) are some of the most basic quantities providing insights into galaxy evolution across cosmic time and enabling a direct comparison between observations and simulations. Here, we present the first [C ii] 158 μm LF at z ∼ 7 from a sizeable UV-selected ALMA sample. Our analysis makes use of 27 galaxies with significant [C ii] emission line detections in the epoch of reionization from the REBELS (Reionization Era Bright Emission Line Survey) ALMA Large Program and its pilot programs. We used these line detections and similar from ALPINE to calibrate UV luminosity-$L_\mathrm{[C\, {\small ii}] }$ and stellar mass-$L_\mathrm{[C\, {\small ii}] }$ relations at z ∼ 7. Given the challenge in precisely defining a selection volume for the REBELS sample itself, we rely on published UV LF and stellar mass function (SMF) determinations at z ∼ 7 and three complementary approaches to derive the [C ii] LF. The UV LF-based method provides a lower limit on the [C ii] LF, due to its missing the most dust-obscured systems. Our SMF-based estimate yields a Schechter function with a characteristic luminosity of $L^*_\mathrm{[C\, {\small ii}] }=10^{9.11_{-0.27}^{+0.11}}\, L_\odot$ and a steep faint-end slope. From z ∼ 7 to z ∼ 5, our inferred [C ii] LF shows an evolution of +0.3 dex in normalisation and +0.1 dex in $L^*_\mathrm{[C\, {\small ii}] }$. Our results indicate a general underprediction from models of the abundance of [C ii] emitters at high-redshift and thus potentially the number densities of massive yet UV-faint systems implied by our SMF-based method. Additionally, they suggest that 63% of the star formation rate density occurs in massive [C ii]-bright systems and that ∼60–90% of [C ii] emitters at z ∼ 7 may be missed by bright UV selections. This highlights the importance of surveys focusing on especially massive, UV-faint sources at z > 6.

items.title: GRB 180620A: Detected Signatures of Precessing Magnetars in the Optical Afterglows of Gamma-Ray Bursts
items.abstract: Abstract Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) powered by precessing magnetars have been extensively studied in the X-ray band, whereas clear signatures of such effects in the optical band have not yet been identified. In this work, we present multiwavelength optical observations of the afterglow of GRB 180620A and investigate the physical origin of its unusual optical behavior. The optical light curve exhibits two bumps: the first peaks at ~ 250 s, and the second extends from ~ 10 3 s to ~ 10 4 s. These features are difficult to explain using the standard external shock afterglow model. By analyzing the temporal and spectral properties of GRB 180620A, we find that the second bump likely shares the same physical origin as the contemporaneous X-ray emission, whereas the first bump does not. Based on this interpretation, we perform modeling and show that the first bump can be explained by forward-shock emission with energy injection, while the second bump can be attributed to emission through spin-down of a magnetar with precession which is analogous to the physical mechanism proposed for the X-ray afterglow. Our results suggest that the effects of magnetar precession can also manifest in the optical afterglow, thereby extending investigations for the influence of magnetar precession on GRB radiation to the optical band.

items.title: Electrostatic high-frequency oscillations in partially ionized two-fluid plasmas
items.abstract: Abstract We report the existence of a new electrostatic mode in an electron-neutral collision-dominated, partially ionized plasma, in which electrons and the neutral gas are coupled through collisions to behave as a single electron-neutral (EN) fluid, and positive ions behave as a separate fluid. Interestingly, the EN-ion plasma collectively oscillates with a frequency close to or higher than the ion-plasma oscillation frequency (ωpi), and the corresponding wave mode appears similar to Langmuir waves in classical plasmas. However, when ions form only a stationary background, the EN fluid oscillates at a frequency much lower than ωpi. Estimates suggest that such high-frequency electrostatic modes may be excited in laboratories and in the solar photosphere.

items.title: The Long‐Term Trend of the Equatorial Electrojet Over Indian Sector
items.abstract: Abstract The upper‐atmosphere cooling trend is well documented, while the long‐term trend of the ionospheric electrodynamics remains poorly understood. Using two geomagnetic observation data sets over Indian sector, we analyze the long‐term trend of the monthly‐median equatorial electrojet (EEJ) in 1967–2015 after removing the solar activity and seasonal signals. During 1967–1999, a period of slow geomagnetic‐equator motion, the residual of the EEJ shows a decreasing trend between 09 and 13 LT and an increasing trend between 13 and 16 LT. Following accelerated geomagnetic‐equator motion after 1999, the afternoon enhanced trend is suppressed, whereas the morning decreased trend is strengthened for the full‐period (1967–2015) data set. The semidiurnal‐like pattern in the EEJ long‐term trend is possibly related to the weakened migrating semidiurnal tide (SW2) caused by the enhanced greenhouse gases as reported in previous studies. Our results disentangle the influences of greenhouse gas and geomagnetic secular variation on equatorial ionospheric electrodynamics, and have potential implications for ionospheric climate and weather.
