items.title: Measuring heart and breath: BRAMS-Bio-Box (B3), a wearable open-source physiology recording platform
items.abstract: Psychology and social neuroscience study the biological basis of real-world interactive behaviors, such as dancing or playing music in groups. Autonomic nervous system reactivity, assessed through cardiac and respiratory signals, plays an important role in these behaviors. However, affordable, scientifically validated, research-grade devices for synchronous, real-time physiological monitoring of multiple individuals in natural settings remain scarce. We propose a wearable open-source physiological monitoring device, the BRAMS-Bio-Box (B3), that can record cardiac and respiratory signals simultaneously from multiple individuals. B3 can be built cost-effectively using open-source blueprints and software we provide to yield a transparent, flexible option for research-grade physiological data collection. We empirically validated B3 against a widely used reference device in nine participants performing various motor and guided-respiration tasks. Heart rate (HR) and heart rate variability (HRV) were derived from electrocardiographic (ECG) signals, while respiratory sensors were evaluated for respiration rate and the accuracy and consistency of exhalation event detection. B3 derived HR and HRV closely matched reference measures across tasks, with high quality ECG recordings and minimal data loss, except during vigorous arm swinging. Respiratory rate and pattern metrics, including exhalation peak timing, also showed strong agreement. The B3 thermistor accurately tracked respiration rate even at higher breathing frequencies, although minor timing offsets occurred during some guided respiration segments. Overall, B3 performed comparably to the reference system for cardiac and respiratory measures, offering an affordable, open-source solution for physiological monitoring in real-world interactive settings.

items.title: Everyone else does it? Self-reported and perceived questionable research practices in music psychology
items.abstract: Questionable research practices (QRPs) may inflate false-positive rates and have been surveyed in psychology, ecology, and education, but not in music psychology. In a survey, 198 researchers who had authored empirical music-psychology work reported how often they had used 22 practices and estimated how many colleagues had used each. Three quarters (75.1%) reported at least one of the 18 practices bearing on false-positive risk, and 82.8% at least one of all 22. The most common were citing irrelevant work to satisfy a reviewer (46.9%) and selecting the most favourable analysis after seeing the results (43.5%). Respondents estimated that colleagues used 20 of the 22 practices more than they did themselves, but this gap is largely produced by the response scale in the survey and is not evidence of under-reporting. Researchers who thought practices were more widespread reported more of them between persons (OR = 2.16, 95% CI [1.74, 2.68]) and within them (OR = 2.62, [2.32, 2.96]), consistent with false consensus as well as descriptive norms. Music-specific practices were reported less often than reporting and analysis practices, though this depended partly on item wording and on whether a practice applied at all. Career stage showed no detectable association with admissions. Researchers reporting more open research practices reported more QRPs, not fewer (OR = 1.28, [1.14, 1.44]), which may indicate differences in disclosure as much as in behaviour. These results provide a first baseline for the field.

items.title: Environment-dependent diversity-stability relationship in microbial communities
items.abstract: Abstract Understanding the biodiversity–stability relationship has been a central challenge in ecology. Classical ecology proposed that diversity stabilize communities by distributing fluctuations across redundant pathways1,2, whereas random-interaction theory predicts that large and complex communities are unstable3,4. Field observations and experiments have reported positive, negative or negligible relationship between diversity and stability5–10. It therefore remains unclear diversity-stability relationship is universal or not and when a particular diversity–stability relationship emerges. Here we show that diversity-stability relationship is not fixed but environment-dependent, by studying bacterial communities under daily dilutions across temperature (10–50 °C) and dilution-rate (10¹–10⁵) gradients. Communities exhibit two distinct fluctuation regimes: collective fluctuations and dominant-species fluctuations. In the collective fluctuation regime, many species interact and fluctuate together, and exhibit a positive diversity-instability relationship and turnover in the most abundant species. In the dominant-species fluctuation regime, only one or a few abundant species fluctuate and exhibit no significant diversity-instability relationship. Single species measurements show that the community fluctuation regime is determined by the balance between species growth and pH-mediated death. We developed a consumer-resource model with pH feedback reproducing both the fluctuation regimes and diversity–stability relationships observed in the experiment. We further tested our theoretical interpretation by performing another experiment tuning the dilution rate to shift between the same two regimes. Our results thus show that two distinct environment-dependent ecological mechanisms and fluctuation regimes lead to different diversity–stability relationships.

items.title: “We Are All Sick”: Sanitation, Structural Neglect, and the Embodied Politics of Informality in Cape Town
items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the relationship between sanitation, systemic neglect, and embodied suffering in the RR Section of Khayelitsha, Cape Town. Drawing on thematic analysis of interviews with 30 residents and 16 activists, supported by computer-assisted coding in ATLAS. ti 22, it centres the statement of a resident - “We are all sick” - as a lens into perceived illness, infrastructural decay, and environmental degradation. Testimonies reveal how inadequate sanitation systems, including open toilets, bucket disposal, and stagnant wastewater, exacerbate illness and psychosocial stress in densely packed dwellings. Although authorities acknowledge the crisis, the continued classification of the settlement as “temporary” perpetuates inadequate service provision and entrenches vulnerability. Using Urban Political Ecology, the concept of slow violence, and embodied urbanism, the study demonstrates how informality produces material precarity and political marginalisation. Residents’ accounts highlight not only exposure and illness but also fragmented grassroots organising, civic disillusionment, and episodic resistance. These narratives transform private suffering into collective political speech, challenging invisibility and asserting claims to recognition and citizenship. The study contributes to debates on sanitation justice, health equity, and the politics of informality in African cities, advocating for infrastructure to be recognised as a fundamental right of urban citizenship rather than a conditional privilege.

items.title: The Evolutionary Self: Adaptive Prioritization as a Framework for Personality Structure and Change
items.abstract: Abstract Personality psychology has produced increasingly sophisticated accounts of individual differences through trait, motivational, interpersonal, developmental, and evolutionary approaches. Yet an important theoretical question remains: what principles organize these diverse sources of variation into coherent patterns of behavior across situations and over time? This integrative review proposes the Evolutionary Self, a framework that conceptualizes personality as a dynamic system of adaptive prioritization. Whereas existing models primarily describe personality traits, motivational systems, or the processes producing state variation, the Evolutionary Self focuses on how competing adaptive demands are weighted and coordinated when they cannot be simultaneously maximized. Drawing on evolutionary psychology, behavioral ecology, reinforcement sensitivity theory, attachment theory, self-determination theory, interpersonal models of agency and communion, and dynamic approaches to personality, the framework identifies three candidate domains of recurrent adaptive tension: Opportunity–Protection, Control–Accommodation, and Connection–Self-Reliance. These dimensions are not proposed as mutually exclusive psychological systems. Rather, they represent domains in which individuals must coordinate competing adaptive demands. The framework distinguishes capacities, priorities, states, positions, and trajectories. Capacities describe what an individual can potentially do; priorities describe which motives receive greater weight when competing demands become salient; states describe momentary configurations; position describes the person’s characteristic center of gravity; and trajectory describes systematic movement through adaptive space across situations and developmental periods. The model is offered as a theoretical synthesis that generates testable hypotheses concerning personality structure, contextual variability, development, stress response, and behavioral flexibility.

items.title: From Forest to Remedy: Medicinal Plants and Indigenous Therapeutic Knowledge among Naga tribes of Manipur, Indo-Myanmar Biodiversity Hotspot
items.abstract: Abstract Background The Rongmei and Tangkhul Naga tribes of Manipur are forest-dwelling communities that have traditionally relied on medicinal plants for primary healthcare. Ethnomedicinal knowledge has been documented for these tribes in the Tamenglong/Noney and Ukhrul districts, respectively, but populations in the ecologically distinct Churachandpur and Kamjong districts remain undocumented, and no study has applied a quantitative framework to compare the two tribes and prioritize species for pharmacological validation. We documented medicinal plant use among both tribes in these districts and evaluated informant consensus and cross-cultural patterns to inform pharmacological and conservation priorities. Methods Field surveys were conducted from July 2024 to April 2025 across ten villages using multistage sampling. Data were gathered from informal interviews and focus group discussions using modified semi-structured questionnaires, and plants were identified using regional floras and consultation with taxonomists. Relative frequency of citation (RFC), use value (UV), fidelity level (FL), and informant consensus factor (ICF) were used to assess species importance; the Jaccard Index (JI) and Rahman's Similarity Index (RSI) were used to assess cross-cultural similarity in taxa and therapeutic use. Informants were general community members rather than specialized healers, and because each tribe was sampled in a single district, tribal identity, local ecology, interviewer, and sampling intensity could not be disentangled. Effect sizes, an overlap coefficient that adjusts for unequal inventory size, and exact confidence intervals were added to the comparisons Results Among 373 informants (aged 21–86 years), gender, age, and education were not significantly associated with plant-use knowledge in either community. We recorded 131 taxa from 117 genera and 57 families, used to treat 83 human ailments, including a distinctive Rongmei practice of using burnt Goniothalamus sesquipedalis ash for gastritis, fever, and warding off evil spirits. Species overlap between communities was low (JI = 16.03%), and RSI (9.16%) indicated modest concordance in therapeutic use of shared taxa. Plant-part use differed significantly in five of ten categories, though leaves dominated in both. Brassaiopsis glomerulata , Phlogacanthus thyrsiformis , Mikania micrantha , Goniothalamus sesquipedalis , Zanthoxylum acanthopodium , and Clerodendrum colebrookeanum emerged as the strongest candidates for pharmacological screening based on RFC and FL. Several taxa, including Aquilaria malaccensis (Critically Endangered), are of global conservation concern. Conclusion The study documents rich community-level ethnomedicinal knowledge among the Rongmei and Tangkhul Naga and shows that low taxonomic overlap can coexist with substantial agreement in the use of shared plants. Pharmacological validation and safety screening of promising species, targeted conservation of threatened taxa, and community-controlled benefit-sharing are needed to safeguard this cultural and botanical heritage.

items.title: Twenty Years of Agricultural Mechanization Practices in Northern Nigeria: Bibliometric Insights into Research Trends, Productivity, Labor, and Technology
items.abstract: Abstract Agricultural mechanization significantly boosts farm productivity, reduces labor effort, and promotes rural development, especially in developing economies. This study investigated trends in mechanization, productivity, labor, and technology in northern Nigeria. A total of 735 open-access articles published in English from 2004 to 2025 were extracted from the Dimensions.ai database and analyzed using R's Biblioshiny package ver.5.0. The tools of analysis used include co-authorship networks, keyword co-occurrence, citation patterns, co-citation, and word cloud generation, etc. The results show a 20% annual growth rate and a peak in 2025 with 138 publications, reflecting increasing academic, policy interest in mechanization and agricultural modernization. The average citation count was 14.82, highlighting the relevance of the field. Collaboration involved 4,530 authors, with an average of 6.84 co-authors per-paper and 16.55% international partnerships, highlighting global cooperation. Chinese scholars dominate publication volume. With citation analysis, the distribution of research impact by region is seen to be diverse from Asia, Europe, and Africa. Mechanization’s impact on sustainability and livelihoods is illustrated in the research clusters identified and the core themes of agriculture, employment and climate change. The word-cloud analysis reveals that mechanization research in northern Nigeria is multi-faceted, local, and integrative, connecting technology, socio-economics, sustainability and ecology. The results indicate the influence of mechanization in rural development in different ways, so region-specific results are necessary. It is necessary to have policies and investments in local research for effective implementation. Inclusive mechanization policies should promote smallholder farmers, dissemination of knowledge, and resource access in region for sustainable rural development.

items.title: Reevaluating Body Size in Fossil Physeteroids Using Cranial Proportions
items.abstract: Fossil physeteroids exhibited substantially greater diversity in body size and feeding ecology than their extant relatives, yet body-length estimates for many taxa remain dependent on incomplete skeletons and proportional scaling from a limited number of reference species. This study reassesses body-size estimates in fossil physeteroids using a cranial proportion-based framework centered on bizygomatic width (BZW) and condylobasal length (CBL). The reference body lengths of Zygophyseter varolai and Brygmophyseter shigensis were reevaluated using published vertebral measurements, preserved skeletal length, and scale-bar-based skeletal data, and were conservatively set at approximately 6.5 m and 6.0 m, respectively. These revised reference values were then used to generate updated body-length estimates for a broad sample of extinct physeteroids. Revised estimates indicate that large-bodied physeteroids were relatively uncommon. Among the non-kogiid genera examined, only seven reached or exceeded 6 m in estimated total length, whereas Livyatan and Eophyseter were the only fossil genera estimated to exceed 9.5 m. Macroraptorial physeteroids ranged from approximately 4.0–4.3 m in Acrophyseter spp. to approximately 15–16 m in the giant Livyatan melvillei. The results further suggest that large body size evolved under multiple ecological regimes. Some large-bodied physeteroids were macroraptorial predators, whereas others show adaptations consistent with suction feeding or predation on smaller prey. The temporal distribution of giant forms is therefore more consistent with repeated, independent increases in body size than with a single evolutionary trend toward gigantism. However, incomplete preservation and uncertainty in the body lengths of reference taxa remain important limitations. The framework presented here provides a more consistent basis for reassessing body-size diversity in fossil physeteroids and can be refined as more complete cranial and postcranial material becomes available.

items.title: Transparency Is Necessary but Not Sufficient for Trust: Information Leakage and Procedural Overfitting in Supervised Machine Learning for Psychology
items.abstract: Min et al. (2026) provide a timely checklist for improving the transparency and trust of supervised machine learning (ML) research in psychology. I strongly endorse this goal and recognize that their focus on retrospective reporting is both valuable and the appropriate scope for an article. However, I suggest that two related issues warrant greater emphasis in their framework: information leakage and procedural overfitting. Both can produce optimistic estimates of model performance despite apparently transparent reporting. I propose two extensions to the checklist: reporting requirements that make information leakage auditable and prospective specification of key analytical decisions through preregistration. I argue that these additions would further strengthen the ability of readers and reviewers to evaluate the trustworthiness of supervised ML analyses in psychology. Moreover, comprehensive guidelines that do not sufficiently emphasize these issues may create unwarranted confidence that threats to valid model evaluation have been ruled out, allowing information leakage or procedural overfitting to remain undetected.

items.title: More Visibility for Diversity? A Systematic Review of LGBTQ+ Representation in Educational Psychology Journals
items.abstract: Students identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or otherwise non-heterosexual or non-cisgender (LGBTQ+) are increasingly represented. However, they still face additional challenges in educational settings, so Educational Psychology needs to research these issues. In this preregistered systematic scientometric literature review, we investigate (a) the extent of LGBTQ+ centered research in Educational Psychology journals, (b) common themes and trends, and discuss systematic gaps for future research. After searching all 41,992 articles on ERIC, published in the most impactful (Q1 and Q2) Educational Psychology journals, we combined scientometric-quantitative and qualitative methods to review 68 eligible articles. We found a surge in publications from 2000 onward, driven by special issues. For almost half of these high-impact journals, we found no published articles on LGBTQ+ issues on ERIC; most publish only a few per thousand, even though this topic falls within their scope. Most often, these articles were empirical, correlational, and US-based, with inconsistent measures of LGBTQ+ identities. Through qualitative thematic analysis, we identified seven research themes and highlighted pertinent research gaps. To strengthen the evidence base in the field, future research should conduct rigorous longitudinal and intervention studies with culturally diverse samples and adhere to open science standards.

items.title: Artificial Agents as Leaders and Followers: An Integrative Role-Congruity Review
items.abstract: Artificial agents such as algorithms, virtual agents, and robots increasingly occupy organizational roles as leaders, followers, and partners. However, evidence on how people evaluate these nonhuman role occupants is mixed. We systematically review 107 empirical studies across management, psychology, engineering, and computer science through a role-congruity lens. A consistent pattern emerges: Artificial agents in leader roles face role incongruity, driven largely by perceived deficits in morality (e.g., fairness, trustworthiness). Agents in follower roles are evaluated as largely congruent with role expectations. Agents in partner and teammate roles show conditional congruity that depends on task context and design-based social cues (e.g., appearance, voice). We integrate these patterns into the Artificial Agent Role Congruity (AARC) model, a conceptual model that extends role congruity theory to artificial agents: perceived role (in)congruity occurs when observers compare role prescriptions with the attributes they ascribe to an agent from its design-based cues along a task dimension (competence, assertiveness) and a social-emotional dimension (warmth, morality). Based on this synthesis, we outline theoretical extensions, an agenda for future research, and guidance for managers and designers deploying artificial agents in organizational roles.

items.title: Avoiding the worst leaders is more important than getting the best
items.abstract: Society and organizations invest heavily in selecting the best leaders 1, and existing research shows a positivity bias by focusing on the bright side of leadership 2–4. Yet, according to Popper 5, the central question of institutional design is not who should rule, but how to prevent bad leaders from doing too much damage. This raises the question of which approach is more consistent with human psychology: Aim for the best leaders, or avoid the worst? We provide robust evidence for an “avoid-the-worst” principle in human leadership preferences. Although text analyses indicated that the top 100 business schools emphasize good leadership far more than the prevention of bad leadership, actual employee experiences from 9.9 million Glassdoor reviews show that people mentioned their leader 70% more often in the negative than positive section, and negative leader mentions predicted company ratings 1.5 times more strongly. Providing causal evidence, five high-powered experiments across 40 countries (N = 51,433) revealed that people were more willing to sacrifice time and money to avoid a bad leader than obtaining a good leader—across morality and competence, hypothetical and incentivized choice, ideology and culture. People care more about avoiding the worst leaders than getting the best.

items.title: The Prevalence of Bayesian Inference, Preregistration, and Open Data in Psychology, 2004-2024
items.abstract: Psychology has undergone substantial methodological changes in the past two decades. We tracked the adoption of Bayesian inference and two open science practices across 28,738 articles from six ‘top-tier’ (15,634 articles) and six ‘mid-tier’ (13,104 articles) psychology journals in 2004–2024. In ‘top-tier’ journals, human (50%) and LLM-assisted (50%) full-text coding revealed that in 2024, 26% of articles reported a Bayesian analysis, 41% included a preregistration, and 73% provided open data. In ‘mid-tier’ journals, LLM coding showed corresponding rates of 16%, 18%, and 40%. From 2004 to 2012, these practices were virtually nonexistent. Bayesian logistic growth modeling suggests further increases, although their extent remains uncertain. Mixed-effects models became more prevalent, software reporting improved, with greater use of R and less reliance on SPSS, but estimation-focused (vs. hypothesis-testing-focused) reporting showed only modest gains. Despite heterogeneity across journals, psychology articles published in 2024 differ markedly from those published only a decade earlier.

items.title: Sleep quality, chronotype, and psychological distress in adults with chronic conditions: independent associations and nonlinear sleep-quality gradients
items.abstract: Abstract Background We examined associations of sleep quality, chronotype, and chronic-condition burden with psychological distress in adults with chronic conditions and explored nonlinearity. Methods We analysed cross-sectional data from the Sichuan component of the 2023 Psychology and Behavior Investigation of Chinese Residents (PBICR-2023), collected from June to September 2023. Of 1,932 Sichuan respondents, 611 adults with at least one chronic condition were included. Chronotype, sleep quality, depression-anxiety symptoms, and perceived stress were assessed using the reduced Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (rMEQ), Brief Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (B-PSQI), Patient Health Questionnaire Anxiety and Depression Scale (PHQ-ADS), and four-item Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-4), respectively. Hierarchical multivariable linear regression with HC3 robust standard errors estimated adjusted associations. Unadjusted four-knot restricted cubic splines characterised nonlinear association patterns. Results PHQ-ADS and PSS-4 differed by age, household registration, income, education, body-mass-index category, relationship status, debt, recent life events, and chronic-condition count. They were strongly correlated ( r = 0.795; P P P P = 0.027); its PSS-4 association did not reach conventional significance (B=-0.31; 95% CI, -0.64 to 0.03; P = 0.075) and attenuated after broader adjustment. Splines indicated nonlinear B-PSQI associations with both outcomes ( P for nonlinearity P = 0.029), with fitted minima near 2.96 and 2.65, respectively. rMEQ nonlinearity was not statistically significant. Conclusions In this cross-sectional sample, Poorer sleep quality and greater chronic-condition burden were consistently associated with greater psychological distress. Morningness showed a weaker inverse association that attenuated after broader adjustment. Longitudinal studies with objective sleep and circadian measures are needed.

items.title: A complex systems approach to health workforce modelling: Simulating regional psychology workforce capacity and mental healthcare access to 2050
items.abstract: Abstract Background. Mental health workforce projections estimate future workforce supply and demand for services but seldom represent nonlinear feedback and behavioural adaptation through which population need, workforce capacity, service access, and system performance change over time. We examined these dynamics within a community-based psychological treatment pathway funded through Australia’s universal health insurance system and delivered by a Primary Health Network in southern Queensland. Methods. We developed and calibrated a 2013–2050 system dynamics model using workforce, Medicare-funded psychological therapy and population time series data. Model parameters were optimised against observed data, and uncertainty analyses identified plausible parameter combinations. The calibrated model generated a business-as-usual (BAU) projection and three stress test scenarios: (i) a future ceiling on workforce recruitment; (ii) increasing pressure from rising mental ill-health driven by compounding effects on onset; and (iii) their combination. Paired simulations compared each stress test with BAU. Results. The model reproduced broad historical trajectories. By 2050, mean paired differences from BAU under the recruitment ceiling were − 163 clinical FTE [-420, 0.0] and − 4,800 monthly services [-12,500, 0], with poorer access and workforce indicators despite a smaller visible treatment queue. Compounding onset pressure increased the population living with mental ill-health by 32,100 [24,100, 42,600]; workforce and services expanded but did not fully offset rising need. Combined pressures produced the clearest deterioration: +38,200 people living with mental ill-health [24,900, 55,200], -147 clinical FTE [-421, 84] and − 4,000 monthly services [-12,500, 2,900], alongside lower supply-demand balance and greater care-seeking suppression and pipeline attrition. Conclusions. BAU stability depended on recruitment keeping pace with demand. The combined pressures produced the clearest overall system-wide deterioration and showed that smaller queues can coexist with poorer access. Interpreting FTE, service volume and waiting alongside care-seeking, attrition and workforce conditions could support more complete whole-of-system planning. More broadly, these findings suggest that human resources for health planning may benefit from approaches that explicitly represent feedback processes, delays, behavioural adaptation, and other emergent system dynamics that influence how workforce capacity, service demand, and access evolve over time.

items.title: Beyond Correct Letters: Cognitive Foundations of Spelling in Multilingual African Contexts
items.abstract: Abstract Spelling is frequently characterised as the accurate reproduction of conventional written forms, a definition that can obscure the cognitive and linguistic mechanisms underpinning its acquisition and development. This conceptual article reframes spelling as an integrated cognitive–linguistic process and considers what this means for multilingual education in African contexts. Drawing on a qualitative, theory-driven synthesis of literacy studies, cognitive psychology, linguistics, and multilingual education, it combines research on phonological, orthographic, and morphological awareness with evidence on memory, vocabulary, and multilingual resources. The synthesis advances the position that spelling competence arises from dynamic interactions among these component systems rather than from a strictly linear process of grapheme sequencing. It also argues that multilingualism is not mainly a source of cross-linguistic interference; rather, it offers resources learners strategically draw on across languages to develop literacy. With specific attention to African educational contexts in which learners negotiate languages differing in orthographic depth, morphological structure, and instructional status, the article proposes a Multidimensional Cognitive–Linguistic Spelling Framework that embeds core cognitive processes within multilingual ecologies and schooling conditions. The proposed framework aims to guide empirically grounded spelling instruction and assessment by considering learners’ linguistic repertoires and the cognitive processes underlying orthographic learning.

items.title: A Multi-Stakeholder Survey Examining Incident Review Processes in a National Healthcare System: A Study Protocol
items.abstract: Background: Incident reporting is central to patient safety, yet translating review findings into systemic learning remains challenging. Within the Irish Health Service Executive (HSE) 2020 Incident Management Framework (IMF), Improvement Planning and Monitoring (Step 6) is where findings are intended to become service change. How well reviews achieve this, and how the review methodologies in use shape that performance, has not been systematically examined. This protocol sets out a study examining how these methodologies operate in practice and the perceived quality of the recommendations they produce, by capturing the accounts of multiple stakeholders linked to the same reviews, with particular attention to human factors in the transition from learning to action. Methods The study uses a cross-sectional, mixed-methods survey design. A stratified random sample of 96 incident reviews will be drawn from the National Incident Management System (NIMS): 48 Category 1 (major/severe harm) and 48 Category 2 (moderate harm), equally divided between acute and community settings. Seven role-tailored instruments, mapped to four stakeholder categories (reviewers and commissioners; clinical staff; implementers; patients, service users and families), combine rating-scale and written-response questions organised around the six IMF principles. Quantitative data will be analysed using descriptive and non-parametric methods, qualitative data using reflexive thematic analysis, and the two strands integrated through joint displays. Ethics and dissemination Ethical approval has been granted by the School of Psychology Research Ethics Committee at Trinity College Dublin and the HSE National Research Ethics Committee. A pilot phase of five reviews will precede national administration. Findings will be disseminated through peer-reviewed publication, conference presentation, and a summary report to the HSE, and are intended to identify systemic barriers to improvement planning and inform a national logic model for shared learning.

items.title: Using Arabian Sea Coastal Water as a Model to Study Plasmid-mediated AMR Dissemination driven by Anthropogenic Impacts
items.abstract: Background: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a growing global public health threat. The water bodies act as both reservoirs and medium for dissemination of AMR. Coastal water driven by anthropogenic effects accumulate antibiotics, heavy metals, microplastics, and disinfectants which act as stressors, increasing the overall AMR. Therefore, it is necessary to understand the AMR entities and its transmission in coastal water bodies. Methods and Results Mumbai, mirroring most cosmopolitan cities of the world, was used as a model to understand how rapid urbanization disseminate AMR in coastal waters of the Arabian Sea and can pose substantial risk to human health. Bacteria isolated from coastal waters were screened and found to be multi-drug resistant. Several isolates carried multiple plasmids of high molecular weight (>10 kb). Plasmid sequencing and analysis using various bioinformatic tools identified plasmid replicons like IncFIA, IncFII, rep7a and repUS43. Analysis showed a high burden of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) conferring resistance to antibiotic classes such as monobactams (blaTEM-116), carbapenems (blaNDM-5), vancomycin (vanA), disinfectants and antiseptics (qacG). Additionally, clinically relevant mecA and mecR1 associated with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus sp., rpsL associated with streptomycin resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis and the colistin-resistance genes mcr-10.1 and mcr-10.4 were also detected. We also report for the first-time presence of a plasmid-borne mupB gene in coastal waters, that confers high resistance to mupirocin. Conclusions Despite the moderate sample size, the presence of diverse plasmid replicons and clinically important ARGs suggests urban coastal environment as a potent reservoir of AMR, with potential for global transmission through active waterway trade and transport.

items.title: Shared landscapes, shared risk: Echinococcus multilocularis infection in coyotes is linked to agricultural land and altered green space in a major U.S. metropolitan area
items.abstract: Alveolar echinococcosis (AE), caused by the tapeworm Echinococcus multilocularis, is among the most lethal zoonotic helminthic diseases affecting humans. Historically rare in North America, human and canine AE cases have risen sharply over the past decade, coinciding with the spread of a more virulent European-type haplotype and the emergence of coyotes (Canis latrans) as a principal definitive host in and around urban centers. Despite growing recognition of E. multilocularis as an emerging public health concern, the host- and landscape-level factors that concentrate infection risk within urban environments remain poorly understood. We used monitoring data from the Chicago metropolitan area to assess E. multilocularis prevalence and test demographic and land cover predictors of infection among urban coyotes. Fecal samples from 85 coyotes were screened via real-time PCR, and land cover association with E. multilocularis infection within individual home ranges or capture-based buffers was investigated using generalized linear models. Overall, 27.1% of coyotes were infected. Infection status was unrelated to age or sex, but coyotes with a greater proportion of agricultural land or altered open land cover, such as golf courses, cemeteries, and manicured parks, within their home ranges had significantly higher odds of infection (ORagriculture = 2.84; ORaltered open spaces = 2.07). These landscapes are also heavily used by people and domestic pets, suggesting elevated potential for zoonotic spillover in human-dominated areas rather than natural or forested habitat. Our findings identify specific, human-accessible landscapes that sustain E. multilocularis transmission in a major U.S. metropolitan area and provide a framework for prioritizing surveillance, targeted anthelmintic intervention, and public health outreach in expanding urban coyote populations across North America.

items.title: Undeclared Kratom Alkaloids and Tianeptine in Products Labeled as Cat's Claw
items.abstract: Background: High-concentration 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) products have been described by the US Food and Drug Administration as an emerging public health concern, and in August 2026 the Drug Enforcement Administration temporarily placed mitragynine pseudoindoxyl (MP), MGM-15 (dihydro-7-hydroxymitragynine), and MGM-16 in schedule I. Since July, Utah and Tennessee officials have reported overdoses, deaths, and laboratory findings involving tablets labeled as cat's claw (Uncaria tomentosa), an herbal supplement without known opioid activity. Chemical data on such products are scarce, and consumers cannot tell from the label which opioid-active compounds they contain. Methods: In a cross-sectional analysis, we purchased 46 chewable or unit-dose products labeled as containing cat's claw from online retailers and 3 gas stations in Mississippi during September 2026. The products represented 17 brands. Methanol extracts were analyzed by ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography with photodiode array detection and compared with a methanol extract of botanically verified U tomentosa bark. Liquid chromatography quadrupole time of flight mass spectrometry identified additional compounds, and compounds were quantified against authentic reference standards. Proportions are reported with exact (Clopper-Pearson) 95% CIs. Results: None of the 46 products declared kratom alkaloids or their derivatives, yet all contained at least one component. Mitragynine was quantified in 41 products (89%; 95% CI, 76% to 96%), 7-OH in 35 (76%; 95% CI, 61% to 87%), MGM-15 in 24 (52%; 95% CI, 37% to 67%), and MP in 22 (48%; 95% CI, 33% to 63%). A total of 39 products (85%; 95% CI, 71% to 94%) contained MP or MGM-15, which are temporarily controlled in schedule I. Tianeptine, an antidepressant not approved in the US, was present in five products (11%; 95% CI, 4% to 24%) at 27.9 to 40.2 mg per unit. The 7-OH content ranged from 0.01 to 95.4 mg per unit. Eight products carrying claims such as "NO KRATOM and No 7-OH" or "NO 7-OH" contained mitragynine, 7-OH, and 3-dehydromitragynine. Conclusions: Labels gave consumers no reliable guide to exposure. Clinicians evaluating unexplained opioid toxicity after use of a cat's claw product should consider kratom-derived opioids and tianeptine. Regulators may need product testing and label enforcement in addition to scheduling of individual compounds.

items.title: Shared Data As a Mechanism for Integration between Housing and Health Sectors: A Qualitative Interview Study in the UK
items.abstract: Background: Data sharing is widely positioned as a key mechanism for enabling integration between health and non-health sectors, particularly in relation to wider determinants such as housing. However, there is limited empirical understanding of how cross-sector data sharing is enacted in practice. Methods: Semi-structured interviews were undertaken with professionals from housing, NHS, public health and voluntary and community sector organisations in the UK. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, informed by Normalisation Process Theory. A typology of data sharing models was developed inductively. Results: From 27 interviews, six models were identified through which data sharing enabled and sustained integration across sectors. Models ranged from referral pathways supporting individual-level coordination to linked datasets supporting population-level service planning and monitoring. Participants balanced potential benefits against concerns relating to privacy, trust and organisational capacity. While initiatives supported improved coordination and greater recognition of housing as a determinant of health, some remained emergent and unevenly embedded. Discussion: Integration depended not only on digital infrastructure, but on the relational and organisational work required to legitimise and operationalise data sharing. Conclusion: Policies emphasising digital infrastructure as a means to integration should be complemented by attention to the relational, organisational and ethical conditions required to support effective cross-sector data sharing.

items.title: Temporal associations between pain and anxiety/depression in young people: A systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal, prospective, population- and community-based studies
items.abstract: Pain, anxiety, and depression are common among young people, frequently co-occur with each other, and may be longitudinally related. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to synthesise the direction and strength of the temporal associations between pain and anxiety/depression among young people. PsycINFO, Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, Proquest Dissertations and Theses, Google Scholar, and OSF Preprints were searched from inception until 3 July 2026. Additional studies were identified through citation searching and references of existing systematic reviews. Longitudinal, prospective, population- or community-based studies examining temporal associations between pain and anxiety/depression among young people (0-24 years) were included. Two independent reviewers screened studies, extracted data, assessed risk of bias using ROBINS-E, and evaluated certainty of evidence using GRADE. Data were synthesised using three-level meta-analysis and narrative synthesis. Forty-two studies from 31 longitudinal cohorts were included. Anxiety, depression, and combined anxiety/depression were positively associated with subsequent pain. However, after adjustment for confounders, only depression remained significantly associated. Pain was positively associated with subsequent anxiety, depression, and combined anxiety/depression both before and after confounder adjustment. Heterogeneity was moderate to considerable and was partly explained by sex, baseline age, follow-up duration, pain type, pain informant, pain and anxiety/depression operationalisation, and risk of bias. Two of 14 outcomes had high quality of evidence, whereas the remainder ranged from very low to moderate quality. These findings highlight longitudinal associations between pain and anxiety/depression among young people and should be considered in the screening, treatment, and public health management of these problems.

items.title: Acceptability and perceived effectiveness of health warnings and calorie labels on alcohol products: An online experimental study
items.abstract: AimsImproved alcohol labels are a population-level intervention with the potential to reduce selection and consumption of alcohol. The primary aim of this study was to assess the acceptability of implementing (i) alcohol calorie labelling, (ii) alcohol health warning labels (HWLs), and (iii) both types of labels combined, each presented with or without images. The specific labels used were based on those being proposed for national implementation in Ireland.MethodsParticipants (n=994) were randomly assigned to one of six groups in an online experiment with a between subject 3 (Label Type: HWL only; calorie labelling only; combined label [HWLs and calorie labelling]) x 2 (Message Type: description; description plus example image) factorial design. The primary outcome was acceptability of implementing the labelling policy. Secondary outcomes were perceived effectiveness and potential harms. Free-text comments were analysed using content analysis.ResultsThere was a significant main effect of Label Type (F(2, 990)=4.27, p=0.014, ηₚ²=0.01), with acceptability lower for HWLs (p=0.01, d=0.23). There was no main effect of Message Type or interaction. All types of labels were perceived as relatively acceptable. There were no overall differences in perceived effectiveness or harms of the labels. ConclusionsHWLs and calorie information were both perceived as relatively acceptable, although HWLs were less accepted. The way the labelling policy was presented did not affect acceptability. Although further evaluation with other labelling interventions is warranted, this suggests giving the public more detailed and visual information about a labelling policy does not decrease acceptability of the policy. items.title: Prevalence of dementia and mild cognitive impairment in Morocco: A population-based study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Dementia and mild cognitive impairment (MCI) represent growing public health concerns, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, where population-based epidemiological data remain limited. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of dementia and MCI among Moroccan adults aged ≥ 60 years and to examine associated sociodemographic and health-related factors. Methods A nationwide cross-sectional telephone survey was conducted between March and June 2025 among 1,662 adults aged ≥ 60 years across all 12 administrative regions of Morocco. The target sample was allocated proportionally to regional population size, and mobile telephone numbers were randomly selected within regional pools using computerized selection. First-stage cognitive screening was conducted in Moroccan Darija using the telephone version of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (T-MoCA) and the AD-8. Participants were considered screen-positive if they had a T-MoCA score ≤ 16 or an AD-8 score ≥ 2. All screen-positive participants underwent a second-stage telephone assessment conducted by neurologists under the supervision of a senior professor of neurology. Diagnoses were established within the DSM-5 framework based on cognitive and functional assessment. Results Among the 1,662 participants, 388 screened positive and underwent second-stage assessment. Of these, 85 met the criteria for dementia and 303 for MCI. The crude prevalence of dementia was 5.1% (85/1,662; 95% CI: 4.15–6.28) and increased to 11.6% (95% bootstrap CI: 8.8–14.5) after weighting for age, sex, and region according to the 2024 Moroccan General Population and Housing Census. The corresponding crude and population-weighted prevalence estimates for MCI were 18.2% (303/1,662; 95% CI: 16.45–20.16) and 23.6% (95% bootstrap CI: 20.5–26.9), respectively. Conclusion This nationwide study provides epidemiological data on dementia and MCI among adults aged ≥ 60 years across all 12 administrative regions of Morocco. The findings indicate a substantial burden of cognitive impairment in the study sample and may contribute to future research and healthcare planning.

items.title: A Dual-Track Knowledge Graph for Evidence-Based Pediatric Medication Management in Neurological Disorders: Implications for Rational Drug Use and Public Health Governance
items.abstract: Abstract Background Pediatric neurological disorders represent a leading cause of chronic childhood de integrity of domestic pediatric drug indicisability and necessitate long-term standardized pharmacological intervention. Current clinical practice for pediatric neurological disorders is constrained by fragmented research evidence, incomplete pediatric drug labeling specifications, prevalent off-label drug use, and the scarcity of age-appropriate pharmaceutical formulations, resulting in inconsistent clinical medication standards and persistent pediatric medication safety risks. As an efficient tool for integrating heterogeneous biomedical data, the knowledge graph facilitates standardized medication management and evidence mining for public health research. This study constructed a dual-track knowledge graph framework centered on clinical practice guideline evidence and semantic-derived potential medication associations. The framework systematically organizes multi-dimensional medication evidence for pediatric neurological disorders, identifies critical gaps in pediatric medication resources, and provides empirical support for optimized evidence-based medication management and refined pharmaceutical public health governance. Methods This study synthesized multi-source authoritative data, including global clinical practice guidelines for pediatric neurological disorders (2008–2025), official drug approval labeling documents, and professional pharmaceutical databases. A dual-track evidence integration framework was implemented for standardized knowledge organization in pediatric neurological evidence-based medication management. The primary track extracted explicit disease–drug therapeutic associations recommended by clinical practice guidelines to form authoritative, standardized clinical medication evidence. The auxiliary track supplemented potential rational medication associations via textual semantic similarity analysis, expanding the coverage of medication evidence for pediatric neurological disorders. Multi-dimensional safety filtering rules were established to guarantee the rationality of exploratory evidence. All structured evidence was visualized and quantitatively analyzed using the Neo4j platform to elucidate the current status and structural deficiencies of existing pediatric medication resources. Results The established dual-track knowledge graph covered 32 common pediatric neurological disorders and 7,847 standardized drug specifications, encompassing 1,549 authoritative disease–drug relationships validated by clinical practice guidelines and 3,300 clinically viable latent medication associations. Quantitative analysis identified three prominent structural deficiencies in domestic medication resources for pediatric neurological disorders: insufficient officially approved pediatric drug indications for first-line therapeutic agents, severe shortages of child-adapted dosage forms, and inequitable cross-border accessibility of specialized pediatric medications. The dual-track framework achieved hierarchical classification of authoritative consensus evidence and exploratory potential evidence, enabling comprehensive integration and traceable management of evidence-based medication management resources. Conclusions This study proposed a targeted dual-track knowledge graph framework for evidence-based medication management in pediatric neurological disorders, effectively addressing the fragmentation and ungraded classification of existing pediatric medication evidence. The framework not only supports standardized clinical evidence-based medication and expands individualized medication reference schemes for complex conditions but also quantitatively identifies key gaps in pediatric drug approval, dosage form allocation, and public health resource distribution. It provides reliable empirical evidence for optimizing pediatric pharmaceutical governance, promoting rational pediatric drug use, and constructing a refined digital public health service system for pediatric medication management.

items.title: The Relationship Between Problematic Social Media Use and Sleep Quality Among University Students : A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Abstract Problematic social media use has emerged as a significant global public health concern, particularly among university students. This systematic review synthesizes contemporary evidence across diverse geographical contexts to evaluate the relationship between social media addiction and objective sleep quality parameters. Following strict inclusion criteria, ten high-quality empirical studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses published between 2023 and 2026—representing populations in Bangladesh, China, India, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, the United Kingdom, Nigeria, and Brazil—were synthesized. The collective findings across a cumulative sample size of over 40,000 participants demonstrate a robust, negative correlation between excessive digital exposure and sleep duration. Late-night screen time, driven by Fear of Missing Out (FoMo) and digital fatigue, severely alters circadian rhythms and suppresses melatonin secretion, leading to fragmented sleep, daytime sleepiness, and heightened depressive symptoms. While protective behavioral strategies like physical exercise offer a viable mitigation buffer, their efficacy is heavily undermined by extreme digital dependencies. In conclusion, unregulated social media consumption poses an escalating threat to student well-being. Immediate multi-sectoral interventions, digital literacy programs, and campus-based health policies are required to safeguard the physical and psychological health of the higher education workforce.

items.title: Locally-informed risk maps for yellow fever: a modelling study in Ghana
items.abstract: Abstract Yellow fever (YF) outbreaks continue to occur in Africa and South America despite an effective vaccine. Knowing where and when certain areas are at greatest risk for YF could enable targeted allocation of resources for outbreak prevention and detection. While global risk maps of YF and other epidemic-prone pathogens exist, more granular models are needed for decision-makers. Therefore, we constructed a process for co-developing infectious disease risk maps with national experts and applied this process to model YF risk in Ghana. We collected local-level data on 14,534 patients tested for YF and eco-epidemiological covariates in Ghana from 2005–2024. We then created subnational risk maps for YF using ecological niche models that combined spatial epidemiological analysis and feedback from public health experts in Ghana. These risk maps can be used to inform targeted vaccination campaigns and diagnostic resource allocation. Our results demonstrate how local public health data can be combined with high-resolution earth observation data and expert feedback to create risk maps for infectious diseases such as YF that can directly inform subnational and national policy decisions.

items.title: Body Composition and its correlates in children and adolescents living in Germany: An updated cross-sectional replication study based on the MoMo 2.0-Study
items.abstract: Abstract A population’s body composition and its interplay with health-related correlates should be monitored continuously to inform public health strategies and track potential changes. We conducted a cross-sectional replication study using data from 2.930 children and adolescents aged 6–17 years participating in the nationwide [replication study blinded for peer review] (2022–2025) and compared the findings with 2.869 participants from [original study blinded for peer review] (2014–2017). Overall, 98 of 108 predefined hypotheses (90.7%) were replicated, including 39 hypotheses that were supported and 59 that were consistently not supported across both studies. Physical fitness again showed the strongest and most consistent associations with body composition parameters across age groups and sexes. Compared with the earlier cohort, participants in the [replication study blinded for peer review] exhibited generally lower fat-free mass index and phase angle. These findings demonstrate a high degree of reproducibility of the reported associations between body composition and its correlates while indicating potentially unfavorable between-wave differences in body composition among German youth.

items.title: Transforming Child Nutrition Planning Through a Localized Data Driven Costing Model in Southern Bangladesh
items.abstract: Abstract Malnutrition remains a critical public health challenge in Bangladesh, specifically among children under 5 years of age in coastal and climate vulnerable regions. The study aims to explore and analyze the changes in children under 5 years of age nutrition status alongside the increased budget allocations for nutrition at the union level. The study was conducted in selected coastal upazilas of southern Bangladesh, guided by the UNICEF Conceptual Framework. A survey of 922 households was carried out using a semi-structured questionnaire, FGDs and KIIs were conducted. The study shows notable improvements in the nutritional status of under-five children from 2022 to 2023, with severe stunting dropping from 16.4% to 6.7% and severe underweight from 5.1% to 3.1%. A key finding is the strong positive correlation between increased nutrition and WASH budget allocations and reduced stunting and underweight. The study suggests that formalizing local budgets for nutrition and WASH can guide policy in South Asia to reduce child malnutrition. The Bangladesh National Nutrition Council (BNNC) endorsed Child Profile Estimates & Costing Model (CPE&CM) marks a critical step toward institutionalization, contributing to the Second National Plan of Action for Nutrition (NPAN2). This innovative tool guides local to central authorities in implementing need-based nutrition interventions with accurate cost estimates.

items.title: AI-Enabled Early Prediction of Lassa Fever: A Clinical Decision Support System for Endemic Settings
items.abstract: Abstract Lassa fever remains a major public health challenge in West Africa, where early clinical symptoms frequently overlap with other febrile illnesses and laboratory confirmation may be delayed. This study developed and evaluated an AI-enabled Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) to support early triage of suspected Lassa fever cases using a retrospective clinical surveillance dataset from Irrua Specialist Teaching Hospital, Nigeria, spanning 2015 to 2025, one of the largest longitudinal clinical surveillance datasets for Lassa fever. The final cohort included 31, 277 patient encounters, with 3, 359 laboratory-confirmed cases (10.7% prevalence). To ensure real-world deployability and the prevention of data leakage, only variables available at initial clinical presentation, including demographic characteristics and reported symptoms, were used for model development. Four supervised models (logistic regression, random forest, gradient boosting, and XGBoost) were evaluated using temporal validation, with recent years reserved for independent testing. On the temporal test set, the selected XGBoost model achieved ROC-AUC of 0.664, AUPRC of 0.137, and Brier score of 0.057. Predicted probabilities were stratified into Low ( 0.155) risk categories, with observed positivity ratesincreasing across bands (3.9%, 8.7%, and 16.1%, respectively). The model was deployed as a lightweight web-based CDSS with integrated feature-level explanations, which demonstrated the feasibility of the real-time AI-assisted triage using routine clinical surveillance data in endemic settings. Our findings highlight the potential of AI-driven tools to support early decision-making and optimise resource allocation for Lassa fever control.

items.title: Reflections from lived experience contributors and researchers on effective collaboration in the trial of a digital parenting intervention: exploring unexpected outcomes of patient involvement and engagement.
items.abstract: Abstract Background Patient and public involvement and engagement (PPIE) has become an integral part of health and social care research. The limited existing evidence suggests that it can improve the quality and relevance of research and the experiences of study participants, PPIE contributors, and researchers. However, further research to better understand effective collaboration between researchers and PPIE contributors and its importance to research is needed. Methods This paper explores the experiences of PPIE contributors (n = 11) in the OPTIMA trial of a digital parenting intervention for families of children on a child mental health services waitlist, and the research team. The PPIE contributors were themselves parents who had sought psychological support for their children. Feedback was gathered from PPIE contributors at two timepoints via group discussion and emails, specifically focusing on the professional skills development and personal outcomes reported by both PPIE contributors and researchers, and on their experiences of working together. Results PPIE contributors highlighted developing valuable research skills, including qualitative analysis, editing and academic and non-academic writing. Beyond professional skill development, PPIE contributors described developing a strong sense of community and purpose and the opportunity to give back to other parents with shared experiences. Researchers reported an increased understanding of participant-sensitive communication and emphasised the substantial contribution of PPIE in informing key decisions of the study. Conclusion These findings contribute to a growing body of literature on meaningful PPIE in research, illustrating not only its value in improving research processes but also the personal and professional benefits generated through co-design and collaboration between researchers and those with lived experience.

items.title: Silent Circulation of Rickettsia Spp. In a Non-Endemic Area of Northeastern Brazil Revealed by Molecular and Serological Evidence in Animals From Probable Sites of Human Spotted Fever Infection
items.abstract: Abstract Spotted fever is a severe zoonotic disease, and Alagoas State has historically been classified as a silent area for human rickettsioses. This study aimed to investigate the occurrence of and exposure to bacteria of the genus Rickettsia in Alagoas to support epidemiological surveillance and assess public health risks. We collected 114 blood samples from animals, including 95 dogs and 19 horses, alongside 146 ticks, across four municipalities: Maragogi, Palmeira dos Índios, São José da Tapera, and Senador Rui Palmeira. Samples were tested for antibodies against Rickettsia rickettsii , R. parkeri , and R. amblyommatis by indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA). DNA from blood clot and tick samples was extracted for molecular analyses using real-time PCR (qPCR) and conventional PCR targeting gltA and ompA genes. IFA revealed significant exposure to these agents (p R. parkeri , followed by R. amblyommatis and R. rickettsii . Of the 146 ticks, 111 (76.0%) from dogs were identified as Rhipicephalus sanguineus , and 35 (24.0%) from horses were Dermacentor nitens . All tick samples tested negative for Rickettsia by qPCR. However, Rickettsia DNA was detected in a blood clot sample from a dog from the municipality of Maragogi. This study provides the first molecular and serological evidence of silent Rickettsia spp. circulation in Alagoas, a non-endemic region for spotted fever. The high seroreactivity demonstrates active exposure, highlighting dogs and horses as sentinel species within an integrated One Health framework.

items.title: Sport Is Social Medicine: A Conceptual Review of Loneliness and Social Health
items.abstract: Abstract Background Loneliness has emerged as a major public health challenge associated with adverse biological, psychological, and social outcomes. Although traditionally conceptualized as an individual psychological experience, contemporary perspectives increasingly emphasize social connection and social health as important determinants of well-being. Sport and physical activity have received growing attention as potential strategies for addressing loneliness; however, the mechanisms through which sport may influence loneliness and social health have not been clearly synthesized within a single conceptual framework. This review aimed to examine how sport participation may contribute to reducing loneliness through biological, psychological, and social pathways and to explore its potential role in promoting social health. Methods This study was conducted as a conceptual review using a narrative synthesis approach. Literature related to loneliness, social connection, social health, physical activity, sport participation, social prescribing, and relevant theoretical frameworks was reviewed across multiple disciplines. Evidence was examined and synthesized to identify the biological, psychological, and social mechanisms through which sport may influence loneliness and social health. Based on this synthesis, a conceptual model was developed to explain the relationships among sport participation, social connection, social health, and loneliness. Results The reviewed evidence suggests that sport participation may influence loneliness through interconnected biological, psychological, and social pathways. Biological mechanisms include improved stress regulation, reduced inflammation, and enhanced cognitive health. Psychological mechanisms involve greater self-efficacy, self-esteem, resilience, and well-being. Social mechanisms include strengthened social support, belongingness, social identity, and community participation. Building upon these findings, the Biopsychosocial Loop Model is proposed to explain how sport participation may strengthen social connection, promote social health, and reduce loneliness through mutually reinforcing processes. The review further introduces the Sport is Social Medicine (SSM) perspective, which conceptualizes sport as a social health resource that extends beyond its traditional role in physical and mental health promotion. Conclusions Current evidence suggests that the relationship between sport and loneliness cannot be explained through a single mechanism. Rather, sport appears to operate through interconnected biopsychosocial pathways that strengthen social connection and support social health. The proposed Biopsychosocial Loop Model and Sport is Social Medicine perspective provide complementary conceptual frameworks for understanding how sport may contribute to addressing loneliness and promoting social health across the lifespan. These frameworks may inform future research, public health strategies, and community-based interventions aimed at strengthening social connection and well-being.

items.title: Disease activity and functional trajectories with biologic DMARDs in Brazil's public health system: the REAL study, 2015--2017
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Real-world evidence on biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (bDMARDs) in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is abundant but derived almost entirely from high-income countries; longitudinal Brazilian data are scarce. The trajectories of disease activity and functional capacity were analysed in Brazilian patients with RA receiving bDMARDs within the Unified Health System (SUS). Methods: This was a retrospective cohort analysis of the REAL, Rheumatoid Arthritis in Real Life, study, a nationwide prospective multicentre cohort of Brazilian patients treated at public referral centres. Sixty-two patients receiving bDMARDs at 8 centres, with complete data across three protocol-driven visits over approximately 12 months (186 observations), were included. Disease activity was assessed by DAS28-CRP, DAS28-ESR, SDAI, CDAI, and RADAI, and functional capacity by the HAQ. Patients received tumour necrosis factor inhibitors (TNFi; n = 31) or non-TNFi agents (n = 31). Linear mixed-effects models with nested random intercepts (patient within centre) were fitted for each outcome. Results: Rather than improving, disease activity remained stable between the first two visits and then rose significantly at the final visit relative to baseline for DAS28-CRP (p = 0.011), SDAI (p = 0.013), and CDAI (p = 0.019); functional capacity did not improve. Drug class was significantly associated with HAQ (p = 0.007), with the TNFi group showing lower disability, and TNFi patients maintained stable DAS28-CRP remission rates (approximately 55 percent) while non-TNFi patients declined from 35.5 percent to 19.4 percent. However, no visit x drug class interaction was significant (nearest trend: SDAI, p = 0.076), indicating broadly parallel trajectories, and the between-class difference is likely confounded by indication and treatment line. Smoking was associated with worse HAQ (p = 0.004), and corticosteroid use with higher SDAI (p = 0.003), CDAI (p Conclusion: In this Brazilian real-world cohort of long-standing RA treated in the public health system, disease activity was not consistently sustained over 12 months, while functional capacity remained largely unchanged. Effectiveness estimates from other health systems should not be assumed to transfer to the SUS, and closer structured monitoring with timely therapeutic adjustment is warranted.

items.title: Prevalence and Temporal Trends of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Among Adults in Cameroon: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is an increasing public health challenge in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). In Cameroon, its prevalence remains uncertain due to heterogeneous evidence across populations and geographical settings. This systematic review and meta-analysis estimated the pooled prevalence of T2DM among adults in Cameroon and examined variations by demographic, geographic, and study characteristics. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, WHO Global Index Medicus, and the Virtual Health Library was conducted from database inception through 14 March 2026. Eligible studies were population- or community-based observational studies reporting the prevalence of T2DM among adults (≥18 years) in Cameroon. Pooled prevalence estimates were obtained using a random-effects meta-analysis of proportions with inverse-variance weighting, logit transformation, restricted maximum likelihood estimation, and Hartung-Knapp confidence intervals. Heterogeneity, publication bias, subgroup analyses, meta-regression, and sensitivity analyses were performed. The review protocol wasregistered in PROSPERO (CRD420251274750). Results: Eleven studies comprising 20,559 adults were included. The pooled prevalence of T2DM was 3.5% (95% CI, 2.1-5.7%), with substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 92.7%). The 95% prediction interval ranged from 0.7% to 16.6%, highlighting substantial variability in T2DM prevalence estimates across different settings in Cameroon. Prevalence increased markedly with age, from 2.0% (95% CI, 1.0-4.0%) among adults aged Conclusions: . These findings provide the most comprehensive synthesis to date of T2DM burden and temporal trends in Cameroon and highlight the urgent need for strengthened surveillance, targeted prevention strategies, and early detection programs to address the growing diabetes epidemic.

items.title: Prevalence, Socioeconomic Determinants, and Health-System Factors Associated with Laboratory-Confirmed Renal Impairment Among Adults Attending Tertiary Referral Hospitals in Mogadishu, Somalia: A Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is an important and growing public health challenge that disproportionately affects populations in low- and middle-income countries. Limited diagnostic capacity, constrained access to care, and socioeconomic disadvantage contribute to delayed diagnosis and poor clinical outcomes. In Somalia, evidence describing the burden and determinants of CKD remains limited despite the increasing prevalence of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and other non-communicable diseases (NCDs). This study estimated the prevalence of renal impairment among adults attending tertiary referral hospitals in Mogadishu, identified associated socioeconomic and clinical factors, and examined health system barriers to kidney care. Methods A hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted between April and July 2026 in two tertiary referral hospitals in Mogadishu, Somalia. Systematic sampling was used to screen 312 adult outpatients, resulting in 200 participants with complete clinical, laboratory, and questionnaire data for analysis. Renal function was assessed using serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), urine protein dipstick testing, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) calculated using the 2021 CKD-EPI race-free equation. Multivariable binary logistic regression was performed to identify factors independently associated with renal impairment, with results reported as adjusted odds ratios (aORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Results Among the 200 participants, 145 (72.5%) had reduced eGFR ( p = 0.003), hypertension (aOR = 3.15; 95% CI: 1.58–6.28; p = 0.001), diabetes mellitus (aOR = 2.48; 95% CI: 1.25–4.92; p = 0.009), frequent use of non-prescribed non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) (aOR = 2.21; 95% CI: 1.12–4.36; p = 0.022), and treatment non-adherence (aOR = 1.95; 95% CI: 1.02–3.73; p = 0.043). Conclusions Renal impairment was common among adults attending two tertiary referral hospitals in Mogadishu and was strongly associated with established cardiometabolic risk factors, frequent non-prescribed NSAID use, and indicators of socioeconomic disadvantage. These findings suggest opportunities to strengthen early detection and management of kidney disease through integration of routine renal assessment within primary care and NCD services, expansion of diagnostic capacity under Somalia's Essential Package of Health Services (EPHS 2020), improved regulation of nephrotoxic medications, and enhanced community-based screening and referral within the national Universal Health Coverage (UHC) agenda. Trial registration: Not applicable

items.title: Democratising patient and public involvement – A case study from the RELAX (Reducing Levels of AnXiety) randomised clinical trial
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Perinatal anxiety is a public health concern, affecting over one fifth of women during a vulnerable life stage. The RELAX randomised clinical trial tested a psychological training designed to prevent escalating anxiety. This paper describes and appraises the patient and public involvement (PPI). Objective: PPI aims were to: 1) make the trial relevant and acceptable for participants; 2) reduce barriers to engagement among those often underrepresented in research, including Black and Asian women; 3) assist recruitment; and 4) develop and promote PPI good practice. Methods : We used co-production values, and Guidance for Reporting Involvement of Patients and the Public (GRIPP2-SF) for planning the PPI. We carried out a PPI reflections survey with open and closed questions and drew on research records. Reflexive thematic analysis was used to analyse PPI advisers’ reflections. We adopted a realist research perspective, describing the PPI context and processes, reporting PPI outcomes and considering what worked for whom, and why. Results: Key PPI themes were: (1) feeling valued, gaining confidence; (2) achieving something good from bad experiences; (3) making a difference to the study; (4) supporting equity and inclusivity; and (5) being part of a community. PPI began with extensive consultation (7 meetings). A large, diverse PPI advisory group was active throughout the study (14 meetings, mean attendance: 11 PPI advisers). Innovations: focus on diversity and inclusion; employment of a service-user researcher to facilitate public involvement; a WhatsApp group for communication and support; researchers’ responsiveness to PPI ideas, publicity contributions, co-analysis and co-authorship. Limitations: limited PPI input into study methodology; PPI wish for training to be accessed via smartphone was not permitted, and some advisers felt shy in online meetings. PPI enhanced trial recruitment; ethnic diversity and high retention. Conclusions: PPI contributed to research quality in this trial and empowered PPI advisers. During the study PPI became increasingly democratised, moving from consultation , to collaboration , and some co-production as a result of principal investigator support for PPI; an experienced service-user researcher to lead and promote PPI good practice; and RELAX researchers’ flexible responsiveness. A focus on equity and diversity, and relationship-building innovations contributed to overall success. Plain English summary: One in five pregnant women experience anxiety disorders during pregnancy and many more distressing anxiety symptoms. The RELAX study aimed to help pregnant women and birthing people have less anxiety. Researchers asked a diverse group of parents with experience of anxiety in pregnancy to help them design and carry out the study. This is called public involvement (PPI). Researchers and PPI advisers worked together to make the RELAX website and training relevant and accessible. We checked the language was easy to understand and made videos about the study. Public advisers shared information on social media and locally to help with recruitment. This case study is a positive example of PPI in a trial, with useful learning points. Good practice: a large, diverse public involvement advisory group, advisers always paid for their time, childcare and travel costs, and continuous support. Innovations: diversity and inclusion; employment of a service-user researcher to facilitate public involvement and advise on good practice; use of WhatsApp for team-building and support; researcher responsiveness to demand for frequent advisory group meetings; and involvement of public advisors in analysis and authorship. Progression during the study from consultation, through collaboration to co-production. Limitations: limited in-depth involvement prior to funding, advisers’ wish for training to be accessed via smartphones was not permitted, and some advisers felt shy to speak in meetings. Impact: Evaluating public involvement creates useful learning. Advisers felt respected and valued; research quality and learning about co-production increased. The training will soon be offered on a new smartphone app. Trial registration: ISRCTN 12754931. Registered 25th May 2023.
