items.title: Dry-season malaria transmission and associated risk factors among urban residents of Jabi Tehnan District, northwest Ethiopia
items.abstract: Abstract Background Dry-season malaria transmission is a growing public health challenge in urban areas of Ethiopia. However, concrete evidence on its magnitude and associated factors remains scarce. The present study, therefore, assessed the extent of malaria transmission and identified factors associated with malaria among urban residents of Jabi Tehnan District during the dry season. Methods A community-based cross-sectional study was conducted in March 2026 among 335 residents of Finote Selam, Mankusa, and Jiga towns. One eligible adult from each selected household was tested for malaria using a CareStart™ Malaria Pf/Pv Ag Combo rapid diagnostic test (RDT). Sociodemographic and malaria-related data were collected using a pretested structured questionnaire. Associations were assessed using multivariable logistic regression and reported as adjusted odds ratios (AORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Statistical significance was considered at p Results Malaria prevalence was 17.6% (59/335), with cases detected in all urban centers of the district. Plasmodium falciparum was the predominant parasite identified (59.3%), while mixed P. falciparum/P. vivax infections accounted for 6.8% of cases. Individuals engaged in farming activities (AOR=3.575; 95% CI: 1.218-8.858), houses with eave openings (AOR=9.635; 95% CI: 2.718-34.155), and inadequate knowledge about malaria preventive measures (AOR=2.218; 95% CI: 1.011-5.301) appeared as significant explanatory risk factors associated with increased odds of malaria. In contrast, insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) utilization was associated with reduced odds of infection (AOR=0.076; 95% CI: 0.011-0.525). Conclusion Dry-season malaria transmission persists among urban residents of Jabi Tehnan District. Strengthening personal protection during farming activities and ITNs utilization at home, improving housing conditions, and promoting malaria-related health education should be prioritized alongside targeted surveillance and vector-control interventions.

items.title: Accompaniment Planning: Re-sequencing Suicide-Related Care in ClinicalSocial Work Practice
items.abstract: Abstract Social workers frequently encounter suicidal thoughts and behaviors across practice settings. Contemporary standards of care often organize suicide prevention into a protocol-driven sequence that begins with screening and risk assessment. This sequencing rests on the assumption that risk can be identified early and reliably enough to act upon. Such an assumption is challenged by emerging empirical research, critical theorists, and people with suicide-lived experience. The confluence of these perspectives suggests that when clinical encounters are structured around risk identification before relational grounding has been sufficiently established, disclosure becomes perilous rather than relational: some individuals conceal suicidal experiences altogether. This theoretical and practice-oriented article introduces accompaniment, an ethical stance and relational practice that privileges presence over prediction, and translates it into the Accompaniment Planning Template: a structured and collaborative process organized around eight domains. The proposed re-sequencing positions accompaniment before assessment, safety planning, and follow-up, not to delay care but to establish the relational and epistemic conditions under which subsequent intervention becomes meaningful. Implications are discussed for clinical practice, education and supervision, and public health because the relational conditions that support disclosure may improve access to care and outcomes for populations historically marginalized within behavioral health and health care systems. Finally, limitations for this practice and education innovation are identified. Keywords: accompaniment, suicide prevention, therapeutic alliance, clinical social work, critical suicide studies

items.title: A Systematic Review of Social Determinants of Health in Harare, Dissecting the Affordability Dichotomy Between Private and Public Healthcare
items.abstract: Introduction: Healthcare affordability in Harare is shaped by social and economic conditions, including income, employment, insurance status, medicine availability and household insecurity. Public care may offer lower entry costs than private care, but shortages, facility-level price variation and payment mechanisms can generate additional expenditure. Methods: The researcher-selected databases and information sources were Google Scholar, PubMed (MEDLINE) and ERIC. The eligibility protocol restricted publication years to 2020–2026. The exact calendar date of search execution was not recorded in the verified identification provenance; this is distinct from the publication-year eligibility range. Google Scholar, PubMed (MEDLINE) and ERIC were searched using a prespecified Boolean strategy for English-language studies published from 2020 to 2026. Results: The direct Harare evidence was concentrated in qualitative diabetes-care research. Public referral care was described as cheaper and more accessible to low-income and generally uninsured households, but local consultation fees, medicine shortages, transport and searching costs, cash co-payments, exchange-rate disadvantages and possible improper charging weakened effective affordability. Household economic insecurity constrained continuity of chronic disease treatment. Information about medicine sources was enabling, while digital infrastructure and network limitations constrained telehealth. Remittances were associated with greater use of private facilities in wider urban Zimbabwe evidence. Discussion/Conclusion: Affordability in Harare is relative and pathway-dependent rather than determined solely by sector. Public care can reduce initial financial barriers, yet system shortages and payment failures shift costs to households. Confidence is moderated by concentrated disease-specific evidence, thin direct comparison of private and public care, contextual transferability limits and incomplete.

items.title: Did the emergence of the Omicron variant impact the COVID-19 vaccine sentiments in the Arab world? A Twitter-based comparative analysis
items.abstract: Background: Vaccine hesitancy constitutes a major obstacle for achieving herd immunity against coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). Research has shown high vaccine hesitancy rates and low compliance among Arabic-speaking populations in the 2021–2022 period. The aim of this study was to analyze sentiments related to COVID-19 vaccines before and after the emergence of the COVID-19 Omicron variant in the Arab-speaking world. Methods Tweets were collected before and after the Omicron emergence period in the Arab-speaking world using Python-enabled CAMeL Tools (Arabic Natural Language Processing toolkit) libraries. A sentiment analysis on COVID-19 vaccines using Arabic keywords, a sentiment analysis by city, and a time series were conducted. Results The data sets exhibited a shift towards less negativity, more neutrality, and a possible adoption of a pragmatic discourse towards vaccine uptake. Sentiments by city showed the Gulf region registered the most presence in the Twitter data, and the time series demonstrated change in sentiments followed public health events. Conclusions Despite its limitations, the study pointed to change in sentiments in response to vaccine-related events. Increased neutral sentiments and vaccine discourse shifting towards vaccine uptake pragmatism after the onset of Omicron, indicate change is possible. Future research may focus on how change towards more vaccine acceptance can be triggered; on how Twitter vaccine discourse translates within local communities; on including other social media (for instance Facebook); on vaccine discourse analysis to get nuanced insights; and on ethical implications of vaccine policies.

items.title: Digital Transformation of Public Finance and Fiscal Depth: Impact on Spending Efficiency to Achieve the Sustainable Development Goals in Iraq
items.abstract: Background: Digital transformation of public finance is a fundamental pillar for achieving modern and effective public financial management. By enhancing transparency, reducing waste, and improving efficiency in the allocation and use of public resources, digital transformation directly contributes to raising the level of efficiency of public spending. This efficiency, in turn, is a vital factor in countries’ ability to finance and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals, which positively impacts the long-term well-being and sustainability of societies. The research includes an economic analysis of the relationship between the digital transformation of public finances and spending efficiency to achieve sustainable development goals, with a focus on the Iraqi economy during the period 2007-2023. Methodology Using a quantitative analytical approach based on quarterly time-series data (N = 63) covering 2007 Q 3 to 2023 Q 1, this research provides an empirical assessment. Fiscal depth (FD) is employed as a structural proxy for digital financial capacity. Per capita education spending (SE) and health spending (HS) are explicitly defined as quantitative fiscal allocation indicators rather than direct operational efficiency scores. Model lag selection was automatically optimized using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) in EViews Results The results indicate a statistically significant positive dynamic impact of fiscal depth on spending allocation in the short term. However, the bounds test reveals the absence of a long-term cointegration relationship for health spending, demonstrating the structural oil-dependent bottlenecks in Iraq. Model diagnostic issues regarding heteroskedasticity were systematically corrected using Huber-White robust standard errors. Conclusions These findings contribute to policy recommendations urging the Iraqi government to develop clear roadmaps for implementation and address skills gaps in infrastructure and workforce to ensure the sustainability of digital reforms.

items.title: Consumo de alimentos ultraprocesados, coexistencia de aditivos y factores de riesgo asociados entre estudiantes universitarios en Perú
items.abstract: Background: The rising consumption of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) is a global concern, given their poor nutritional quality and the presence of multiple additives that may pose health risks when consumed in excess. Young populations are particularly vulnerable due to lifestyle habits and the widespread availability and accessibility of these products. The present study aimed to assess the consumption of ultra-processed foods (UPFs), taking into account the co-occurrence of additives and their association with risk factors in a young population. Methods A two-phase cross-sectional study was conducted. In the first phase, 500 ultra-processed food products available on the Peruvian market were analysed and classified into five groups: meat products, cereals, confectionery, dairy, and beverages, in order to identify the presence and frequency of additives. In the second phase, a structured survey was administered to 385 students, collecting data on UPF consumption over the previous 24 hours, along with variables related to lifestyle. Chi-square tests and ordinal logistic regression were used to analyse the associations. Results The categories with the highest levels of consumption were carbonated beverages (59.6%), meat products (54.7%), and dairy in various forms (66.3%). A high frequency of co-occurrence was identified between colourings and acidulants, particularly INS 133, INS 150d, and INS 339i. Statistical analysis revealed a significant association between UPF consumption and male sex (OR = 1.603), as well as alcohol consumption (OR = 2.059), while age showed an inverse relationship (OR = 0.756). Other variables, such as physical activity and smoking, did not demonstrate a significant association. Conclusion It is concluded that excessive UPF consumption varies according to age and sex and represents a continuous source of exposure to food additives. In addition, a statistically significant association was observed between UPF consumption and alcohol consumption, which may indicate a relationship of relevance from a public health perspective; however, a causal relationship cannot be established.

items.title: Maltreatment predicts centiles of individual variation from normative brain growth in children
items.abstract: Abstract Exposure to maltreatment in childhood is posited to profoundly disrupt brain development with adverse consequences for cognitive development and health across the lifespan. Here we use “brain charts” from the largest available neuroimaging database to quantify individual brain volumes relative to normative brain growth distributions in 299 children, aged 3 to 13 years, including 123 children with clinically verified maltreatment exposure. Using magnetic resonance imaging, we obtain volumes of cortical grey, total white, and subcortical grey matter and derive chart-based centiles for each child and tissue type. In our sample, children with maltreatment exposure exhibit lower mean brain centiles across tissues than unexposed children. Associations of greater maltreatment severity with lower brain centiles do not survive correction for multiple comparisons. Lower brain centiles are associated with lower intellectual ability and more behavioural problems. These findings provide evidence for widespread differences in brain structure associated with childhood maltreatment and their relevance to intellectual ability and behavioural functioning.

items.title: Experience affects novel object aversion and the use of human cues in rural and urban American crows
items.abstract: Abstract Population differences in behavior can result from experience, which can be drastically different between environments such as urban and rural areas. Urban areas may be more complex, contain more human-made objects but fewer natural objects, or have more non-threatening people. Consequently, animals in urban and rural populations may differ in neophobia levels, what is novel, and attention to human behavior. We conducted two experiments with a common urban bird, the American crow (Corvus brachyrhynchos). On home territories of urban and rural crow family groups, we presented objects that were either equally novel in both environments or more common in one environment than the other. Separately, we measured flight initiation distance (FID) from an approaching person using either a direct or averted, less threatening gaze for individual crows across an urban gradient. We found that urban crows were more neophobic than rural crows, as measured by the probability of feeding near an object that is equally novel in both environments. There were no differences in approach and feeding latencies for the least neophobic family member. Both urban and rural crows were less averse to objects that were more common in their respective environments. In the FID experiment, crows in highly urbanized areas had FIDs 25 m shorter for an indirect gaze, while rural crow FIDs were unaffected by gaze. FIDs were best predicted by crows’ experiences with people in a relatively large area around each trial. These results highlight how experience must be accounted for when considering population differences in behavior.

items.title: A meaningful framework for change for the Police
items.abstract: Background This PhD project evolved from MSc research by the author into stressors in a UK police force. The findings from both the MSc study and existing literature suggested that the UK police need a new way to support their officers and staff in reducing psychological distress. This led the author to want to create a Meaningful Framework for Change, moving the police from being reactive to psychological distress to being proactive and preventative. Aim and Research Question This PhD project aimed to develop a Framework for Change within a specific UK police force to determine its feasibility and identify what might be required to achieve this goal. In this sense, the PhD project is somewhat untraditional, as the author is an applied psychologist and the work is hands-on and practical, involving support methods that are to be tried and tested within the pilot force. Methods Due to its applied and practical nature, the author was embedded with the pilot police force, and the most logical method for this project was to be autoethnographical in its approach. The thesis is subsequently written in the first person and is less traditional than the reader may be used to seeing. Results/Findings The findings showed that it is possible to design a Meaningful Framework for Change for a police force, introducing new methods of supporting officers and staff. The Framework for Change was partially achieved, with some elements still to be developed by the end of the project. Conclusion Although the project was successful, it took longer than the usual three years of full-time PhD study because of COVID delays. However, from a cultural change perspective, the extra time was beneficial in securing the organisational uptake that made a difference for officers and staff, providing a new and meaningful way to support them.

items.title: Developing a multisensory smell retraining programme
items.abstract: Olfactory training (OT) is a well-established intervention for enhancing smell function, but questions remain about the mechanisms underpinning its effectiveness and the features that optimise outcomes. This thesis investigates how factors such as odour pleasantness, training duration, subjective experiences, and multisensory integration contribute to OT efficacy, drawing on both quantitative and qualitative approaches. A systematic review of the OT literature revealed that improvements in olfactory function are influenced by elements such as training duration, odour selection, and adherence. However, the review also highlighted substantial methodological variation across studies, underscoring the need for more standardised and theory-driven approaches. To facilitate experimental control over odour valence in subsequent work, a stimulus set of pleasant and unpleasant odours was developed and validated through hedonic ratings, enabling precise manipulation of this dimension. Building on these foundations, a 16-week longitudinal OT study was conducted with participants with and without olfactory dysfunction who trained using a set of pleasant, unpleasant, or mixed odours. Results indicated that olfactory function improved over time regardless of odour valence, suggesting that a longer training duration may be more influential than odour pleasantness in driving improvement. To better understand the lived experience of individuals undergoing olfactory training, a qualitative study explored participants’ perceptions, and revealed four key themes: lived experiences of olfactory dysfunction; OT challenges; noticeable changes in olfactory function; and training techniques and strategies employed to facilitate training. Finally, a short-term study tested whether visual-olfactory congruency could enhance training effects over a one-week period. No significant gains were observed, indicating that brief multisensory training may be insufficient without longer engagement or additional support. Together, these findings advance understanding of how OT works, highlighting the importance of duration, baseline ability, subjective engagement, and adherence. The work contributes to the development of more effective, personalised OT interventions, particularly for use in clinical settings with individuals experiencing olfactory loss.

items.title: How Australian fire and rescue service personnel would like to improve their decision-making learning and training programs
items.abstract: Effective management of the response to an incident or emergency event is critically dependent on the decision-making skills of incident and emergency management (IEM) personnel. In a series of workshops conducted in 2022 by Natural Hazards Research Australia, priorities were identified that specified future needs for the practice and training of IEM decision-making. The research in this paper contributes to the understanding of how to address these priorities by considering the views of a sample of fire and rescue service personnel about their agency’s current decision-making training program and aspects to improve. This paper provides findings from 34 semi-structured interviews with fire and rescue services personnel in Australia. The sample comprised 29 men and 5 women. Participants worked in rural fire services (n=17), urban fire services (n=9) and State Emergency Services (n=8). The findings suggest that there is need for greater training focus on emergency management decision-making, greater use of exercise-based training activities, a formal approach to mentoring and coaching staff development programs and mandatory refresher courses and review exercises to maintain incident management skills. Australian fire and rescue services agencies need to ensure they are taking a strategic and holistic approach to emergency management learning and development programs.

items.title: Analyzing one’s own and others’ errors in 360° video-based virtual reality: an exploratory pilot study in swiss vocational healthcare training
items.abstract: Abstract Video-based reflection can help learners recognize procedural errors and develop prevention strategies. 360° video-based virtual reality (360°VR) is increasingly used for error analysis, especially in tertiary education, because it can depict authentic professional situations with a high degree of physical realism. However, little is known about whether analyzing one’s own errors differs from analyzing a peer’s errors in 360°VR and about how vocational learners respond to this task. Using a two-condition between-groups design, this pilot study compared two approaches to error analysis in 360°VR: healthcare assistant apprentices analyzed either their own venipuncture procedure (SELF; n = 16) or a peer’s procedure (PEER; n = 17). Outcomes included error-analysis performance, sense of presence, epistemic emotions, motivation, and perceived cognitive demand. Between-group differences were analyzed using Mann–Whitney U tests. SELF participants reported a higher sense of presence and perceived usefulness, but also greater anxiety. Although SELF participants rated the error-analysis task as easier than PEER participants did, performance did not differ detectably and was low in both conditions, suggesting that the task may have been difficult for apprentices. The substantially greater effort required to produce individualized SELF recordings was therefore not matched by any detectable gain in error-analysis performance. Future research should examine whether differences between SELF and PEER observation in 360°VR vary with expertise, guidance, and error salience.

items.title: The Influence of Self-Esteem and Gender on Judgments of Sociosexuality and Romantic Desirability in a Hypothetical Dating Context
items.abstract: In forming first impressions of others, people may notice and attend to cues about the others’ self-esteem, argued to function as a “proxy trait” that can influence inferences of other traits, including relationship desirability (Cameron et al., 2016 ). Our study provided a further test of this lay theory of self-esteem by examining how information about a hypothetical person’s self-esteem not only affects participants’ judgments of the romantic desirability of the target (from a third person perspective), but also estimates of the target’s sociosexuality (degree of being restricted vs. unrestricted in sexual attitudes and behaviors). Using a vignette experimental design, we manipulated the self-esteem (low or high) and gender (man or woman) of a hypothetical target in an online dating profile. Results indicated that a high self-esteem (HSE) target was estimated to be more attractive and desirable to online daters, and also assumed to have higher sociosexuality compared to a low self-esteem (LSE) target. Our study also contributes to the literature on gender stereotypes related to sexuality; a male target was assumed to be more unrestricted in their sociosexuality than a female target. However, the gender of the target did not interact with the self-esteem of the target to affect impressions of targets’ sociosexuality. Beyond extending past research, our results provide implications for interventions in clinical, educational, and relational contexts.

items.title: Khawf, Huzn and Sakinah in Islamic finance
items.abstract: This article analyses the way in which Islamic finance incorporates certain psychological and emotional states known in Islamic thought, namely khawf (fear and apprehension in the face of the unknown future) and huzn (sadness and regret for choices made in the past), within a system of welldefined norms and operational structures. This methodology is compared with that of traditional finance and behavioral finance, stating that the Islamic approach proposes a structurally different solution to economic precariousness. The study adopts a qualitative conceptual methodology that combines Qur'anic textual analysis, regulatory examination of Islamic finance standards issued by the Organization of Accounting and Auditing for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) and the Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB), and contextual analysis of macrofinancial data from international institutions. The focus is on institutional design rather than causal inference. The analysis shows that Islamic finance institutionalizes khawf and huzn as economic constraints through prohibitions of gharar and ribā, risk-sharing, and zakāt. In contrast, conventional finance monetizesfear and regret via debt and risk transfer, while behavioral finance remains primarily descriptive. This article contributes to the literature conceptualizing Islamic finance as a normative institutionalization of behavioral insights and promoting sakinah (tranquillity) as a systemic goal of financial design. The study is conceptual and does not empirically test causal relationships. Selected principles of Islamic finance can inform ethical screening, debt regulation, and financial consumer protection frameworks. By structurally addressing debt-related uncertainty and distress, Islamic finance contributes to financial well-being and social stability

items.title: INTEGRASI NILAI-NILAI BUDAYA LOKAL SUMATERA UTARA DALAM DESAIN PEMBELAJARAN BAHASA INGGRIS BERBASIS KARAKTER
items.abstract: This study aims to develop and evaluate a character-based English language instructional design that integrates the local cultural values of North Sumatra to improve students’ English proficiency and multicultural character. The approach incorporates the traditions and local wisdom of ethnic groups, including the Batak, Malay, Nias, and Karo, to strengthen linguistic competence while fostering cultural awareness and identity. It also seeks to prepare graduates who are globally competitive and remain rooted in their local cultural heritage. The study employed a quantitative approach with a quasi-experimental nonequivalent control group pretest–posttest design. It was conducted during the fifth semester of the 2026/2027 academic year in the English Literature Study Program, Faculty of Literature, Universitas Islam Sumatera Utara (UISU). The sample consisted of 72 undergraduate students, with 36 assigned to the experimental group and 36 to the control group. The experimental group received local culture-based instruction, whereas the control group received conventional instruction. The instruments measured English proficiency through locally relevant cultural content and multicultural character across four dimensions: cultural awareness, appreciation of diversity, cross-cultural empathy, and cultural identity. Data were analyzed using multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) and normalized gain (N-gain). The results indicated significant improvements in English proficiency (F = 29.47, p < .001, d = 0.94) and multicultural character (F = 34.82, p < .001, d = 1.07). The N-gain scores were 0.68 for English proficiency and 0.71 for multicultural character. These findings support integrating North Sumatra’s local cultural values into character-based English language instruction.

items.title: Land-based search and rescue training: evolution and simplification
items.abstract: Land-based search and rescue training in Aotearoa New Zealand has undergone substantial change, yet there has been limited examination of how these changes have affected the analytical foundations of search management. This review was undertaken to identify what concepts, tools and competencies have been retained, modified or lost in the Managing Land Search Operations course that evolved into Manage the Initial Response and Extended Search Planning. Using 8 analytical domains and a continuity scoring approach, this longitudinal review examined the evolution of 3 core courses. Findings indicate improvements in operational rhythm, interoperability, safety and alignment with the country’s Coordinated Incident Management System. However, these gains are accompanied by a reduction in analytical depth, probability-based reasoning and decision traceability. Key frameworks, including the Probability of Success equation and the Bike Wheel model, have been simplified without clear justification. This review concludes with recommendations to restore analytical foundations and strengthen evidence-based decision-making within the search and rescue training system.

items.title: SUPRIATNOKO’S FIVE-FINGERS TECHNIQUE MODEL: INNOVATION IN ENGLISH GRAMMAR LEARNING TO IMPROVE INDONESIAN STUDENTS’ COMMUNICATIVE COMPETENCE
items.abstract: Mastery of grammar, especially English tenses, is a fundamental component in developing effective communication skills among Indonesian EFL students. However, in practice, tenses remain one of the most challenging aspects for students across educational levels to comprehend and apply. Despite the wide range of instructional methods available, tense instruction in Indonesian classrooms still predominantly emphasizes formula memorization rather than functional use in real communication. Consequently, students tend to forget grammatical rules easily, struggle to apply tenses flexibly, and experience low confidence in speaking and writing. This study aims to (1) develop the Supriatnoko Five-Finger Technique Model as an innovative instructional framework for teaching English tenses, (2) examine its theoretical foundations in embodied learning and communicative language teaching, and (3) evaluate its preliminary effectiveness in improving students’ functional use of tenses in speaking and writing. The study employed a research and development (R&D) design combined with a limited pilot implementation. The development phase included conceptual design, model formulation, and instructional material preparation. The pilot implementation involved classroom application at Sekolah Terbuka Madani Depok using a quasi-experimental approach with comparative observation of students’ performance before and after the intervention. Data were collected through speaking and writing assessments, classroom observation, and student feedback questionnaires. The Supriatnoko Five-Finger Technique Model is a visual and kinesthetics’ instructional approach that maps five major English tense categories—present, past, future, perfect, and continuous—onto the five fingers of the hand. Each finger is associated with a distinct communicative question type: WH-questions, Yes/No questions, Negative tag questions, Positive tag questions, and Assumption questions. The novelty of this study lies in its integration of embodied learning, functional tense categorization, and communicative question-based interaction into a single instruction model that operationalizes grammatical tenses to support functional language use, rather than focusing on vocabulary acquisition or classroom commands. Preliminary findings indicate that 97.4% of students demonstrated measurable improvement in their speaking and writing performance compared to conventional teaching methods. Although promising, the model requires further large-scale testing and refinement across diverse secondary and language training contexts to ensure broader applicability and effectiveness.

items.title: Individual differences and grade-related changes in sensitivity to the statistical structure of word forms in a shallow writing system
items.abstract: Abstract The present study investigates a principal mechanism underlying reading development and individual differences in reading skills, namely sensitivity to orthotactic regularities in lexical processing. This sensitivity can be seen as a reflection of statistical learning (SL), as it pertains to accumulated experience with statistical regularities in print. However, empirical evidence regarding the link between such sensitivity and reading skills remains mixed, and it is particularly unclear what role it plays in orthographically shallow languages. The present study addressed this issue by assessing sensitivity to orthotactic regularities in Finnish pseudowords using a lexical decision task, and examining how this sensitivity depends on vocabulary skill and grade by comparing students from grades 3, 4, and 7 ( N = 818). We identified distinct differences between grade levels, with the orthotactic sensitivity effect being significantly stronger in higher grade levels. Furthermore, we observed substantial within-grade individual differences, with higher vocabulary proficiency predicting greater effects of orthotactic regularities in pseudowords. These findings demonstrate a link between sensitivity to orthotactic constraints and linguistic skills. Importantly, our findings indicate that sensitivity to statistical information is critical even in markedly shallow orthographies, challenging earlier literature. We discuss the implications of our findings for SL views of reading. We also discuss whether sensitivity to regularity exists at the level of orthotactics, phonotactics, or both, given that in the shallow writing system of Finnish the distinction between these levels is blurred.

items.title: Delusions and Compelling Experiences
items.abstract: Abstract Delusion is one of the most puzzling doxastic phenomena: on the one hand, the subject appears irrational, holding a delusion despite counterevidence; on the other hand, the subject appears otherwise rational, apportioning their non-delusional beliefs to the evidence. Leading theories of delusion, despite their strengths, still face notable limitations. This article argues that they may benefit from a new empiricist approach. Drawing on insights from Hobbes and Locke, it proposes that the subject may have a distinctive kind of compelling experience that is phenomenologically analogous to, and can effectively be more compelling than, the Cartesian ‘clear experience’. How the experience may, in various ways and to varying degrees, compel domain-specific irrational belief in the face of counterevidence will be articulated.

items.title: ASSESSING THAILAND’S COMMUNITY CRAB BANKS THROUGH INTERNATIONAL CRITERIA FOR SUSTAINABLE MARINE CONSERVATION
items.abstract: This qualitative study evaluates Thailand’s Blue Swimming Crab Bank Expansion Project against five international criteria for sustainable community-based conservation: measurable ecological impact, community participation, scientific credibility, knowledge transfer, and policy alignment. To overcome the persistent limitations of purely narrative assessments, the research systematically triangulates empirical evidence from official operational reports, rigorous peer-reviewed publications, and external international endorsements. The findings show that the project aligns with all five multidimensional criteria. Notably, the initiative transformed local fishers into active co-managers, established fifty-two dynamic learning centers, and demonstrably increased juvenile crab survival rates from one percent to between forty and sixty percent. Furthermore, this robust integration of community empowerment and scientifically verifiable ecosystem recovery contributed directly to upgrading Thailand’s Fishery Improvement Project status from level C to level A. Ultimately, the study argues that international-standard success in marine conservation emerges not from a single isolated factor, but from these five dimensions mutually reinforcing one another. By utilizing this rigorous criterion-based assessment, the framework provides funding agencies and policymakers with a highly replicable, evidence-based tool for designing sustainable natural resource management globally.

items.title: Integrative approach reveals hidden diversity in the Brachionus (Rotifera, Monogononta)
items.abstract: The phylum Rotifera has many species complexes that require integrative analyses to resolve their taxonomic identity. Brachionus angularis comprises different morphotypes. In Aguascalientes, Mexico, we observed two of these morphotypes coexisting. To explore their species identity, we applied an integrative approach that combined taxonomical, ecological, and molecular data. Our results demonstrate taxonomic differentiation in the lengths of females, males, and diapausing eggs between the two morphotypes. We also observed distinct hatching patterns and clearly different ornamentation in diapausing eggs between the two morphotypes. Genetic variation between one monoclonal culture of each morphotype revealed distances of 18.8% for mitochondrial COI and 13.73% for nuclear ITS1 regions. These marked, concordant divergences in mitochondrial and nuclear markers across the closely related Brachionus species, together with diagnostic morphological and ecological differences, support the recognition of the two morphotypes as distinct species. Accordingly, we describe Brachionus agsensis sp. nov. and Brachionus hydrocalidensis sp. nov. as new species.

items.title: Fine-scale characterization of dispersed-village landscapes: data challenges and methodological advances for rural landscape mapping and assessment in Pomerania, Poland
items.abstract: Abstract Dispersed-village landscapes in Pomerania are shaped by local environmental conditions and long-term farming practices, yet standard spatial datasets generalize many fine-scale landscape elements. In this pilot study, we developed and tested a fine-scale mapping and assessment approach at the 64-ha Knyki-1 reference site using a custom 3-level land-use/land-cover (LULC) scheme, an uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV)-derived digital surface model (DSM), field mapping, plant-cover inventories, and GIS analysis. We compared custom mapping with CORINE Land Cover (CLC) and the Topographic Objects Database (BDOT10k) using landscape- and class-level metrics. At the Knyki-1 site, standard datasets strongly generalized or omitted small patches, linear elements, woody structures, and structural transition zones that may correspond to ecotonal structures. The custom mapping represented 21 LULC classes and 148 patches, versus 2–6 classes and 6–28 patches in the standard datasets, showing how dataset choice affects landscape representation and structural inference. Field inventories documented ancient-forest indicators, archaeophytes, and protected vascular-plant taxa across multiple landscape components. The resulting fine-scale baseline may support future repeated monitoring and, after multi-site validation, regional landscape assessment, conservation planning, and management. These natural–cultural rural landscapes remain absent from national landscape classifications and are increasingly vulnerable to pressures from the abandonment of traditional agriculture.

items.title: Population consolidation and head-starting as demographic rescue of a low-density gopher tortoise population
items.abstract: Context Gopher tortoises, Gopherus polyphemus, are a keystone species of south-eastern North America due to their historically high density, grazing habits, and the burrows that they maintain across upland landscapes. Many gopher tortoise populations are demographically non-viable due to low population density and/or population size. Management for this species frequently utilize measures such as translocation and head-starting. Aims Between 2020 and 2024, we used short-distance translocation to consolidate a low-density resident population of gopher tortoises and monitored spatial biology and apparent survival in the translocated animals immediately following translocation. We also conducted head-starting of tortoises collected as eggs from the same site and manipulated head-start release conditions to test whether soft- versus hard-release affected apparent survival. Methods We tracked both wild and head-started tortoises via radiotelemetry for 1 year during and 1 year after penning; we determined apparent survival by direct observation of individuals remaining alive and within the site approximately 1.5 years after all enclosure pens had been removed. Key results Home ranges of free-ranging tortoises were approximately the same in the enclosure pen as they were after the enclosure pen was removed, but apparent survival of free-ranging tortoises at the study site was only 56% after the enclosure was removed. Male adult tortoises had higher apparent survival in the site than did females, and translocation distance was a negative predictor of apparent survival. Release condition did not affect head-started tortoise apparent survival, and overall apparent survival of head-started tortoises was 70% 2 years after release. Conclusions Head-starting and direct hard release of juveniles are likely to be successful tools for gopher tortoise conservation, whereas population consolidation may cause poor adult survival and/or site fidelity. Implications Short-distance translocations of wildlife populations should be further studied before this tool is more broadly applied in conservation projects.

items.title: Contrasting responses to climate change in two Dianthus species of the Irano-Anatolian biodiversity hotspot
items.abstract: The Irano-Anatolian biodiversity hotspot harbors exceptional plant richness and endemism but faces severe threats from climate change. I used MaxEnt-based ecological niche models to evaluate the current and future distributions of two closely related species, Dianthus floribundus and Dianthus szowitsianus . Models were projected for mid-century (2041–2070) and late-century (2071–2100) under SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios. Temperature-related predictors, particularly annual mean temperature (bio1) and temperature seasonality (bio4), were the dominant drivers, yet the species showed markedly different responses to future climates. D. floribundus , characterized by a narrow thermal niche, is predicted to undergo severe habitat contraction (up to 60%) and pronounced elevational and latitudinal shifts toward northern high-elevation refugia, consistent with the “escalator to extinction” paradigm for cold-adapted mountain taxa. In contrast, D. szowitsianus displayed a broader modeled climatic suitability, maintaining most of its core range while expanding into newly suitable habitats, with projected gains exceeding 50%. These asymmetric outcomes highlight the species-specific nature of climate change impacts even among closely related endemics and forecast a decoupling of historical assemblages, with potential consequences for montane community structure and species interactions. Moreover, the reduction of overlap between the two species and the limited representation of persistent habitats within current protected areas underscore the urgent need for forward-looking conservation strategies. My findings emphasize that conserving montane biodiversity in global hotspots requires species-focused vulnerability assessments, identification of future refugia, and adaptive management frameworks to mitigate differential risks and preserve endemic diversity under climate change.

items.title: Standardizing freshwater macroinvertebrate taxonomy: a Lithuanian operational taxa list for ecological quality assessments and biodiversity research
items.abstract: Taxonomic discrepancies pose a significant barrier to national data synthesis and accurate biomonitoring reporting. We compiled a standardized operational taxa list of freshwater macroinvertebrates known to occur in Lithuania, with the goal of improving comparability and ecological quality assessment reliability of biomonitoring data. A national list of freshwater macroinvertebrates was created by synthesizing literature and biomonitoring data. We standardized the synthesized taxa list according to contemporary nomenclature and integrated ecological and genetic information for each species. Using a rule-based approach, we assigned operational taxonomic units to each validated taxon according to the taxonomic level required within each of the Lithuanian river macroinvertebrate index’s constituent metrics. We tested the impact of operational taxonomic unit assignment on the calculation of ecological quality using national biomonitoring data from 401 sites (931 samples) collected between 2014 and 2022. Three out of four tested metrics were practically indistinguishable from the originally reported ecological status values, with the final ecological status classes matching in 91.4% of samples. For the fourth metric, which encompasses the proportional contributions of Malacostraca (formerly Crustacea), we found taxonomic inconsistencies in originally reported results, with recalculated values for this metric being consistently lower. Our findings indicate that Lithuania’s current ecological assessment method is not adversely sensitive to changes in taxonomic resolution, even when standardization led to a 61.3% reduction of taxonomic richness across all groups of macroinvertebrates. The present study is a step toward more reliable and consistent biomonitoring in Lithuania, especially with the anticipated uptake of DNA-based monitoring methods.

items.title: Resistance to capitalist-oriented agrarian development: A case study of the “Matigsalug” in Mindanao, Philippines
items.abstract: For generations, “Matigsalug” traditional farming has been the foundation of sustainable development in their ancestral domain, sustaining livelihoods, preserving cultural traditions, and nurturing ecological wisdom in their farmlands. This study examines “Matigsalug” resistance to capitalist-oriented agrarian development, as evidenced by the proliferation of the Green Revolution in their farmlands. This qualitative study adopted a case study design combined with Indigenous methodologies, drawing on practices such as storytelling, visiting, and sharing circles to foreground participants’ self-determination, autonomy, and identity throughout the research process. The theoretical framework of Green Marxism was also used to critically analyze the voices, choices, and agency of the “Matigsalug” in their quest for indigeneity in their farmlands. The critical perspectives on “Matigsalug” farmland are as follows: (1) capitalist disempowerment of traditional farmers; (2) dependence on Westernized forms of development through the Green Revolution; (3) displacement due to unsustainable modern farming; (4) resistance to capitalist-oriented agricultural practices; (5) resistance through regenerative agriculture; and (6) resistance through the rejection of the Green Revolution. This study contributes to an understanding of the provenance of the “Matigsalug” ontology, epistemology, and axiology, enabling a deeper evaluation of reciprocity and relationality with the land. The indigenous worldview of the “Matigsalug” also conveys the cultural and emotional significance of their interactions with the environment, through which they develop meaning and identity. The study sheds light on the complex interplay among negotiated ecological spaces, traditional narratives, memories, and values associated with their farmland, offering valuable critical insights into their relationship with the land.

items.title: Practical Tools for Fire Risk Assessment in Mediterranean Open Woodlands Using Handheld Laser Scanning and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Photogrammetry
items.abstract: Abstract Mediterranean forests are becoming increasingly vulnerable to wildfires. Given this, there is an urgent need for accurate, high-resolution data on canopy fuel characteristics to facilitate fire behavior modeling and guide risk mitigation efforts. This study assesses the performance of handheld mobile laser scanning (HMLS) and low-cost unmanned aerial vehicle digital aerial photogrammetry (UAV-DAP) in estimating key canopy fuel parameters and stand structural attributes, including canopy base height, stand height, canopy fuel load, canopy bulk density, and canopy cover. Field data were collected from 12 circular plots in open woodlands ( dehesas ) dominated by Quercus suber or Quercus ilex in the southwest of the Iberian Peninsula. Each plot was surveyed using traditional forest inventory, HMLS with a GeoSLAM ZEB Horizon scanner, and UAV DAP with RGB imagery processed using structure-from-motion techniques. In both cases, the resulting point clouds were processed using LiDAR360 software to extract canopy fuel parameters. HMLS yielded the most accurate estimates for most variables, with relative root mean square error (RMSE%) values ranging from 4% for canopy fuel load to 23.3% for canopy base height. UAV DAP showed a wider range of RMSE% values, from 5.9% for stand height to 41.2% for canopy bulk density, and was notably less effective for variables that require the characterization of subcanopy structure, such as canopy fuel load and canopy bulk density. These findings suggest that HMLS is a reliable and efficient tool for under-canopy data acquisition for small-scale forest managers to assess fire risk and provide reference data for high resolution fuel mapping, while UAV DAP may be a viable option for managers operating in areas that are difficult to access or require low-cost inventories.

items.title: Enabling fire-safe gardens: a case study from Greater Hobart
items.abstract: Garden management plays a crucial role in reducing bushfire risk at the wildland-urban interface, yet implementation of fire-safe practices remains challenging. An analysis of garden assessments and in-depth interviews with 23 property owners in Greater Hobart, Tasmania, examined how technical, social and emotional factors influence garden bushfire adaptation decisions. Using the Cynefin framework and complexity theory, this study demonstrates that successful adaptation addresses multiple domains of complexity, from straightforward vegetation management to complex socio-emotional attachments to garden spaces. Findings reveal that while personalised garden assessment reports can motivate change, their success depends on a broader set of conditions. Barriers include practical constraints (e.g. green waste management), emotional attachments to garden elements and difficulties obtaining context-specific guidance. By applying the As Low As Reasonably Practicable (ALARP) principle, this study identified cost-effective interventions across the 4 avenues of institutional support and resource management, individual garden bushfire adaptation, personalised technical guidance and community support networks. This research suggests that creating fire-adapted gardens requires coordinated support systems that address both practical implementation challenges and emotional connections to garden spaces.

items.title: Evidence of Birgus latro (Linnaeus, 1767) population in Surigao del Sur, Mindanao, Philippines
items.abstract: The general distribution pattern of coconut crab or Birgus latro (Linnaeus, 1767) shows patchy and insular populations which are influenced by ecological needs and human pressures. Historical records in the Philippines, including global occurrence databases (GBIF 2026) indicate a handful of intermittent sightings of the species in the country. The research note documents a newly recorded population of the B. latro in Surigao del Sur, Mindanao, Philippines. Random field surveys and interviews with key informants conducted from October 2024 to April 2025 confirmed the presence of individuals of B. latro in three different coastal and islet limestone, ultramafic forests in Surigao del Sur, indicating evidence of a population of the species. This record expands the known population and distribution of B. latro in Mindanao, where previous reports suggest a discontinuous national distribution, extending to southern Sulu and Batanes on the Northern Pacific coast and island regions. The finding is significant for both scientific inquiry and conservation, given the vulnerable status of the species within its known population and distribution range in the country. The confirmed population in Surigao del Sur represents an important record that fills the gap in the occurrence and distribution of B. latro on the Pacific seaboard of Mindanao, Philippines, which could serve as a basis for localized species and habitat management.

items.title: Species of the genus Gibberula Swainson, 1840 (Gastropoda: Cystiscidae) from Namibia
items.abstract: The marine gastropod fauna off Namibia (SW Africa) has hardly been explored. The current study on species of the genus Gibberula Swainson, 1840 is part of an inventory of marine gastropods from Namibia. Four species are described as new, all endemic to Namibia: Gibberula oshishani sp. nov., G. evukule sp. nov., G. ehodhi sp. nov., and G. heyali sp. nov. One additional species was also known from South Africa: G. cf. bensoni (Reeve, 1865). None of the species known from Angola was found in Namibia. Apparently, the Kunene River delta forms a biogeographical dividing line for species of Gibberula (and many others).

items.title: How Changes in Elephant-Handling Practices Shape Human Perceptions of Their Wild Conspecifics
items.abstract: Opportunities for direct experience with wildlife shape human perceptions and behaviors, influencing human-environment relationships. These perceptions vary across communities according to lived experiences and the assessed costs and benefits of living with wildlife. In a changing global context, a “perception-practice loop” emerges, where shifts in local practices directly affect attitudes toward wildlife. This study uses a mixed-methods approach - combining qualitative and statistical analysis of semi-structured interviews - to examine how evolving elephant handling practices in Laos influence direct interactions with and perceptions of wild elephants. Our findings indicate that owners adapt their strategies to diverse socio-ecological contexts driven by recent global pressures. These practices, often grounded in reciprocity, shape perceptions and levels of tolerance toward wild individuals. The results indicate that tolerance depends less on aggressive elephant behavior and more on the perceived balance of costs and benefits. While wild elephants impose psychological or delayed burdens, they also provide tangible and symbolic benefits, such as mating opportunities and conservation value. We conclude that fostering reciprocal relationships and integrating traditional knowledge can enhance human-wildlife coexistence, supporting both biodiversity and local well-being.

items.title: Dear Sloane: a letter to my granddaughter
items.abstract: Milestones in life invite reflection on the past and consideration of the future. At retirement, I reached a troubling conclusion: I had played a part in a largely unsuccessful effort to protect coral reefs (particularly in the Western Atlantic, where most of my career played out) from decades of stressors driven or intensified by human development and exploitation. Those of us responsible for management did not do enough to control them, and reefs paid the price. An apology to my granddaughter is an admission that my dream career ultimately left her generation with less than it deserves. But is all lost, or can we recover from past mistakes, use what we’ve learned, and help restore biodiversity and ecological function to the world’s reefs? We know the causes of decline, and we have decades of coral reef science and management experience to guide us. We also have powerful new technologies, and an ally in Nature 1 itself, which has a remarkable capacity to recover when stressors are reduced. Restoration of Nassau grouper populations in the Cayman Islands provides a compelling example. And a few coral reefs remain in remarkably good condition. By protecting them, we can learn what works, use them as benchmarks for restoration elsewhere, and demonstrate what remains possible under current environmental conditions.

items.title: Nano‐Biochar‐Assisted Intercropping Alleviates Fusarium Wilt of Faba Bean by Enhancing Rhizosphere Soil Health in Long‐Term Continuous Cropping Soil
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Long‐term faba bean ( Vicia faba L.) monocropping degrades soil and promotes Fusarium wilt. Intercropping and nano‐biochar (N‐BC) can improve soil health and suppress soil‐borne diseases. However, their combined effects on Fusarium wilt in faba bean remain unclear. This study assessed whether combining intercropping with N‐BC could improve faba bean rhizosphere soil health and reduce Fusarium wilt under prolonged continuous cropping. A pot experiment was conducted to compare faba bean monocropping with faba bean–wheat intercropping under an unamended control, biochar (BC), and N‐BC treatments. Fusarium wilt incidence and rhizosphere physicochemical and biological properties were assessed. Intercropping reduced disease incidence and disease index by 8.57%–34.53% and 8.32%–30.20%, respectively. Under intercropping, BC reduced these measures by 14.95% and 15.17% compared with the control. N‐BC further reduced them by 50.02% and 54.74% compared with BC. The combined treatment increased soil water content, macroaggregate proportion, organic matter, dissolved organic carbon, ammonium nitrogen, nitrate nitrogen, available phosphorus, sucrase, urease, neutral phosphatase, catalase, and polyphenol oxidase. It decreased bulk density and benzoic, cinnamic, p‐hydroxybenzoic, ferulic, and vanillic acids. These changes coincided with higher relative abundances of potentially beneficial bacteria, including Pseudomonas , and a lower relative abundance of Fusarium . Combining faba bean – wheat intercropping with N‐BC amendment mitigated Fusarium wilt while improving rhizosphere soil structure, nutrient status, and enzyme activity, reducing phenolic acid accumulation, and reshaping microbial composition. These findings support a soil‐health‐based strategy for sustainable continuous cropping management.

items.title: Abyssal Cretaceous Varicolored Clays of the Northern Apennines of Italy: mineralogical, geochemical and paleontological insights
items.abstract: Abstract. The deep seafloor is one of Earth’s least observed environments and modern abyssal plains remain difficult to investigate directly. Here we present an integrated mineralogical, geochemical and paleontological study of the Cassio Varicolored Shales (AVV) of the Northern Apennines, interpreted as Cretaceous deep-marine deposits accumulated below the CCD and later incorporated into an accretionary prism. Although the analyzed shales share a broadly clay-rich composition, they record distinct diagenetic pathways controlled by redox conditions, organic matter availability, sediment input and pore-water circulation. Red shales represent an oxidized, organic-poor abyssal clay end-member, while black shales preserve Mn-carbonate trace fossils and tabular crusts formed through early Mn cycling, microbial organic matter degradation and rhodochrosite-rich carbonate precipitation. The three-dimensional preservation of pellet-rich burrows suggests rapid early cementation linked to macrofaunal activity and microbial Mn reduction. Gray-green shale records a carbonate-rich system influenced by sulphate reduction, with early calcite veins preserving pyrite framboids and carbon filaments. Overall, the AVV provides an ancient analogue for the small-scale heterogeneity of modern abyssal plains and shows how benthic activity, microbial metabolism, redox cycling and authigenic mineralization can be preserved in ancient deep-sea sediments.

items.title: BOERHAVIA DIFFUSA: A POLYPHARMACOLOGICAL HERB BRIDGING ETHNOMEDICINE AND MODERN THERAPEUTICS
items.abstract: As per WHO reports, around 70-80% of people residing in developing nations rely upon herbal medicines as a source for their health care needs.There are countless medicinal plants that have been used throughout the world, but one of them is Boerhavia diffusa L., which belongs to family Nyctaginaceae.Its common name is Punarnava, and it is considered as a medicinal plant.Boerhavia is named after Dutch botanist and physician Hermann Boerhaave.The meaning of Punarnava in Sanskrit is "renewed again" (Punar=again, Nava=new).Among the total number of about 40 species of Boerhaavia, six species are found in India, that include Boerhaavia diffusa, B. erecta, B. repanda, B. chinensis, B. hirsuta, and B. rubicunda.Boerhaavia diffusa is referred to as Punarnava, and it grows in two types: namely, Rakta Punarnava (red type) and Shweta Punarnava (white type).It holds great medicinal importance due to its high content of phytochemicals and nutritional constituents.It is composed of various bioactive substances, for instance, 15 amino acids in the whole plant (six being essential amino acids) and 14 amino acids in the roots (seven of them being essential).Furthermore, it includes fatty acids and their derivatives such as isopalmitate acetate, behenic acid, arachidic acid (6.3%) along with other saturated fatty acids (around 38%).The use of medicinal herbs is known since antiquity and is practiced for disease prevention and treatment.A lot of knowledge regarding medicinal herbs was gained from indigenous communities.Boerhaavia diffusa (Punarnava) is a medicinal herb and has gained popularity in the traditional medical system for the treatment of many chronic and metabolic diseases.It contains a good number of secondary metabolites such as alkaloids (punarnavine), flavonoids, rotenoids, lignans, steroids, and glycosides.It is used in Ayurveda, Unani, and Siddha for the management of its diuretic, nephroprotective, cardioprotective, hepatoprotective, anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, antimicrobial, antioxidant, and anticancer inflammation.Another point covered by the review is the present use of B. diffusa and its presence in some of the commercially sold medicinal products.The increasing significance of the herb in healthcare practice today has been emphasized.

items.title: Assessing threats to freshwater ecosystems: implications for water security management in Spain
items.abstract: Human threats to freshwater ecosystems overall compromise water security, and identifying these threats is essential to set up the required strategies in managing water resources. The article focuses on Spain as the region of study since this country maintains a long-lasting conflict between the use of water resources and the impacts on freshwater ecosystems. Spain has a double-sided water reality, both in spatial (dry Mediterranean versus humid Atlantic ecoregions) and in temporal terms (interannual climate variability). Up to 30 threats for freshwater ecosystems have been identified and prioritized after a deliberative process composed by three main methodological stages aimed at (I) documenting, (II) screening, and (III) assessing based on academics and water managers perspectives. Climate and land use change are the highest-ranked threats, while pollution is ranked lower. Overall, quantity issues lead to concern among both the experts and Júcar River Basin managers, whereas quality-centred threats displayed discrepancies between the two perspectives. These observed discrepancies between academic and managerial priorities underscore the challenges of operationalizing Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM), highlighting the need for enhanced knowledge co-creation in water governance. Thus, this twofold assessment, as a co-creation and prioritization exercise, establishes a new knowledge co-creation approach and represents a potential framework in designing strategies for assuring freshwater ecosystem preservation as a foundation for water security.

items.title: Performance Evaluation and Late Blight Reaction of Advanced Potato Genotypes for Yield and Quality Traits in Bekoji, Southeastern Ethiopia
items.abstract: The research aimed to assess potato genotypes that possess high yield and tuber quality characteristics and yield traits. The study was arranged by randomized complete block design with three replications and was executed at the Bekoji substation during the main cropping seasons of 2022 and 2023. The results revealed that all the traits except days emergence showed significant differences among the genotypes. The genotypes varied for dry matter content, specific gravity, and total starch content, which ranged from 18.32% to 23.66%, 1.07 to 1.097 g/cm^3^, and 12.03% to 17.08%, respectively. The genotype CIP315009. 71 had the highest specific gravity, dry matter content, and total starch content. The four advanced clones CIP315003.132, CIP315008.30, CIP315009.71, and CIP315004.61 produced a total tuber yield that exceeded the released variety, Burka. The identified genotypes may provide useful breeding material for improving yield and processing-related tuber quality.

items.title: Effects of functionally diverse seed mixtures on dry matter yield and forage quality of a central European grassland
items.abstract: The debate on balancing agricultural production and biodiversity conservation has intensified in response to increasing global livestock production and more intensive grassland use. This is because productive grasslands show high yield but low species diversity. Increasing the forage quality by improving low-diversity grasslands may be an option to combine agricultural needs with biodiversity promotion. Reseeding species-poor swards with legumes and non-legume forbs has become feasible with the increasing commercial availability of native seeds. Thus, functionally diverse mixtures should be developed and tested, since there is little knowledge on the establishment of such species and their effects on yield and forage quality. Therefore, we designed four legume and forb-rich seed mixtures (‘toppings’) and tested them in combination with two standard grass-based agricultural mixtures (‘grass mixtures’) during a four-year mesocosm experiment that simulated agricultural management through cutting and fertilizing. Plant establishment, dry matter yield, metabolizable energy (ME) as a measure of forage quality, and functional diversity (richness, divergence, evenness) were recorded every year. We further asked whether season (spring, summer, autumn) moderates the effects of community composition and functional structure on dry matter yield and forage quality. The experiment showed that season was the dominant source of variation in both dry matter yield and ME. Dry matter yield decreased with increasing cover of legumes and forbs, while harvest season was the dominant driver of productivity, with the highest yields in spring and the lowest in autumn. Metabolizable energy of pooled samples for each topping × grass-mix combination tended to increase with legume-forb cover, whereas the effects of functional diversity were inconsistent and depended on mixture composition and harvest season. Nine of 13 introduced species established, with Trifolium pratense , Galium album , Lotus corniculatus , and Plantago lanceolata being most abundant, identifying them as candidates for further field evaluation rather than immediate large-scale recommendation.

items.title: Regulation penetrating the countryside and the persistence of habitus: governance tensions and smallholder practices in the modernisation of the Enshi tea industry
items.abstract: This study examines a characteristic agricultural industry in an ethnic minority region of southwestern Hubei, China, exploring the structural tensions between state-led agricultural modernisation and the practices of smallholder farmers. Drawing on fieldwork conducted in Enshi City in 2023–2024, including semi-structured interviews with actors across the tea value chain and analysis of local gazetteers, policy documents and heritage archives, the study examines how GI standardisation is negotiated in cultivation, processing and marketing. The findings show that local governments have sought to incorporate traditional tea production into a modern governance framework through geographical indication certification, the standardisation of intangible cultural heritage techniques and the integration of production and marketing networks. These measures have aimed to construct a public branding regime centred on “varietal purity” and “technological orthodoxy,” embedding local tea production within a framework of institutional rationality. Drawing on their adaptive knowledge of mountainous ecologies, however, tea farmers have developed forms of selective compliance to standardised governance. These include mixed cultivation of local tea varieties, flexible adjustments to processing techniques and the reconstruction of rural relational networks. In cultivation, farmers retain local varieties to mitigate market risks and manage seasonal labour demands. In processing, they rely on embodied knowledge, making tea according to leaf conditions rather than mechanised parameters. In distribution, they preserve market flexibility through informal transaction practices, including relationship-based pre-sales and customised private-domain marketing. The study reveals that state-led policy penetration has improved short-term economic returns through brand premiums and industrial integration. Yet, by overlooking the role of local knowledge in ecological adaptation and cultural transmission, such governance has produced a structural mismatch between institutional provision and farmers’ practical needs. The case suggests that agricultural modernisation requires a dynamic balance between technical standardisation and ecological diversity, and between policy rigidity and practical flexibility. Only through adaptive shifts in governance paradigms can regulation and habitus achieve a more sustainable form of co-development.

items.title: Geospatial approaches to mapping invasive alien plants: the neglected role of soil in remote sensing and GIS-based distribution models
items.abstract: Introduction Invasive alien plants (IAPs) pose significant ecological and socio‐economic threats by disrupting native biodiversity, ecosystem functioning, and land productivity, underscoring the need for robust spatial tools to guide management interventions. Using a systematic literature review approach guided by the PRISMA framework, this study examines geospatial techniques for modelling Invasive Alien Plant (IAP) distributions, focusing on how climatic, land use/land cover (LULC), and soil variables are integrated to explain habitat suitability. Methods Across reviewed studies, remote sensing and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) emerged as central tools for multi‐scale monitoring and predictor integration. Medium‐resolution satellite imagery (Sentinel‐2, Landsat) commonly supported regional assessments of vegetation change and land-use dynamics, while very‐high‐resolution imagery enabled finer species‐ and structure-level discrimination, though at greater cost. These data streams were increasingly coupled with machine learning and statistical approaches to improve classification accuracy, though performance remained dependent on input data quality and adequate representation of key environmental drivers. Results A notable methodological imbalance emerged in predictor selection. Among the 24 studies included in the soil‐variable integration analysis, 71% (n = 17) excluded soil variables, relying instead on spectral, thermal, and structural proxies, land surface temperature, and canopy characteristics. Only 29% (n = 7) incorporated measured edaphic variables, such as soil pH, texture, and soil classification, which typically require field integration if observations, soil survey data, and digital soil maps within GIS-based frameworks. Discussion This omission stemmed largely from remote sensing’s inability to directly observe below‐ground properties and the logistical challenges of acquiring spatially explicit soil data. The review suggests that the limited integration of soil variables may constrain the ecological realism of geospatial invasion models, particularly in environmentally heterogeneous landscapes. Greater integration of soil, climate and LULC frameworks has the potential to improve ecological realism and predictive capability and warrant further investigation, particularly in under‐studied regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa.

items.title: Psychological Well-Being among Fisher Women: A PRISMABased Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Fisher women (FSW) are major contributors to the coastal economies in fish catching, processing, marketing and management of household affairs.Although they make significant socioeconomic contributions, they are disproportionately vulnerable to occupational stress, livelihood insecurity, gender discrimination, climate related disasters and lack of access to health care and social protection, which negatively impact their psychological wellbeing.This is a systematic literature review which aimed to synthesize the existing evidence on the psychological well-being of FSW and the major determinants influencing their mental health and quality of life.The review was carried out as per PRISMA 2020 guidelines.Literature search was carried out in Google scholar, PubMed and Semantic scholar, which resulted in 800 records.After duplicate removal, title and abstract screening, and fulltext eligibility assessment, 100 peer-reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2026 were included in the qualitative synthesis.The results show that the main causes affecting the psychological well-being of FSW are occupational stress, poverty, financial instability, family burden and gender inequality.Emotional distress and livelihood insecurity is also compounded by climate change, coastal disaster, environmental degradation and diminishing fisheries resources.In contrast, factors such as resilience, social support, community engagement, empowerment of women, livelihood diversification, and coping mechanisms emerged as protective factors that promote psychological well-being.The review also points to important areas of research that are currently underdeveloped, such as a lack of standardization of the psychological assessment tools, limited longitudinal studies, and weak incorporation of mental health in fisheries and coastal development policies.To enhance the psychological well-being and quality of life of FSW, there is a need to strengthen gender responsive health policies, occupational safety, community-based resilience programmes and psychosocial support services.There is a need for future interdisciplinary research to produce strong evidence for sustainable and inclusive policy development.
