items.title: Modulating hydrodynamic flow by modifying the active patch of a colloid
items.abstract: We have developed a simulation model to study the hydrodynamic flow fields around Brownian colloidal particles with an active surface patch. Hydrodynamics is introduced by modeling low-Reynolds-number fluid flows around a colloid using multi-particle collision (MPC) dynamics and allowing momentum exchange between the MPC fluid and the colloid. This approach provides good estimates of both near- and far-field flows around the colloid. The size of the active patch is varied to generate different fluid flow fields around the colloid. In this framework, the fluid in the vicinity of the active patch is driven radially away from (or toward) the surface, and an equal and opposite momentum is imparted to the colloid to ensure momentum conservation. The resulting surface-driven flow generates self-propulsion of the particle, thereby converting an otherwise Brownian colloid into an active Brownian particle. Interestingly, as we systematically vary the surface area of the active patch on the colloid, the nature of the generated flow field changes from that of a pusher to a puller. To model such surface activity-driven flows, we developed a hybrid boundary condition that ensures a no-slip condition while incorporating momentum exchange between the flowing fluid and the colloid surface. This scheme integrates the advantages of bounce-back and stochastic boundary conditions while mitigating their respective limitations. Thus, in future studies, the effective hydrodynamic interactions between an active and a passive colloid, or between two active colloids, can be modulated by adjusting the size of the active patch.

items.title: DynaFilter: Cloud-driven Dynamic Filtering for Satellite Edge Intelligence
items.abstract: Modern satellite edge systems, including those performing remote sensing tasks such object detection and tracking, are characterized by severely limited bandwidth and intermittent connections, making continuous data transmission to the cloud impractical. Existing edge-cloud systems, however, either require heavy pre-processing before analysis, for instance, full decompression of imagery data, or transmit all compressed data regardless of relevance. To address these challenges, we design DynaFilter, a dynamic filtering technique that enables satellite edge devices to perform selective region-of-interest (RoI) inference directly in the compressed-domain, without full decompression. Our key insight is that low-level compression syntax, specifically DC coefficients/AC energy in JPEG images and motion vectors in video streams, exhibits strong correlations with high-level semantic queries. By establishing a precise mapping between cloud query semantics and multimodal compressed-domain features, DynaFilter enables the edge to identify and transmit only relevant data associated to RoIs. Extensive evaluations show that DynaFilter reduces the total volume of pixel data for decoding and subsequent inference by 1.6x-7.1x for images, and achieves 92.0% bandwidth savings for video streams compared to state-of-the-art baselines. Furthermore, it decreases energy consumption by 43.1-88.6% on target devices and achieves a 1.6x-3.0x speedup in inference latency.

items.title: Causal Discovery in Photospheric Magnetic Field Time Series for Interpretable Solar Flare Prediction
items.abstract: Abstract Deep learning has proven to be a vital advancement in many fields that present difficult classification and prediction tasks. This includes astrophysics, particularly space weather prediction, where accurate modeling has become essential for protecting satellite and ground infrastructure from the impacts of solar flares and solar energetic particle events. Despite their strong predictive ability, one issue with deep learning as a method for space weather prediction is the poor interpretability of these “black box” methods. A possible solution to this comes in the form of a structured deep learning framework named Amortized Causal Discovery (ACD), which aims to enforce an easily interpretable layer in the neural network that represents the causal summary graph. We apply this method to the Space Weather Analytics for Solar Flares dataset, a rich source of multivariate time series (MVTS) data of solar active regions, to demonstrate that high-intensity solar flares can be detected ahead of time by comparing their causal summary graphs with those of other flare events. In this work, we use graph metric statistics as well as objective performance tests against state-of-the-art classifiers to demonstrate the depth of insight that ACD can produce into differences between MVTS samples in the context of solar flare prediction.

items.title: LeanStream: A Speculate-and-Refine Streaming Framework for Efficient on-Device LLM Inference
items.abstract: On-device LLM inference is attractive for privacy and responsiveness, but remains challenging on mobile and embedded devices because model weights far exceed available DRAM. Prior systems exploit activation sparsity and offload weights to SSD or flash storage, but face a fundamental systems trade-off: accurate sparse execution decisions require the latest context, whereas efficient computation-I/O overlap requires early prediction. As a result, existing designs either serialize execution or incur redundant weight fetches, extra computation, and large cache overheads. We present LeanStream, a streaming speculate-and-refine framework for efficient on-device LLM inference. LeanStream progressively refines computation, loading, and cache-retention priorities using partial GPU results, enabling fine-grained overlap between GPU execution and storage I/O. We implement LeanStream on both mobile and embedded platforms. Compared with prior on-device LLM inference systems, LeanStream reduces memory usage by 4.8$\times$ to 7.5$\times$ at the best throughput achieved by prior work, while further improving token generation throughput by 1.6$\times$ to 2.1$\times$.

items.title: SOVABIDS: EEG-to-BIDS conversion software focused on automation, reproducibility and interoperability
items.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) recordings are stored in many vendor-specific formats and lab-specific folder structures, making them difficult to organize, share, or compare across studies.SOVABIDS is an open-source tool that converts EEG data into the Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) (Gorgolewski et al., 2016), a standard that promotes FAIR data practices (Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reusability).Rather than manually renaming files or writing dataset-specific scripts, users define conversion rules in human-readable YAML configuration files, which SOVABIDS applies across the dataset (Figure 1).It can be used as a Python package, a command-line tool, or an experimental terminal user interface (TUI), and its API supports integration with graphical frontends.Documentation and tutorials are available at sovabids.readthedocs.io.

items.title: Task load and phase relevance modulate primary flight display change blindness: evidence from flight simulator, eye-tracking, and fNIRS.
items.abstract: Change blindness (CB) during Primary Flight Display (PFD) monitoring threatens aviation safety, yet the roles of flight phase and parameter relevance remain unclear. This study examined cognitive-neural correlates of PFD change blindness in experienced commercial pilots. Experiment 1 (N = 14) found change location had no influence on detection performance but demonstrated a three‑way interaction among task load, flight phase and parameter type. Under high load, pilots detected attitude and descent rate more accurately during landing, and speed and altitude more accurately during cruise. Experiment 2 (N = 34) focused on landing with an auditory-load PFD change-detection task. High-relevance parameters boosted detection accuracy under high load alongside longer fixations. Enhanced Superior Parietal Lobule (SPL)/Inferior Parietal Lobule (IPL) activation and modulated dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dLPFC) activity correlated with reduced CB under high load. Findings indicate task load and phase relevance jointly shape PFD monitoring performance.

items.title: Informal Caregivers' Administration of Opiate, Benzodiazepine, and Antipsychotic Medications to Home Hospice Patients Experiencing Hyperactive Delirium in the Last Week of Life.
items.abstract: PurposeWhile hospice-prescribed comfort medications are used to manage hyperactive delirium (HD), the relationship between caregivers' administration of these medications and HD is not well established, especially for patients receiving care in home settings.MethodsA retrospective chart review was conducted on medication records of home-hospice patients (N = 19) experiencing HD in the last week of life. Medication use included scheduled and prn medications administered and converted to opiate, benzodiazepine, and antipsychotics dose equivalencies. A binomial generalized linear model predicting HD incidents by dose equivalencies and time from death was followed by Spearman correlation lag analyses to characterize associations between HD and medications.ResultsThere were 2016 documented medication administrations and 133 HD incidents in the last week of life. After adjusting for covariation in measurements by patient, no medication class was a strong, independent predictor of HD. Opioid dose had a significant but modest positive association with HD incidents, but trends varied across patients. Shift-level lag analyses revealed HD episodes correlated with opioid and benzodiazepine doses in subsequent shifts more so than with doses in prior shifts, but neither lag transformation correlated more strongly than concurrent shift dose administration and HD.ConclusionsThe results highlight the intensity of pharmacologic management informal caregivers can face when managing HD in the last week without clinical staff on site. None of the 3 drug classes studied showed an inverse relationship to HD, raising questions about the efficacy of these medications for managing HD at the very end-of-life.

items.title: Public mental health: The case and required actions across the European region.
items.abstract: Despite the existence of effective public mental health (PMH) interventions, only a minority across the European region receive treatment for mental health conditions (MHCs). Even fewer receive interventions to prevent MHC-associated impacts, with negligible coverage of interventions to prevent MHCs, or promote mental well-being and resilience. Various reasons account for implementation failure which breaches the right to health and results in population scale preventable suffering, broad impacts and associated economic costs. Public mental health involves a population approach to improve coverage, outcomes and coordination of PMH interventions. Required actions to scale up PMH implementation include effectively making the case through assessment of PMH need, highlighting economic impacts of PMH implementation failure and improved coverage, and coordinated advocacy and leadership. Public mental health practice involves the use of PMH needs assessment to inform choice of interventions, policy development, and required coverage and resources for effective PMH intervention delivery by different sectors. This is supported by the collection of PMH-relevant data. Further actions to scale up PMH implementation include adopting human rights-based approaches and legislation, PMH training to different sectors and improved population PMH literacy, maximizing existing resources, settings-based and integrated approaches, use of digital technology, prioritizing interventions with large population impact, and implementation-focused research. Scaled up PMH implementation results in broad population impacts, achievement of a range of policy objectives, sustainable reduction in impacts of MHCs and promotion of mental well-being across the population of the European region. Associated economic savings also make PMH practice an essential part of sustainable economic development.

items.title: Spatial Memory Guides Attention before Object Recognition: Evidence from Lateralized N1pc Responses.
items.abstract: Visual search is facilitated when targets reappear within invariant distractor layouts (contextual cueing). Although contextual cueing can bias attention within 150 msec, it remains unclear whether this guidance relies on global spatial configuration or requires object identity. We recorded ERPs while participants searched for targets in repeated versus novel arrays. Critically, each trial began with a placeholder display that conveyed only spatial configuration, preceding the search display by 500 msec. Following learning, targets were relocated and swapped their locations with a distractor in the opposite visual field, such that the overall search layouts remained unchanged. ERPs time-locked to placeholder onset revealed an early poster contralateral negativity (N1pc, 140-160 msec) for repeated contexts, despite the absence of target-specific object information. After relocation, this effect reversed polarity, indicating persistent orienting to the learned target location. A second N1pc, followed by N2pc and CDA, emerged only after search onset. These findings show that learned spatial structure rapidly guides attention, whereas effective selection requires additional processing of object information.

items.title: Confounds in Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging-Part II: Modifiers.
items.abstract: In the first part of this three-part series, we reviewed the mechanisms that cause nuisance signals in fMRI data. Here, in the second part of the series, we review "human factors" that modulate these confounding mechanisms. The modulators may be trait characteristics such as age or bodyweight, or they may be state dependencies that alter the relative contributions of nuisance signals in the fMRI data. A wide array of psychological (e.g., motivation/arousal, cognitive strategy, task engagement), lifestyle (e.g., exercise, sleep, and dietary habits), experimental (e.g., scanner anxiety, task-related movement), and situational (e.g., prandial state, time of day, menses) factors can affect the brain state directly as well as via changes in systemic physiology mediated by autonomic nervous responses.

items.title: Confounds in Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging-Part I: Mechanisms.
items.abstract: In this review, the first in a three-part series, we consider the origins of confounding in fMRI. We review the signal properties of an fMRI experiment and the intended sensitivity to neurovascular coupling, the hemodynamic response function, and the spatial-temporal biases imposed by the heterogeneous anatomy of the vascular system. We then explore the various mechanisms that can leave nuisance signals, often termed physiologic noise, in fMRI data. All mechanisms having a biological dependence are considered, including mechanical effects from head motion and respiration, blood gases, brain motion from the cardiac pressure wave, blood pressure, and scanner instabilities that couple with the participant's body.

items.title: Ultra high-density, 4096-channel intraoperative neurophysiological brain mapping for functional localization of the human central sulcus.
items.abstract: Objective. Intraoperative localization of the central sulcus (CS) using somatosensory evoked-potential (SSEP) phase reversal (PR) is routinely performed with sparse subdural strip electrodes. We evaluated whether a multi-array, 4096-channel surface micro-electrocorticography ( μ ECoG) configuration could provide dense two-dimensional sampling of stimulus-dependent sensorimotor responses within a standard neurosurgical workflow. Approach. Four Precision Neuroscience Layer 7 μ ECoG arrays (1024 platinum electrodes per array on a flexible polyimide substrate, 400 μ m electrode pitch, ∼1.5 cm 2 active area per array) were deployed during resection of a right parafalcine meningioma in a 56-year-old male. Two arrays were placed horizontally on the exposed precentral gyrus; two were inserted under the intact dura overlying the postcentral gyrus, using a custom flexible stylet. Somatosensory evoked potentials (SSEPs) were recorded across five contralateral stimulation conditions (median nerve, ulnar nerve, index finger, middle finger, ring finger). Per-electrode SSEP responses were classified without anatomical labels, and spatial organization was quantified across stimulation conditions. Stimulus-locked high-gamma activity, digit-response maps, and signal quality across micro- and macroelectrodes were also evaluated. Main results. Aggregate channel yield was 91.3% (3739/4096) at a 2 MΩ impedance criterion (per-array range 86.7%-97.0%). Per-electrode amplitude maps resolved continuous phase-reversal contours with stimulus-specific spatial structure; reversal latencies were 19, 21, 25, 26, and 25 ms for median, ulnar, index, middle, and ring stimulation respectively. PR occurred within a single array in eight of ten sensory-array recordings, with the phase-reversal pattern varying across stimulation conditions. Digit responses showed measurable spatial differentiation within substantially overlapping response fields. Automated classification of the phase-reversal responses recovered the expected motor and sensory organization, consistent with the standard-of-care intraoperative localization performed in the same case. Significance. The deployment shows that a four-array Layer 7 μ ECoG configuration can be used within a standard neurosurgical exposure and provides dense two-dimensional sampling of stimulus-dependent phase-reversal patterns across the peri-Rolandic recording field. The measured responses were correlated across approximately 3-4 mm of cortex, an order of magnitude coarser than the 400 μ m electrode pitch, so the contribution demonstrated here is dense spatial sampling rather than submillimeter physiological resolution. Dense sampling rendered the polarity transition as a continuous two-dimensional boundary across the recording field rather than as a reversal between two adjacent contacts. The platform supports future evaluation of high-density surface μ ECoG for intraoperative mapping and chronic brain-computer interface applications.

items.title: Assessing the Effects of Hurricane Hazards on Hospitalization or Death Among Older Adults Using Electricity-Dependent Medical Devices.
items.abstract: Background To evaluate short-term effects of Hurricanes Matthew (2016) and Florence (2018) on hospitalization or death among older adults using electricity-dependent durable medical equipment (edDME) in North Carolina, and to assess how hurricane exposure definitions influence associations. Methods We conducted controlled interrupted time series analyses using NC Medicare data (2015-2019). Monthly cohorts of beneficiaries aged ≥ 65 years with recent edDME use were classified as hurricane-exposed or unexposed using FEMA county-level disaster declarations. Exploratory analyses applied North Carolina Flood Extent Archive (FLDEX) to define exposure by residential flooding thresholds. The primary outcome was 30-day all cause hospitalization or death. ARIMA models estimated immediate level changes and sustained trends, including race-stratified analysis. Results Using FEMA definitions, we observed no significant immediate changes following either hurricane, but a sustained increase in hospitalization or death after Hurricane Matthew. FLDEX-based analyses showed stronger and more consistent exposure-outcome associations, particularly at higher flooding thresholds and among Black beneficiaries. Conclusions Coarse FEMA disaster designations may obscure important dose-dependent and racially patterned health effects of hurricanes. Higher-resolution exposure metrics may improve disaster surveillance and targeting of preparedness resources for medically vulnerable populations.

items.title: Natural products shape microbial ecology and disease in the cystic fibrosis airway.
items.abstract: Covering up to 2026Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a life-shortening autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutation in the gene encoding the CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR). Dysfunction in CFTR leads to the accumulation of thick and dehydrated mucus in the respiratory tract, which serves as a substrate for a complex microbiota that includes commensal oral and respiratory bacteria and opportunistic pathogenic bacteria and fungi. During chronic infections, these microbes persist in the airways and contribute to progressive lung tissue damage, ultimately leading to respiratory failure and premature death. Within this environment, microbes synthesize a diverse repertoire of natural products, including antimicrobials, siderophores and other metallophores, signaling molecules, toxins, and other virulence factors. In this review, we thoroughly discuss natural products produced by members of the CF airway microbiota, primarily the bacterial pathogens Burkholderia spp., Pseudomonas aeruginosa , and Staphylococcus aureus and the fungal pathogens Aspergillus fumigatus and Scedosporium spp. When known, we describe the biosynthesis and roles of these natural products in microbial persistence, interspecies interactions, and virulence in the CF airway. When these roles are unknown, we infer potential roles based on evidence from the literature in different disease contexts. Finally, we briefly highlight natural products produced by the CF microbiota as novel sources for developing new antimicrobials and as drug targets to treat disease.

items.title: Women Among Top-Cited Scientists: Authorship Patterns, Career Length and Disciplinary Distribution in the 2025 Single-Year Citation Database
items.abstract: Background: Women are a minority among highly cited scientists, and it is unclear how those who reach this group differ from men. Methods: We analyzed 159,112 authors in the 2025 single-year database of top-2% scientists whose gender could be inferred from first names (21.1% women). Women and men were compared within Science-Metrix fields using fixed-effects regression, adjusting for career length, publication volume and first-publication cohort. Results: Women were concentrated in Public Health, Social Sciences and Psychology and scarce in Mathematics, Physics and Engineering (dissimilarity index 0.21). Within fields, women had careers 4.4 years shorter, 24% fewer papers, a lower share of single-authored papers (−1.4 percentage points; absent in the first decade of careers and growing thereafter) and less often multi-country careers. Citations per paper were higher, but total citations did not differ after adjustment, and composite scores gave no general evidence that women faced a higher selection bar. Self-citation did not differ; first- and last-author differences disappeared with career stage. Conclusions: Within the top group, differences mostly reflect cohort, volume and field, with a persistent single-authorship gap. Findings are cross-sectional and rely on inferred gender.

items.title: A critical implementation gap in suicide prevention in oncology: Systematic review and content framework of training programs for healthcare professionals.
items.abstract: Cancer patients face elevated risk of suicidality, yet suicide prevention remains inconsistently implemented in oncology care. Training healthcare professionals is widely recommended, but it is unclear whether existing programs address oncology-specific needs. In this pre-registered review (PROSPERO-ID: CRD42023393187), we systematically searched PubMed/Medline, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science. Oncology reports were examined closely using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. A qualitative content-analysis synthesized training contents. Of 6,526 reports identified; 351 met inclusion criteria, including 202 programs in healthcare settings. Only eight addressed oncology, just two fulfilled nearly all quality criteria. Most programs were evaluated (84.16%). Content-analysis of 129 studies focused on assessment, risk management, and intervention/referral strategies. Professionals' development and theoretical knowledge dominated, ethics and standard procedures appeared less often. While structured suicide prevention training exists in general healthcare, oncology remains largely unintegrated. This synthesis provides a framework that may inform adaptation and implementation.

items.title: Implicit Prejudice Differentially Predicts Placement Into Valuable and Scarce Opportunities.
items.abstract: Racial excellence gaps persist, partly due to unequal participation in advanced learning opportunities. Guided by the opportunity hoarding framework, this research investigates whether White Americans' pro-White/anti-Black prejudice differentially predict simulated Advanced Placement (AP) course admission decisions, and under what conditions-when the opportunity is valuable, scarce, or both. Across two experiments, we observed an unexpected overall pattern in which Black students were placed into higher priority tiers than White students. Nonetheless, greater implicit prejudice predicted larger White-Black differences in placement decisions, explained by placing Black students into lower tiers rather than White students into higher tiers. Critically, we found preliminary evidence that this pattern emerges only when AP participation was described as both valuable and scarce. Explicit prejudice showed less consistent associations with differences in placement decisions across studies. The valuable and scarce nature of advanced learning opportunities may amplify the effect of implicit prejudice in deciding who deserves access.

items.title: Less Is More: Why and When Having Less Signals Competence.
items.abstract: Living with less has become increasingly popular in contemporary culture. It can simplify people's lives and enhance their well-being. Beyond these intrapersonal benefits, we document a novel, interpersonal benefit of having less: individuals who own fewer possessions are perceived as more competent than those who own more. This effect arises because observers infer that they rely more on reasoning rather than feelings in decision-making. We further develop a three-condition descriptive model specifying that the effect emerges when having fewer possessions appears voluntary, when the possessions are primarily non-hedonic, and when the quantity of possessions is sufficient to meet minimum needs. This research extends the literature on the benefits of having less from an intrapersonal to an interpersonal perspective and identifies possession quantity as a new cue for perceived competence.

items.title: Between-case incidence rate ratio for single case experimental designs with count outcomes: A Monte Carlo simulation with conditional and marginal models.
items.abstract: Calculating design-comparable effect sizes in single-case experimental designs (SCEDs) is essential for research synthesis to identify evidence-based practices that integrate findings from both SCEDs and group-based designs. The field has made significant progress in developing additive design-comparable effect sizes in recent years. This study aims to evaluate the statistical properties of a newly developed proportional estimator, the between-case incidence rate ratio (BC-IRR), for SCEDs with count outcomes. Two analytical frameworks are introduced for estimating BC-IRR: generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) and generalized estimating equations (GEEs). A large-scale Monte Carlo simulation is conducted to assess the bias of the point estimate, the standard error bias, mean squared error, and coverage rate. We also demonstrate the estimation of BC-IRR using GLMMs and GEEs with real data. Based on the simulation and demonstration results, we provide recommendations for applied researchers, discuss limitations, and outline directions for future research.

items.title: Germany's Verschickungskinder: parent-child separation and mental health.
items.abstract: Background: Parent-child separations have been associated with adverse health and well-being, with most research focusing on prolonged separations driven by war, famine or disease. Verschickungskinder ('sent-away children') - the eight to twelve million German children who, in the decades following World War II, were separated from their families for several weeks to stay in so-called children's health resorts - represent a largely overlooked case of short-term separation. Despite growing recognition of adverse experiences and abuse in these settings, little is known about the long-term mental health of this population or which characteristics of the sent-away experience are associated with these outcomes. Objective: To examine whether sent-away children show more depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, and stress overload compared with peers, and to identify which characteristics of the sent-away experience are associated with these outcomes. Method: An anonymous online survey was conducted with 334 sent-away children and 77 participants in a convenience comparison group ( M = 61.1 yrs.; 72.7% female). Linear regression models, adjusting for ACEs and sociodemographics, examined group differences and associations between characteristics of the sent-away experience (age at separation, sex, number of separations, emotional memory) and these outcomes. Results: Sent-away children reported more depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, and stress overload than comparison participants (all p p = .02) and anxiety symptoms ( p = .009). Conclusions: Findings highlight the potential long-term mental health relevance of the sent-away experience, particularly among those with very negative memories of their experiences.

items.title: Adolescents' positive and negative reactions to participation in trauma-focused research and their associations with PTSD and complex PTSD.
items.abstract: Background: Previous studies have investigated the levels of distress reported by children and adolescents while participating in trauma-focused research. However, the role of complex PTSD in responses to participation in trauma-focused research is unknown. The aim of the study was to investigate adolescents' positive and negative reactions to trauma-focused research and their associations with lifetime trauma exposure, PTSD, and complex PTSD. Methods: The sample comprised 834 school-based adolescents (40.9% boys), aged 13-18 years ( M = 16.17, SD = 1.34) from the general population. Lifetime trauma exposure was measured using the Child and Adolescent Trauma Screen (CATS); PTSD and complex PTSD were measured with the Child and Adolescent version of the International Trauma Questionnaire (ITQ-CA). Positive and negative responses to research were measured with the short version of the Reactions to Research Participation Questionnaire for Children (RRPQ-C). Results: Most adolescents reported neutral or positive reactions to participation: 73.4% did not feel upset or sad, 81.4% did not regret participating, 34.3% reported being glad about participating, and 61.0% felt good about helping. 6.6% reported feeling upset. Lifetime trauma exposure was reported by 74.5% of participants ( M = 2.18, SD = 2.18); 6.8% met criteria for PTSD, and 13.1% for complex PTSD. Lifetime trauma exposure, PTSD, and complex PTSD were associated with feeling upset or sad, as well as being glad to participate. PTSD increased the odds of negative reactions to research 2.07 times, and complex PTSD 5.78 times. On the other hand, 42.2% of those with complex PTSD reported being glad they had participated. Conclusions: Adolescents generally responded positively to participating in the study. However, complex PTSD was associated with a higher likelihood of research-related distress, highlighting the need for tailored safety and risk protocols for adolescents with complex PTSD.

items.title: Athletes and Medical Staff in Elite Contact Sports: a Quantitative Analysis of Use, Knowledge, and Attitudes Regarding Cannabinoids.
items.abstract: Background Cannabis use among elite contact sport athletes increases with legal reform and commercial availability. Limited education in cannabinoid pharmacology, use, and risk persists among athletes and medical staff, fostering stigma and reducing evidence-based guidance and communication. Hypothesis Athletes use cannabis but perceive stigma and discomfort discussing cannabis with medical staff. Study design Quantitative, descriptive cross-sectional surveys. Level of evidence Level 4. Methods Two anonymous online surveys were administered to elite and professional contact sport athletes (Canada, United States, Australia) and medical and training staff (February 2023 to July 2024). Descriptive statistics assessed demographics, use patterns, knowledge, education needs, attitudes, stigma, communication, and league policies. Results A total of 166 athletes (89.7% male, 35.2% aged 18-23 years) and 64 medical staff (physicians, athletic therapists, strength and conditioning coaches, etc) responded. Knowledge (pharmacology, interactions, dosing) was low. Overall, 56% of athletes currently used cannabinoids (81% having ever used), but only 21.7% knew the endocannabinoid system and 67.4% were unfamiliar with therapeutic dosing. Among medical staff, 59.5% were unfamiliar with mechanisms, only 14% were familiar with dosing protocols, and 71.4% lacked confidence in making treatment plans. Of the athletes, 86.5% believed cannabis had therapeutic value, 72.3% wanted education, and 74.1% favored qualified scientists as instructors. Of the medical staff, 79.5% reported strong educational need, with 100% of staff desiring athlete-specific cannabinoid education. Stigma and communication barriers were substantial: 81.3% of athletes perceived public stigma, 66.1% perceived staff stigma, and only 21.4% felt comfortable discussing cannabis with medical staff. Staff believed athletes would be honest if approached; however, Conclusion Athletes and medical staff exhibit parallel knowledge gaps and strong educational needs amid high interest, use, and significant communication barriers. Evidence-informed education and stigma-reducing strategies are urgently needed. Clinical relevance Athletes increasingly use cannabinoids for pain, sleep, and recovery, while medical staff report insufficient training and low confidence. System-level education, communication, and policy updates may improve safety, decision-making, and trust.

items.title: NMR-Based Structural Elucidation of a New Dihydroisocoumarin and Related Polyketides From a Mangrove-Derived Fusarium sp.
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) remains one of the greatest global public health challenges of the 21st century, compromising the effectiveness of current therapies and highlighting the urgent need for new antibacterial agents. Natural products from bacteria and filamentous fungi continue to represent an invaluable source of structurally diverse bioactive metabolites. In this study, a library of 56 extracts obtained from mangrove-associated ascomycetes was screened against a panel of multidrug-resistant bacterial pathogens. Bioactivity data were integrated with LC-MS/MS-based molecular networking to prioritize extracts for chemical investigation. This approach identified Fusarium sp. IQ-1921 as one of the most promising candidates, leading to the isolation of a new dihydroisocoumarin (1) and four known analogues (2-5). The structures of all isolated metabolites were elucidated by 1D and 2D NMR spectroscopy and high-resolution mass spectrometry (HRMS). All compounds were evaluated against multidrug-resistant strains of Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae, and Staphylococcus aureus. Compounds 1 and 3-5 exhibited moderate antibacterial activity, with compound 1 displaying the broadest inhibitory profile. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating metabolomics with bioactivity-guided prioritization for the discovery of antibacterial natural products and further highlight the indispensable role of NMR spectroscopy in the structural elucidation of closely related fungal metabolites.

items.title: It's All in Your Head: A Qualitative Examination of the Help-Seeking Experiences of Women Suffering Postpartum Psychosis.
items.abstract: Background Postpartum psychosis (PPP) is a rare, yet severe, perinatal psychiatric disorder that typically presents abruptly within several days after childbirth and requires urgent in-patient psychiatric care. Despite its severity, postpartum psychosis remains underrepresented in research and can be poorly understood in clinical healthcare settings, particularly regarding the detection of the disorder. Aims This exploratory qualitative analysis examines lived-experience perspectives on help-seeking, including barriers encountered when help-seeking, to develop a clearer understanding of the current pathways to detection and diagnosis of PPP. Design A qualitative study design was used to analyse interview transcripts. Methods Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 15 participants during 2024 which were thematically analysed. Findings Four key themes were identified: (1) recognising the unnameable (women's early insights and difficulties in articulating their experiences and symptoms), (2) invisible until visibly unwell (barriers to recognition of PPP healthcare professionals), (3) speaking without being heard (Frequency of misdiagnosis and lack of thorough medical investigation) and (4) falling through the cracks (the Australian healthcare systems inadequate capacity to support women experiencing PPP). Conclusion Unintentional medical gaslighting, which is the dismissal, reframing or invalidation of symptoms and or patient experiences, was evident through the frequent reframing and dismissal of the women's experiences and led to a disconnect between them and the Australian healthcare system. Misrecognition was evident across multiple dimensions including interpersonally and institutionally. It delayed access to care, fractured relationships and trust within the healthcare system and exacerbated psychological distress. Implications for the profession and/or patient care This study emphasises that enhancing outcomes for women affected by postpartum psychosis requires increased focus within both research and clinical domains, ensuring that maternal distress is accurately identified, comprehended and validated. Impact This study examined the help-seeking experiences of women experiencing postpartum psychosis in Australia. Medical gaslighting and frequent dismissal and reframing of the women's experiences by healthcare professionals were evident, which led to a disconnect between the women and the Australian healthcare system. This disconnect can impact the mother, the infant, the whole family unit by increasing psychological distress, the burden on family members, and disruptions to the mother-infant attachment, and the healthcare systems collectively. It emphasises that research and clinical domains need to focus on ensuring maternal distress is accurately identified, comprehended and validated. Reporting methods This study adhered to the COREQ for reporting interview-based qualitative research. Patient or public contribution This study did not include patient or public involvement in its design, conduct or reporting.

items.title: Habitual tea consumption is associated with lower cardiovascular disease risk.
items.abstract: Background Tea consumption has been associated with vascular health, but evidence regarding multidimensional tea-drinking characteristics and their joint associations with other lifestyle factors remains limited. Objectives To examine associations of multidimensional tea-drinking characteristics with vascular disease (VD) and assess joint associations and interactions with smoking and physical activity (PA). Methods We included 485,934 participants from the China Kadoorie Biobank (CKB). Multivariable Cox models were used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for total VD and 12 subtypes. Dose-response relationships and joint associations and interactions of tea consumption with smoking and PA were evaluated. Results During a mean follow-up of 9.05 years, 14,863 incident VD cases occurred. Habitual tea consumption was associated with lower total VD risk (HR = 0.888, 95%CI 0.857-0.921) and several major cardiovascular and cerebrovascular outcomes. Associations varied by tea-drinking characteristics: Black tea showed more consistent inverse associations than green tea, moderate-strength tea was associated with lower risk, whereas 'burning hot' tea was associated with higher VD risk (HR = 1.160, 95%CI 1.090-1.236). Tea intake showed non-linear dose-response associations, with the lowest estimated risk at approximately 6-8 cups/day among weekly drinkers. The combination of habitual tea consumption, non-smoking and high PA was associated with the lowest VD risk (HR = 0.548, 95%CI 0.492-0.609), with evidence of sub-additive tea-PA interaction. Conclusion Habitual tea consumption was associated with lower VD risk, with associations varying by drinking characteristics and intake level. Tea consumption combined with non-smoking and high PA was associated with the lowest risk. These findings support considering multidimensional tea-drinking and lifestyle patterns in vascular health research.

items.title: Targeted therapy use following Medicare's coverage expansion for next-generation sequencing in older adults with lung cancer.
items.abstract: Purpose To examine whether Medicare's 2018 National Coverage Determination (NCD) for next-generation sequencing (NGS) was associated with changes in the use of targeted oral anticancer therapies among older adults with lung cancer. Methods Retrospective cohort study. Multivariable logistic regression was used to estimate the probability of initiating an oral targeted therapy within 12 months of diagnosis. Key exposures were (1) diagnosis before versus after the NCD and (2) residence in a region with versus without pre-NCD NGS. Data were drawn from the SEER-Medicare linked data with Part D claims, including diagnosis years 2016-2019 with follow-up through 2020. The analytic sample included Medicare fee-for-service Part D beneficiaries aged 65 years or older with newly diagnosed lung cancer. Results Among 30,855 Medicare fee-for-service Part D beneficiaries with lung cancer, 7.1% used targeted oral anticancer therapies. The NCD was not associated with a significant overall change in targeted therapy use (0.4 Percentage Point; 95% CI, -1.6 to 2.4; p = 0.71). Before NCD implementation, targeted therapy use was 1.0 PP higher in regions with pre-NCD NGS coverage than in regions without such coverage (95% CI, 0.2-1.9; p = 0.015). In stage-stratified analyses, the additional post-NCD change was significant among patients with distant-stage disease (3.2 PPs; 95% CI, 2.6-4.0; p Conclusions Medicare's NCD for NGS was not associated with a significant overall increase in targeted oral anticancer therapy use but was associated with increased use among patients with distant-stage disease. items.title: Caring across borders: ageing and digital technology in transnational families.
items.abstract: Background and objectives The rise of transnational families has generated new care arrangements in which migrant children use digital technologies to support ageing parents across borders. While the functional role of digital technologies in facilitating remote care is well documented, their relational and culturally embedded dimensions remain less understood. This review synthesises recent evidence on how digital technologies shape transnational caregiving. Research design and methods Eight electronic sources were systematically searched for studies on transnational families, ageing, digital technology (including artificial intelligence-AI), and care, published between 2020 and 2025. Eligible studies were extracted, coded, and analysed using thematic analysis. Results Fourteen studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the analysis. Five themes were identified: 1) adoption and challenges for transnational ICT-mediated care; 2) ambivalence towards digital intimacy; 3) emotional labour and strategic concealment in transnational family care; 4) cultural norms and moral hierarchies of digital care; 5) structural inequalities in transnational care. Digital technologies both foster connection and amplify separation, serving as symbolic markers of family devotion and tools for managing information across generations. Rather than democratising care, technologies often reinforce existing global North-South, gendered, and class-based inequalities. Discussion and implications Digital technologies both sustain and transform transnational care, yet digitally mediated care remains relational and structurally constrained. Stronger digital inclusion and coordinated cross-border care infrastructures are needed to support ageing transnational families, while avoiding the reproduction of existing social, gendered, and global inequalities, and enabling older adults to age with dignity, connection, and security.

items.title: What Patients See Before They See the Surgeon: Bariatric Surgery on TikTok.
items.abstract: BackgroundTikTok is a rapidly growing audiovisual social media platform and an emerging source of health information, including bariatric surgery content that may influence patients' expectations before consultation with clinicians. This study aimed to characterize the engagement patterns and themes of bariatric surgery-related TikTok videos to inform clinical practice.MethodsA comprehensive search identified the 10 most frequently used bariatric-related hashtags on TikTok. For each, the 10 most liked videos (n = 100) were extracted. Videos were included if they contained English, Spanish, or Portuguese content referencing bariatric surgery. Quantitative engagement metric analysis and qualitative thematic analysis were performed.ResultsMost videos were created by patients (92%) and most creators were female (83%). Content was overwhelmingly positive (79%) and focused primarily on vertical sleeve gastrectomy (61%), with limited representation of alternative procedures. No videos meaningfully discussed risks or differences between surgical options. The most common themes included body image and identity (59%), often with before and after images, and lifestyle adaptation (19%). Educational and promotional content was significantly longer (74.8 seconds, Kruskal-Wallis test: P = 0.002) without a statistically significant difference in engagement.DiscussionBariatric surgery content on TikTok is characterized by patient-generated, visually driven narratives that emphasize transformation and empowerment, with limited discussion of risks or procedural complexity. These findings suggest TikTok may shape narrow perceptions of bariatric surgery for patients. Clinicians should address social media-shaped expectations when counseling patients and use short-form, visually engaging, and patient-partnered content when posting educational content on TikTok to enhance engagement.

items.title: Association of Antihypertensive Medications with Orthostatic Hypotension among OIder Adults.
items.abstract: Background Orthostatic hypotension (OH) is common among older adults actively prescribed hypertension pharmacotherapy. Associations between antihypertensives and OH are inconsistent, due to differences in drug classes and OH assessment protocols. Methods Three supine and six standing blood pressures (BPs) were measured over 6 minutes, timed to initiate immediately (0 minutes) and 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 minutes after standing. OH was defined as a drop of systolic/diastolic BP ≥ 20/10 mmHg upon standing from the supine position. OH phenotypes were initial (immediately after standing), early (within 3 minutes), late (after 3 minutes), and sustained (during 6 minutes of standing). Participants were asked about orthostatic symptoms experienced during OH assessment. We investigated associations of antihypertensive classes with OH phenotypes and orthostatic symptoms via multivariable logistic regression. Results Of 863 participants (mean age 84 years), 41% had initial, 24% early, 18% late, and 17% sustained OH; 81% used antihypertensive medications. First-line antihypertensives (renin angiotensin aldosterone system blockers, dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers, and thiazide diuretics) were not associated with OH or orthostatic symptoms. Among non-first-line, alpha blockers were significantly associated with initial OH (OR 1.80, 95%CI 1.07, 3.01) and orthostatic symptoms during postural change (OR 2.64, 95%CI 1.34, 5.23), whereas combined alpha-beta blockers were significantly associated with early, late, or sustained OH (2.24 [1.15, 4.37], 2.50 [1.21, 5.17], 2.99 [1.41, 6.30], respectively) and experienced symptoms while standing (3.08 [1.10, 8.65]). Conclusions First-line antihypertensives are not associated with OH among older adults, which does not support their discontinuation in the setting of non-neurogenic OH.

items.title: The Magnusian generator for dissipative systems and application to leading 2.5PN radiation-reaction dynamics
items.abstract: A bstract The Magnusian is a phase-space function that generates finite-time evolution through nested Poisson brackets. It is related to several familiar generators of classical dynamics, including the radial action, the eikonal phase and related quantities. In this work, we extend the Magnusian framework to systems with dissipation and nonlocal-in-time interactions using the in-in formalism, also known as the Schwinger-Keldysh or Galley formalism. This framework is particularly natural for binary dynamics, where integrating out the mediating gravitational field can produce both dissipative radiation-reaction effects and hereditary, nonlocal-in-time interactions. We derive the generalized Magnusian and show that it continues to generate finite-time evolution. As an application, we construct the Magnusian for Newtonian bound motion subject to the leading 2.5PN radiation-reaction force. The resulting generator defines a discrete evolution map from one cycle to the next and describes the evolution of the system in agreement with numerical solutions.

items.title: Gate-Based Feature Importance in Simulation-Based Inference for EEG: A Cautionary Tale
items.abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) provides a powerful way to fit mechanistic models to data, but offers little insight into which information in the data shapes the inferred parameter values. It could therefore benefit from robust and inexpensive interpretability methods. Learned weighting mechanisms such as feature gates provide a potential route to low-cost interpretability, although their interpretation assumes that predictive training reveals which inputs drive performance. We examined this assumption in a computational neuroscience setting, where neural posterior estimation (NPE) is used to infer four physiological parameters of a dynamical model of interacting neuronal populations (Jansen-Rit). We tested whether the learned gate weights captured feature importance by comparing them with a retrain-based ablation benchmark, in which each feature was removed in turn and the NPE retrained. We considered two jointly trained gates: independent sigmoid weights and competing softmax weights. If these reliably reflect feature importance, they should align with the ablation-based estimates. Across nine independent training seeds, however, gate-based and ablation-based importance were negatively correlated (Spearman's rho approximately -0.61 for sigmoid gating and -0.56 for softmax gating). The feature that ablation identified as most important, total signal power, was among the features the gate down-weighted most, despite gating costing negligible predictive accuracy. These results extend a pattern previously documented for attention mechanisms in natural language processing and for explainability methods in electroencephalography (EEG) deep learning to the simulation-based inference setting, and suggest caution when interpreting learned gate weights as measures of causal feature importance in scientific machine-learning pipelines.

items.title: The medium is the message: How neurometabolic entanglement generates conscious experience
items.abstract: Most neuroscientific accounts of consciousness assume that conscious experience is constituted by the information conveyed between neurons. The physical-chemical details of the metabolic and physiological processes that convey this information are correspondingly presumed to be relevant only insofar as they support the organization of information processes. We describe an alternative perspective that denies this presumed independence of the processing of neural information and the metabolic-physiological details of these processes. We call this alternative paradigm the theory of neuro-metabolic entanglement (NME). NME proposes that mental experience exemplifies the inseparability of the organization of neural information processes from the constraints imposed by the material-energetic properties of the neural medium itself. Central to this account is a recursive, Möbius-like loop of neural connections that entangles patterns of forebrain information processing with midbrain regulatory systems that modulate forebrain metabolism. This enables patterns of neural activity to indirectly modify the global distribution of metabolic resources underlying these information processes. It also constitutes a bottleneck that integrates diverse neural processes into an adaptively relevant unitary experience organized in terms of the global redistribution of metabolic support. Computational models of neural function cannot treat energy supply as a fixed background parameter; our proposed Möbius-like loop of neuro-metabolic entanglement offers a framework for future models in which neural activity is dynamically and recursively modulated by the network's own metabolism. Recognizing this entanglement is a first step toward dissolving the explanatory gap highlighted by the so-called "hard problem" of consciousness.

items.title: Quasi-Localization of Short-Wavelength Perturbations in Softened Laplace-Lagrange Chains
items.abstract: We examine the long-term evolution of localized eccentricity perturbations in a softened Laplace-Lagrange chain. The secular coupling between mass elements is long-ranged, suggesting that any disturbance imposed at a single radius should disperse rapidly across the chain. We show that this expectation fails once the secular interaction is regularized by a finite softening length $β$: while broad eccentricity profiles propagate smoothly, as textbook secular theory anticipates, narrow profiles remain confined to their launching site for millions of secular periods. The origin of this quasi-localization lies in the dispersion relation of the softened chain. The group velocity of eccentricity waves collapses by orders of magnitude on spatial scales below the softening length, so that narrow perturbations project almost entirely onto a nearly flat sector of the band, where little differential precession is available to disperse them. Propagating the initial wavenumber spectrum through the dispersion relation reproduces the retained fraction of angular momentum deficit across the full range of perturbation widths with no adjustable parameters. The confined perturbation is flanked by an apsidally polarized (oppositely-aligned) response, which we show to be the real-space imprint of this spectral projection. The softening length therefore sets a dynamical scale below which eccentricity perturbations spread only on timescales far longer than the secular period.

items.title: Simulations of a Conducting Sphere Moving through Magnetized Plasma II: Effect of Internal Magnetic Fields and Enhancement of Alfvénic Drag
items.abstract: Magnetic interaction between astrophysical objects can play an important role and produce electromagnetic radiation in various systems, ranging from planet-moon and star-planet systems to binary compact objects. We extend our previous numerical study of an ideal magnetized plasma flowing past a conducting sphere to the case where the sphere is magnetized. Such a flow generates magnetic disturbances and produces a drag force on the sphere. We examine the drag coefficient as a function of the strength and orientation of the conductor's internal magnetic field relative to the background magnetic field. We find that a strong internal magnetic field that is aligned with the background field significantly enhances the drag coefficient compared to the unmagnetized case; this enhancement is related to the increased magnetic flux that connects the conductor and the open, external field region. We also explore how the drag coefficient changes as the flow transitions from the sub-Alfvénic to the super-Alfvénic regime. Our results suggest that magnetic interaction may play a larger role in orbital evolution of some binary systems than previously expected.

items.title: Ellipsoidal Modeling Framework for TNOs: the triaxial shape of (50000) Quaoar and its implications for Weywot and the dynamical environment
items.abstract: The three-dimensional shapes of Trans-Neptunian Objects (TNOs) are notoriously difficult to determine due to their slow orbital motion and minimal variations in aspect angle over human timescales. To overcome this geometric degeneracy, we developed a versatile modeling framework capable of deriving ellipsoidal shapes by simultaneously combining stellar occultations and rotational light curves, including parameterizations of localized surface albedo. We applied this methodology to the large TNO (50000) Quaoar, jointly modeling 37 stellar occultation events and two photometric datasets. Our MCMC analysis demonstrates that Quaoar is best represented by a triaxial shape with equatorial semi-axes $a = 620.7^{+3.3}_{-2.8}$ km and $b = 546.5^{+6.0}_{-5.6}$ km, and a polar semi-axis $c = 511.5^{+5.3}_{-5.5}$ km, yielding a bulk density of $1.663 \pm 0.127$ g cm$^{-3}$. By isolating Quaoar's barycentric motion from the astrometric offsets, we determined the mass of its satellite, Weywot, to be $(1.485 \pm 0.360) \times 10^{18}$ kg, corresponding to a system mass ratio of $q = 0.0012 \pm 0.0003$ and a satellite bulk density of $0.95 \pm 0.60$ g cm$^{-3}$. Furthermore, dynamical simulations using the derived triaxial gravitational field reveal that potential additional satellites can only maintain stable orbits beyond 2.4 Quaoar radii, as inner bodies would be strongly perturbed. Regarding the ring system, particles at the location of the secondary ring (Q2R) location exhibit libration associated with the 5:7 spin-orbit resonance (SOR). Similarly, particles at the location of the main ring (Q1R) location show libration of the 2:6 SOR angle for orbital eccentricities larger than 0.2, providing a plausible mechanism for the azimuthal width variations observed in Q1R.

items.title: The Pandora SmallSat: post-launch operations and mission update
items.abstract: The Pandora SmallSat is a NASA flight project designed to study the atmospheres of exoplanets. Transmission spectroscopy of transiting exoplanets provides our best opportunity to identify the makeup of planetary atmospheres in the coming decade, and is a key science driver for HST and JWST. Stellar photospheric inhomogeneity due to star spots, however, has been shown to contaminate the observed spectra in these high-precision measurements. Pandora will address the problem of stellar contamination by collecting long-duration photometric observations sampled over a stellar rotation period with a visible-light channel and simultaneous spectra with a near-IR channel. These simultaneous multiwavelength observations will constrain star spot covering fractions of exoplanet host stars, enabling star and planet signals to be disentangled in transmission spectra to then reliably determine exoplanet atmosphere compositions. Pandora will observe exoplanets with sizes ranging from Earth-size to Jupiter-size and host stars spanning mid-K to late-M spectral types. Pandora was selected in early 2021 as part of NASA's inaugural Astrophysics Pioneers Program. Herein, we present an overview of the mission, including the science objectives, operations, the observatory, science planning, and upcoming milestones as we prepare for launch readiness in 2025.

items.title: A Technical Reanalysis of the Viking Carbon Assimilation-Pyrolytic Release Experiment
items.abstract: The 1976 Viking Carbon Assimilation-Pyrolytic Release (CAPyR) experiment tested whether carbon from $^{14}$CO$_2$ and $^{14}$CO entered Martian soil during a 120-hour incubation in a form retained during a 120 $^\circ$C purge but released by pyrolysis at 635 $^\circ$C. Untrapped radioactivity was measured as Peak 1; material retained in an organic vapor trap was oxidized and measured as Peak 2. Net Peak 2 was intended to represent synthesized reduced organic carbon. Seven of nine usable incubations at Chryse and Utopia Planitia yielded significant net Peak 2 signals, including the dark U1 run. An underreported Viking Lander 2 gas leak introduces uncertainty into U1-U3. The C1 signal corresponds to approximately 10 or 30 pmol of carbon, assuming derivation entirely from CO or CO$_2$, respectively. We reassess these results in light of the possible presence of perchlorate salts in Viking soils. Oxidation of fixed organic radiocarbon during pyrolysis could have shifted label from Peak 2 to Peak 1, a perchlorate-specific effect not considered in previous CAPyR analyses. Hubbard's (1979) mineral-substrate experiments produced abiotic Peak 2 signals without reproducing the heat sensitivity. No demonstrated abiotic mechanism has reproduced all CAPyR observations under Mars-relevant conditions. The observations remain consistent with a biological carbon-assimilation system whose relevant activity survives C5's 120 $^\circ$C/90 $^\circ$C pretreatment but is strongly impaired by C2's 175 $^\circ$C pretreatment. Together with the Labeled Release experiment, CAPyR suggests oxidative and reductive chemistry in separate aliquots from common Martian soil acquisitions. Metabolically active life combines these processes; a quantitative abiotic explanation of their combined heat-labile response patterns remains to be demonstrated.

items.title: OGLE-2012-BLG-0563: Relative Proper Motion Constraint from Keck Follow-up finds the correct Lens
items.abstract: We present Keck/NIRC2 adaptive optics imaging results of planetary microlensing event OGLE-2012-BLG-0563. We find that the OGLE-2012-BLG-0563L planetary system consists of a 1.12 +/- 0.09 Jupiter-mass planet orbiting a 0.81 +/- 0.04 solar-mass host star at a distance of 5.49 +/- 0.56 kpc from the Sun. This event has a lens-source separation of 23.28 +/- 0.48 mas, which is the smallest lens-source separation measured to date with Keck AO data. We find that the incorrect solution - which identifies the Northeast (NE) star as the source star - is favored if one only considers the discovery paper, the Fukui et al. (2015) solution, or an unconstrained model. However, by performing an image-constrained light curve model fit using the relative proper motion direction constraint from the Keck follow-up data, we demonstrate that the correct solution identifies the NE star as the lens star. The discrepancy in the unconstrained models is driven by systematics in the FTS and MOA B & C data, alongside the impact of the relative proper motion direction constraints. This outcome offers two important lessons for future Roman data analysis: (1) thoroughly verify systematics across all passbands and identify the precise origin of chi-squared differences, and (2) utilize image-constrained light curve modeling incorporating relative proper motion direction constraints to identify the correct lens.

items.title: The physical and chemical structure of Titan's upper atmosphere: energy balance, photochemistry and Jeans escape
items.abstract: Titan's upper atmospheric layers provide a unique opportunity to study how photochemistry, photoionisation, haze microphysics and escape processes shape its atmospheric chemical structure, providing a unique benchmark for understanding these processes in exoplanets. Using a 1D first-principles approach, we extend the Kompot model to simulate Titan's upper atmosphere and investigate its thermal and chemical structure, and Jeans escape. We performed self-consistent simulations of Titan's upper atmosphere, above the dense haze layer, over a 1D radial grid by solving the coupled hydrodynamics, thermal and photochemical kinetic, and energy balance equations. We considered heating by stellar X-ray and ultraviolet (XUV) and infrared (IR) radiation, and cooling due to radiative emission of methane (CH4) and hydrogen cyanide (HCN). We also included additional nineteen photochemical and 117 thermal reactions to Kompot's standard chemical network. Our modelled atmospheric temperature structures lie within the observed variability of Titan's atmospheric temperature profile. Our simulations reproduce observed nitrogen (N2) and CH4 densities in the upper atmosphere, and abundance of minor chemical species also broadly agree with observationally derived abundances. Near the exobase, our CH4 mixing ratio overlap with Cassini-Huygens results, and our model H2 mixing ratios also exhibit broad agreement with observations. Our simulations suggest no significant thermal loss of CH4, even under the conditions of an early Sun's XUV environment.

items.title: The coupled impacts of atmospheric dynamics and cloud microphysics on hot Jupiter atmospheres. I. An application to WASP-43b
items.abstract: Understanding the influence of cloud-circulation feedback on planetary climates is crucial to interpreting solar system and extrasolar planet observations. Hot Jupiter phase curve observations have reported westward optical phase curve offsets and weak absorption features, which may be explained by the presence of clouds. JWST observations have also revealed tentative silicate cloud absorption features in emission and transmission spectroscopy. While a number of 3D atmospheric dynamics models of hot Jupiters and microphysical models describing cloud formation exist, few combine these two approaches. To help elucidate the impact of clouds on hot Jupiters, we introduce a post-processing scheme with the 3D GCM ADAM with SPARC (formerly SPARC/MITgcm), the 1D microphysical cloud model CARMA, and the radiative transfer code PICASO. We first simulate the cloud-free atmosphere of WASP-43b with ADAM, then incorporate resulting thermal profiles into CARMA to simulate WASP-43b's cloud structure, and finally generate phase-dependent emission spectra from our results with PICASO. By comparing to JWST observations, we infer that WASP-43b has a cloudy nightside, a mostly clear morning and evening limb with patchy clouds, and a clear dayside at the level of the photosphere. Our microphysical model predicts the condensation of five cloud species, including silicates, but overestimates the cloud opacity at all phases compared to observations, requiring additional modeling to explain. The results from this post-processing setup are promising for more meaningful characterization of WASP-43b's atmosphere, and will serve as a comparison baseline for our upcoming indirect coupling of both models, as well as for other future studies.

items.title: EXPRESS: How error rates scale with chance rate among dogs following human pointing gestures, and why it matters.
items.abstract: Humans use pointing gestures to communicate with dogs. However, efforts to study how dogs receive this communicative signal have produced ambiguous results. Prior work presenting a choice between two options has shown that dogs choose the pointed-to option at above chance levels, but just barely. With only two options, the high probability of choosing correctly by chance weakens the signal. After replicating the 2-option task, we changed the task's parameters by presenting dogs with six options. We compared two models that make divergent, quantitative predictions on how the success rates will relate on the two tasks. One model stresses that multiplying the options should reduce the number of correct choices made by chance at a higher rate than instances of genuine communication. A second model that involves no understanding of referents, but just a systematic shift in attention, predicts the effect size to remain constant irrespective of the number of options. Dogs chose the location pointed to at barely above chance rates in both the 2-choice and 6-choice tasks. This pattern discourages the view that dogs understand the referential aspect of human pointing. Additional patterns that become visible with more than two options bolster this interpretation. Dogs chose the correct side of the arena and succeeded on second choices disproportionately more often. Dogs succeeded with far and near locations at similar rates. These results challenge the view that dogs interpret human pointing as referring to a specific object, which has implications for claims that point-following evinces intentional capacities among dogs.

items.title: Comparing the coherent point drift algorithm to sliding semilandmark and weighted spherical harmonic whole-bone three-dimensional shape analyses.
items.abstract: The ability to quantify 3D morphologies is critical for anatomical research; however, setting up high-density landmark sets and positioning them on all specimens can represent a substantial challenge. The coherent point drift (CPD) algorithm, a technique for registering two point clouds based on the Gaussian mixture model, was recently used to investigate human variation; however, its performance has yet to be compared to other 3D shape analysis methods. Here we compare the results of a CPD analysis to a sliding semilandmark and weighted spherical harmonic (SPHARM) analysis of the same 60 human and African ape calcanei and a CPD analysis and SPHARM-sliding analysis (a combination SPHARM and sliding semilandmark analysis) of 40 primate third manual proximal phalanges (mPP3s) to determine methodological comparability. Additionally, we run a CPD analysis on a small but wide-ranging sample of primate ulnae to demonstrate its utility for proximodistally long and mediolaterally narrow long bones. All specimens were surface or micro-CT scanned. All calcanei were subjected to a CPD analysis with 2000 semilandmarks, a sliding semilandmark analysis with 1007 semilandmarks, and a SPHARM analysis. All mPP3s underwent a CPD analysis with 2500 semilandmarks and a SPHARM-sliding analysis with 2562 semilandmarks. For the ulna, a CPD analysis with 1252 semilandmarks was run. Shape variation for all analyses was summarized using (separate) principal component analyses (PCAs). Results of the respective analyses for the calcaneus and mPP3 were compared by calculating the maximum and root mean square distances (RMSD) between average taxon shape configurations (scaled based on centroid size) generated from each analysis. All three calcaneus analyses separate taxa along the first two PCs, with humans separating from African apes along PC1 and chimpanzees and gorillas separating across PC2. For the two mPP3 analyses, the three great ape taxa consistently separate along PC1, and Papio separates from the other taxa along PC2. The average RMSD between CPD and sliding semilandmark analyses for the calcaneus was 0.24 mm, and 0.21 mm between CPD and SPHARM analyses. For the mPP3, the average RMSD between CPD and SPHARM-sliding was 0.14 mm. These results indicate that CPD is a comparable 3D shape analysis method to these other approaches. The CPD analysis was also able to place a semilandmark set on primate ulnae ranging from gorillas to tarsiers and capture morphological variations including shaft curvature, relative olecranon process length, and overall robusticity. CPD analyses are less time intensive than sliding semilandmark analyses; however, the sliding semilandmark analysis was better able to capture variation surrounding the borders of the articular facets (although differences were relatively minor), suggesting that these analyses may be better suited when the researcher is interested in a specific anatomical feature. CPD did capture edges better than SPHARM analyses; however, this is likely not an issue for small, relatively round bones such as carpals and most tarsals. In sum, CPD produces similar results to sliding semilandmark, SPHARM, and SPHARM-sliding approaches and has benefits for analyses of long bones with complex morphologies or among taxa that exhibit large amounts of morphological variation.

items.title: Architecture of the Norrin signaling complex and structure-guided surrogate design.
items.abstract: Norrin binds Frizzled 4 (FZD 4 ), tetraspanin 12 (TSPAN12) and low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 5 (LRP5) to regulate angiogenesis and the integrity of the blood-brain barrier and inner blood-retina barrier (BRB). Aberrant Norrin signal causes retinopathies, BRB defects and deafness. Therapeutic mimetics of Norrin are currently in clinical trials for eye diseases. To characterize the mechanism of Norrin signal biogenesis, we determined the structure of a Norrin-FZD 4 -TSPAN12-LRP5 signaling complex using a de novo designed FZD 4 binder as a 'protein glue'. Our structure shows that two curved Norrin homodimers bridge two FZD 4 -TSPAN12 heterodimers. LRP5 LA3 simultaneously interacts with TSPAN12 and two Norrin homodimers, positioning the cytosolic FZD 4 and LRP5 tails for signal activation. On the basis of our findings, we designed FZD 4CRD -LRP5 LA3 bispecific binders that act as Norrin surrogates. Our signaling assays showed that oligomerization of the Norrin surrogate enhances signaling potency. Thus, this work reveals how the Norrin signal is generated and may assist in the development of Norrin/Wnt mimetics.

items.title: Persistent neuronal stress signalling underlies Angelman syndrome phenotypes.
items.abstract: Angelman syndrome is a severe neurodevelopmental disorder caused by the loss of UBE3A, a gene that encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase 1,2 . The mechanisms that underlie Angelman syndrome are not well understood, and in particular, the link between UBE3A substrates and disease phenotypes remains uncertain 3 . Here, using gain- and loss-of-function mutations in UBE3A 4,5 along with unbiased proteomics, we show that asparagine synthetase (ASNS) is a target of UBE3A. We find that ASNS protein abundance is increased in the brains of Ube3a-null mice and in human neurons 6 . Genetic correction of ASNS overabundance rescues microcephaly and many behavioural deficits. Detailed molecular analyses show that ASNS overabundance activates stress signalling and causes a global reduction in neuronal protein synthesis. Our results suggest that loss of UBE3A traps neurons in a state of persistent stress and stunts neuronal growth during developmentally sensitive periods. Moreover, our results indicate that targeting ASNS and the stress response could hold therapeutic potential in Angelman syndrome.

items.title: CD51 delineates functionally distinct astrocyte subtypes in neural circuits.
items.abstract: Astrocytes perform a diverse range of tasks that facilitate brain physiology, raising the possibility that these diverse astrocytic roles are enabled by functionally distinct subtypes 1,2 . Recent studies identified molecular diversity among astrocytes 3 ; however, whether this molecular heterogeneity reflects specialized astrocyte subpopulations with distinct functions remains unclear. Here, on the basis of previous molecular and functional studies 4 , we generated a CD51-FLP mouse line that enables direct comparison of the functional properties between CD51 + and CD51 - astrocyte subpopulations in neural circuits in vivo. We show that CD51 + and CD51 - astrocytes have unique morphological, physiological and developmental properties in both the cortex and hippocampus. Functional studies demonstrate that CD51 + astrocytes selectively promote synapse formation in the developing cortex and circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, we found that CD51 + astrocytes function through glypican 6 to promote synapse formation in the cortex, while CD51 itself drives circuit plasticity in the hippocampus. Applying these findings to brain injury, we found that CD51 + astrocytes promote functional recovery after stroke through enhanced synaptic remodelling. Taken together, our studies identify specialized astrocyte subpopulations that exhibit distinct functional properties in the developing, mature and injured brain.

items.title: Functional architecture of the human insula.
items.abstract: The insular cortex has a central role in pain 1,2 , interoception 3,4 and feelings 5,6 , yet its functional architecture and causal electrophysiological relationships among its subregions remain poorly understood. Here we combine intracranial electrical stimulation and task-based electroencephalography recordings with connectivity mapping within a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the human insula 7-10 in 87 participants implanted with intracranial electrodes, and identify a quadripartite functional architecture comprising four distinct regions: (1) a dorsal-posterior region encoding somatotopically organized nociceptive/thermoceptive and somatosensory signals; (2) a ventral-posterior region with access to somatic information across multiple body parts; (3) a mid-anterior region associated with visceral sensations and anxiety states; and (4) an anterior-polar region, largely silent to direct stimulation, yet showing robust activation during salience detection and change of action mode. Critically, this anterior region, with its strong connections with the prefrontal cortex, including the anterior cingulate cortex, exerts strong and direct influence over other insular regions, while receiving less-strong indirect inputs from them, revealing an electrophysiological pathway for cognitive modulation of pain and bodily perception. Together, these findings define a functional architecture of the human insula that links cytoarchitecture to directed and asymmetric electrophysiological interactions, with mechanistic implications for cognitive modulation of pain and interoceptive experience.
