items.title: Representation in conservation publishing
items.abstract: There is a persistent underrepresentation of marginalized voices in academic literature, including that for ecology and conservation. Such exclusion hampers career progression, perpetuating disadvantages for historically marginalized groups in the field, with implications for the direction of conservation research. Diverse perspectives foster novel thinking, strengthen innovation, and ensure research reflects the full spectrum of challenges faced by communities. To assess this underrepresentation, we analyzed self-reported demographic data for authors of scientific articles to explore demographic trends and how they shifted between 2010 and 2020. The journals chosen were listed as conservation-related by three or more of the five major journal indices. We used the same dimensions of diversity to assess editor demographics in 2021. In total, 2152 authors and 241 editors completed the survey (response rate: 21.5% authors; 29.5% editors). We found that overall author diversity across multiple traits (Rao's Q) increased between 2010 and 2020. Most notably, the representation of women increased from 29.5% to 35.6% of authors. However, women from lower-middle- or low-income countries still represented <1% of authors, and most dimensions of diversity saw little change over a decade. In 2020-2021, 80% of authors and 76% of editors self-identified as White; over three-quarters of respondents across years lived in high-income countries; and nationals of three countries (the United Kingdom, the United States, and Australia) represented 34% of authors and 49% of editors (5% of the global population). Our study findings highlight the importance of considering intersectionality, as respondents spanning multiple marginalized identities were disproportionately underrepresented. Overall, our work highlights how a lack of representation continues to characterize academic publishing in conservation and ecology but shows signs of positive change. There is evidence that gender-based initiatives are having a positive effect, yet more work is needed to enhance representation across other dimensions of diversity.

items.title: Pesticide effects on bee behavior and cognition: a bibliometric analysis of global research (2000–2025)
items.abstract: Bees are essential for ecosystem stability and global food security, yet their populations are declining worldwide, largely due to agrochemical exposure. Traditional pesticide risk assessments have focused on acute mortality, whereas recent ecotoxicological research increasingly emphasizes sublethal behavioral and cognitive effects. This study presents a bibliometric analysis of global research on the impacts of pesticides on bee behavior and cognition, based on 1,418 publications indexed in the Web of Science (2000–2025). Data were analyzed with the Bibliometrix R package and VOSviewer to identify publication trends, collaboration networks, and thematic evolution. Results showed a marked increase in research output after 2015, with peak productivity in 2023. The field is led by international collaborations centered in the United States, China, and Western Europe, with *Apidologie* serving as a key publication outlet. Thematic analyses revealed three major shifts: from mortality-based assessments to behavioral and cognitive endpoints such as learning, memory, and navigation; from traditional pesticides to newer compounds including flupyradifurone, sulfoxaflor, and thiacloprid; and from single-stressor approaches to multi-stressor frameworks integrating pesticide exposure with climate change, nutritional stress, and gut microbiota disruption. These findings highlight the need for regulatory frameworks that incorporate standardized behavioral, cognitive, and multi-stressor assessments to protect pollinator biodiversity and ecosystem services.

items.title: "SPATIAL PATTERNS OF FRESHWATER FISH DIVERSITY AND COMMUNITY STRUCTURE IN THE STREAMS OF THE PALANI HILLS, SOUTHERN WESTERN GHATS, INDIA"
items.abstract: Freshwater stream ecosystems of the Western Ghats support remarkable fish diversity and endemism but are increasingly threatened by habitat degradation and anthropogenic disturbances.The present study investigated the diversity, distribution, and environmental determinants of freshwater fish assemblages in streams of the Palani Hills, Southern Western Ghats, India.Fish sampling was conducted across 23 stream sites representing varying elevational gradients and habitat characteristics between January and December 2019.Different environmental variables were assessed to determine their influence on fish distribution.A total of 16 fish species belonging to 13 genera, 7 families, and 6 orders were recorded.The family Cyprinidae dominated the assemblage, accounting for approximately 73% of the total species composition.Diversity indices revealed greater species richness and abundance in downstream low-elevation streams compared to upstream high-altitude streams.Jaccard similarity and beta diversity analyses indicated moderate faunal similarity among downstream stream systems.Multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) demonstrated that elevation, water temperature, conductivity, total dissolved solids, salinity, and dissolved oxygen significantly influenced taxa richness.Principal Component Analysis (PCA) identified longitude, canopy cover, and substrate composition as important environmental determinants of fish assemblages.The findings emphasize the ecological importance of habitat heterogeneity and environmental gradients in structuring stream fish communities of the Palani Hills.Conservation strategies focusing on riparian vegetation, habitat restoration, and regulation of anthropogenic disturbances are essential for sustaining freshwater biodiversity in the region.

items.title: Impact of Pesticides on Soil Microbial Diversity in Northern India
items.abstract: The widespread application of synthetic pesticides in contemporary agriculture has attracted significant concerns on the influence of synthetic pesticides on the microbial communities of the soil which form a critical part of ecosystem functioning. This was a research project that examined the effect of differential use of pesticides on soil microbial biodiversity and soil microbial community structure in agricultural soils in the northern Indian regions. Samples of soil were sampled on two neighboring farms with differing intensity of pesticide application in December 2024 and June 2025 and the samples were analyzed by 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Microbial diversity declined significantly at high pesticide sites (Shannon index: 3.2±0.4) compared to low pesticide sites (4.1±0.3; p<0.05). Analysis of differential abundance suggested that there was significant change in community structure with a decrease of functional indicators of nitrogen cycling and degradation of organic matter. Mathematical modeling demonstrated an exponential negative relationship between pesticide residues and microbial diversity (R² = 0.84). The findings show that it is necessary to implement the evidencebased pesticide management principles to safeguard the biological health of soil and agricultural sustainability.

items.title: Standardizing deoxygenation studies in coral biology
items.abstract: Abstract Deoxygenation, the global loss of biologically available oxygen (O 2 ) from the world’s oceans, presents a pervasive and intensifying threat for reef-building corals that will require coordinated efforts to understand and manage. However, recent expansion of coral deoxygenation experimentation has produced methodological gaps, limiting collective knowledge generation. Here, we show that growing divergence in this field arises primarily from differences in focal phenotypes, deoxygenation exposures, and experimental execution that together prevent biological from technical variation from being disentangled between studies. To address this, we propose a series of recommendations to establish the foundation for a future standardized framework for coral deoxygenation methodology. Such efforts are critical to establish a robust consensus of scientific data to support effective management of reef deoxygenation. Waiting decades for diverging methodologies to prompt a call for standardization may be imprudent given the urgent threat of deoxygenation and the abundant methodological divergence present in coral deoxygenation experimentation.

items.title: Advances in the study of shallow-water hydrothermal systems and their role in coastal ocean processes
items.abstract: Shallow-water hydrothermal systems (SWHS) occur mainly in submarine volcanic and tectonically active settings and constitute dynamic interfaces between geological processes and coastal marine environments. Despite increasing scientific interest, research has often remained discipline-specific, limiting an integrated understanding of their role in coastal ocean processes. This review synthesizes research on their evolution, proposes an integrative definition and conceptual framework, identifies their distinguishing characteristics and scientific relevance, and addresses the question: What role do SWHS play in coastal ocean processes? A bibliographic research covering 1969–2026 was conducted primarily in Web of Science and complemented with Google Scholar. From 590 initially identified records, duplicates and publications not directly addressing SWHS or not aligned with the objectives of this review were excluded through title and abstract screening and full-text eligibility assessment, yielding 95 publications for the final synthesis; the complete dataset and screening information are provided as Supplementary Material. Four stages of research evolution were identified: (i) field exploration (1969–1994), (ii) geochemical characterization (1995–2005), (iii) molecular and ecological approaches (2006–2015), and (iv) interdisciplinary integration (2016–2026). This synthesis indicates that SWHS are not primary regulators of coastal ocean processes; rather, they act as localized geological–hydrothermal forcing that introduces heat, fluids, gases, nutrients, and minerals and interacts with physical, chemical, biogeochemical, microbiological, biological, and ecological processes. Their influence depends on hydrothermal discharge characteristics and local hydrodynamic conditions, making them valuable natural laboratories for understanding coupled coastal processes.

items.title: The impact of the dynamic shift to organic farming practices in bulukumba regency, Indonesia: evidence from grounded theory research
items.abstract: Background In developing countries such as Indonesia, the agricultural sector remains the backbone of the economy, providing jobs, food, and foreign exchange. However, globalization and developments in the global economic system have put a strain on conventional agricultural practices. The key issue for this sector is to ensure that agriculture continues to contribute to the Sustainable Development Goals by implementing organic farming and profitable agricultural innovations . Objective This study aimed to examine the impact of the dynamic shift of conventional to organic farming practices in Bulukumba Regency, South Sulawesi Province, Indonesia. The research results were expected to provide an empirical-theoretical framework for the management of agricultural resources in rural Indonesia. Methods The primary data were collected through in-depth interviews with 30 participants, including organic farmers, community leaders, and local agricultural officials. The data were then analyzed using the grounded theory research approach. The analysis process was carried out systematically through iterative stages of open, axial, and selective coding. Results One main theoretical category that emerged from the shift from conventional to organic farming practices was socio-ecological rationality, which explains how farmers integrate environmental ethics, economic needs, and socio-cultural norms into their agricultural decision-making. The study showed that ecological awareness, relational solidarity, and moral commitment are the main drivers of farmers’ adaptive resilience in maintaining organic farming practices amid constraints such as market access, certification costs, and suboptimal institutional support. These findings confirm that organic farming practices are not only an economic choice, but also an expression of moral and social values rooted in local culture. Discussions Theoretically, these research results have broadened the understanding of socio-ecological rationality as a relevant conceptual framework in explaining the sustainable behavior of smallholder farmers. In practical terms, this study recommends improving access to certification, strengthening farmer education and training capacities, and strengthening the role of supporting institutions to encourage the sustainability of organic farming systems. The long-term implications emphasize the importance of synergy between public policy, social innovation, and local values in building sustainable agricultural independence in Indonesia.

items.title: Impact of Organic and Chemical Fertilizers on Wheat Yield, Nutrient Uptake, and Soil Biological Properties in the Punjab Agro-Climatic Zone: A Comprehensive Review
items.abstract: The Punjab agro-climatic zone is among the most prolific wheat-producing areas in South Asia and is crucial for maintaining national food security. However, decades of intensive cultivation under the rice–wheat cropping system, coupled with heavy reliance on chemical fertilizers, have contributed to declining soil fertility, nutrient imbalances, reduced soil organic carbon, and deterioration of biological soil health. Sustainable nutrient management has therefore emerged as a critical challenge for maintaining wheat productivity while preserving ecosystem functions. This review critically examines the effects of organic fertilizers, chemical fertilizers, and integrated nutrient management (INM) practices on wheat yield, nutrient uptake, and soil biological properties in the Punjab agro-climatic zone. Evidence from long-term experiments and field studies indicates that the exclusive use of inorganic fertilizers often enhances short- term productivity but may adversely affect soil microbial activity, organic matter content, and nutrient-use efficiency over time. Conversely, organic nutrient sources such as farmyard manure, vermicompost, green manure, poultry manure, and crop residues improve soil structure, microbial biomass, enzymatic activity, nutrient cycling, and soil carbon sequestration, although their nutrient release rates may not always meet crop demand during critical growth stages. The integration of organic and inorganic nutrient sources has been identified as the most effective strategy for sustaining wheat productivity and improving soil health. Integrated nutrient management enhances grain and straw yield, increases nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and micronutrient uptake, and promotes favorable biological indicators including microbial biomass carbon, dehydrogenase activity, phosphatase activity, and soil respiration. Furthermore, INM contributes to improved nutrient-use efficiency, reduced environmental degradation, and enhanced resilience of the rice–wheat production system. The review highlights current knowledge gaps and future research priorities aimed at developing site-specific nutrient management strategies that balance productivity, profitability, and environmental sustainability. Adoption of integrated nutrient management practices is essential for ensuring long-term soil fertility and sustainable wheat production in Punjab under changing climatic and agricultural conditions.

items.title: Achieving sustainable nutrient self-sufficiency in Sweden: a long-term scenario assessment
items.abstract: Introduction Ensuring long-term food security while operating within planetary boundaries requires nutrient management strategies that reduce import dependency without shifting environmental burdens. This study develops and evaluates four contrasting normative scenarios for nutrient management in Sweden in 2045: industrial-scale domestic fertilizer production, industrial-scale nutrient recovery, decentralized “fork-to-backyard” nutrient cycling, and response diversity. Methods The scenarios were assessed using the Sustainability Assessment Framework for Scenarios (SAFS). The framework defines relevant contextual factors and applies a structured qualitative assessment across technological, environmental, and social/governance dimensions. Resource use and circularity were assessed within the environmental dimension, while self-sufficiency was treated as a shared scenario objective. An interrelation analysis and an ordinal scoring scale were used to identify and compare risks, opportunities, trade-offs, and uncertainties without ranking the scenarios. Results The assessment revealed persistent trade-offs that are relevant not only to Sweden but also to other high-input, import-dependent agri-food systems seeking greater nutrient self-sufficiency. Decentralized recycling showed the greatest potential to improve climate and eutrophication outcomes and strengthen democratic participation but involved high implementation and operational complexity, as well as demanding quality assurance requirements. Industrial recovery improved eutrophication performance and circularity while maintaining standardized fertilizer products, but depended on energy and process trade-offs and required substantial investments. Industrial production provided predictable products and perceived safety benefits but risked higher resource intensity and did not inherently reduce pressure on biogeochemical planetary boundaries. Response diversity increased resilience and reduced dependence on single supply pathways but could require greater resource use and coordination. Discussion The combined scenario and SAFS approach clarified key risks, opportunities, and uncertainties, including the influence of electricity mix, achievable nutrient-loss reductions, and contaminant control. The results demonstrate that no single pathway resolves all sustainability challenges and highlight the importance of considering technological, environmental, and governance dimensions simultaneously when designing nutrient self-sufficiency strategies. The approach can support decision-making in Sweden and other regions facing similar sustainability, governance, and supply-security challenges.

items.title: Revision of Alternanthera (Amaranthaceae–Gomphreneae) in the Arabian Peninsula, with nomenclatural corrections and notes on A. pungens and A. sessilis in the Old World
items.abstract: Background and aims – Alternanthera is one of the largest genera in Amaranthaceae, with the primary distribution in the Americas. The identification of some species, including those occurring as alien noxious weeds in the Old World, is challenging because of unstable taxonomy and nomenclature. In addition, their means and history of introduction remain poorly understood. Here, we revise the alien species of Alternanthera in the Arabian Peninsula, providing notes on their morphology, distribution, nomenclature, and dispersal facilities. Material and methods – We analysed type specimens, vegetative, floral and fruit characters, introduction history, and occurrences of four species of the genus in the Arabian Peninsula. Key results – Alternanthera ficoidea is reported for the first time from the Arabian Peninsula, and A. sessilis is newly recorded in the United Arab Emirates. The history and means of the species introduction are discussed. The turbulent nomenclatural history of A. ficoidea and A. tenella is reviewed to resolve the current confusion in their European records, and we propose that the latter name should unambiguously be considered as a synonym of A. ficoidea . The original spelling of Telanthera “ bettzickiana ” and A. “ bettzickiana ” are researched, and the species epithet is corrected to “ bettzichiana ”. A lectotype is designated for A. achyranthes , the generic type of Alternanthera . Detailed morphological descriptions of the propagules of Alternanthera are provided, and their role in the dispersal process are discussed. Conclusion – We noted a recent expansion of Alternanthera ficoidea , A. pungens , and A. sessilis in natural and anthropogenically disturbed plant communities of the Arabian Peninsula, especially across the coastlines of the Arabian Sea and Red Sea, and in foothills of the Sarawat Mountains. Their spread occurs through both vegetative and sexual means of dispersal. Our examination of morphological characters reveals a distinct role of the perianth and pericarp in the propagule dispersal of these species.

items.title: Bleaching and mortality responses of Orbicella annularis during the 2023 mass bleaching event in St. Thomas, USVI
items.abstract: Coral populations can differ in their responses to thermal stress, potentially reflecting environmental history and conditions experienced at transplant locations. We conducted a year-long reciprocal transplant experiment using Orbicella annularis including two inshore reef sites (Rupert Rock and Hassel Island) and two offshore reef sites (Flat Cay and Saba Island) in St. Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands. We examined how source population and transplant location influenced coral growth, bleaching, and mortality during the 2023 global mass bleaching event. The unprecedented thermal stress experienced during the study resulted in all sites exceeding 20 degree heating weeks (DHW). Relative growth increased through time across treatments, but growth trajectories differed among source and transplant locations, with no consistent evidence of a home-site advantage. Bleaching became widespread across all treatments, and neither source nor transplant location had a significant overall effect on bleaching probability. However, fragments originating from Hassel Island reached the 10% bleaching threshold significantly later than fragments sourced from Flat Cay and Saba Island, while maximum bleaching severity did not differ among source or transplant locations. Partial mortality increased through time and varied among source and transplant locations, whereas complete mortality was relatively uncommon, occurring in 9 of 128 fragments. Eight of these mortality events occurred at Rupert Rock, with seven concentrated on a single array; excluding this array eliminated differences in survivorship among transplant locations. Together, these findings suggest that differences in environmental history may be reflected more strongly in the timing of bleaching than its ultimate severity, while transplant conditions may influence growth and mortality under extreme thermal stress.

items.title: A review of country ambition in targeting important areas for biodiversity under the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework
items.abstract: Targets 1 and 3 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF) require actions to focus on areas of importance for biodiversity-a prerequisite for reversing biodiversity loss and halting human-induced extinctions as set out in the Mission and Goals of the KMGBF. There is a need to review progress on how countries are aiming to identify and conserve such areas of importance. We reviewed 97 national biodiversity strategy and action plans (NBSAPs) and 89 country submissions to the Convention on Biological Diversity's (CBD) Online Reporting Tool (ORT) to assess ambition across five targets of the KMGBF. We searched for evidence that countries were considering where to act for Targets 1, 2, 3, 14, 15, and 21. No country defined what constitutes an important area for biodiversity, and any stated focus of planning was limited largely to existing protected areas or ecosystems. Key Biodiversity Areas were identified in 40% of the NBSAPs, yet only 26% included specific targets, actions, or indicators for these globally significant sites. Ambition toward the 30% restoration (Target 2) and 30% protection (Target 3) targets was higher than previously reported but remained low overall. Only half of the countries planned to mandate or encourage business to measure its impacts on biodiversity (Target 15). Across six measures of ambition, an average of 29% of the countries submitting NBSAPs and 31% of the ORT target countries aimed to meet the KMGBF benchmarks, whereas 48% and 53%, respectively, showed no ambition to do so. European countries showed the lowest level of ambition of any region. Much greater levels of ambition and progress are needed to achieve the targets, goals, and vision for areas of importance for biodiversity in the KMGBF by 2030.

items.title: Patterns and Drivers of Sustainable Agricultural Practice Adoption Among Mennonite Farmers in a Closed Endorheic Basin of Northern Mexico
items.abstract: Agricultural sustainability in closed endorheic basins is constrained by periodic water scarcity, hydrological isolation, and the cumulative effects of intensive land use. The Cuauhtémoc region of northern Mexico hosts long-established Mennonite farming communities whose mechanized and irrigation-dependent agriculture constitutes an important component of the regional economy and resource-use system. This study examined the prevalence, diversity, and drivers of sustainable agricultural practices among 95 Mennonite farmers in the Bustillos Lagoon region. Thirteen practices spanning soil and residue management, water conservation, biological soil-fertility management, and agrochemical stewardship were assessed, while a conservation-practice breadth indicator quantified the number of ten resource-management practices used by individual farmers. Among 92 farmers with complete practice data, conservation-practice breadth ranged from 2 to 8 practices (mean = 3.76 ± 1.06). Residue incorporation (98.9%), residue cover (89.4%), and rainwater collection (71.0%) were widespread, whereas zero tillage (1.1%), compost/leachate use (5.3%), mycorrhiza application (5.3%), and reduced tillage (8.5%) were uncommon. Robust Poisson regression showed that technical assistance was associated with a 37.8% higher expected conservation-practice count (IRR = 1.378, 95% CI 1.168-1.626, p < 0.001), while environmental concern was associated with an 18.7% higher count (IRR = 1.187, 95% CI 1.017-1.385, p = 0.030). Water-supply problems, farm area, producer-organization membership, and education showed no independent associations. The findings demonstrate that sustainable management is better characterized as a heterogeneous portfolio of practices than as a binary adoption decision and highlight institutional support and environmental orientation as important correlates of management diversification in water-constrained agricultural landscapes.

items.title: Improved Feed Additives and Grazing Management are Likely Suboptimal Strategies for Reducing the Carbon Costs of Beef
items.abstract: I analyze research thrusts meant to reduce the carbon costs of the most resource intensive food item, beef. Using numerical modeling and data, I analyze the two most vigorously promoted ideas: Improving feed additives for reducing methane emissions, and enhancing soil carbon sequestration via better managed grazing. I find that even with the realistically expected emission reductions of these research thrusts, beef emissions remain higher than those associated with producing alternatives (including pork, poultry, or dairy). I also find that replacing beef with these alternatives is nutritionally adequate (save vitamin B12 for plant based substitutions, which requires supplementation). These sobering novel results are compounded by commercial beef’s well-established high environmental costs beyond emissions alone, and negative public health outcomes. Research into improving feed additives for reducing methane emissions, or into sequestration enhancing grazing management thus stands to benefit society less than dietary shifts. In developed economies, these disappointing results are a major barrier to achieving the emission reductions necessary for keeping global mean surface temperatures below 1.5K or even 2K above preindustrial levels. This reflects the fact that they address the two most enthusiastically publicly celebrated ideas in current agricultural sustainability discourse, and that they address a food item that generates 14-16% of total emissions.

items.title: Spatial pattern analysis of built-up land use and zoning conformity using polygon-based statistics: a case study of Tegal city, Indonesia
items.abstract: Rapid urban expansion in coastal cities increasingly challenges the effectiveness of spatial planning enforcement. Tegal city, located on Java’s northern coast, is experiencing intensive built-up land development accompanied by growing spatial clustering. This study analyses polygon-level built-up land patterns using Ripley’s K-function to identify multi-scale clustering, Global Moran’s I to assess spatial autocorrelation, and Local Moran’s I (LISA) to detect local clusters. Built-up Land Use/Land Cover (LULC) polygons derived from OpenStreetMap (2024) were compared with the official Spatial Plan (RTRW 2021–2031). The objectives are to identify the clustering behaviour of built-up areas and assess conformity between actual land development and planned zoning. The results reveal a concentric-clustered spatial structure and localized zones of spatial non-conformity with the official spatial plan. Transitional areas exhibit significant land-use mismatches, indicating weaknesses in spatial-use control. A Global Moran’s I value of 0.145 (p < 0.05) indicates weak but statistically significant positive spatial autocorrelation. These findings highlight the importance of strengthening zoning enforcement and updating detailed spatial plans (RDTR). The study demonstrates how integrated polygon-based spatial statistics can support routine spatial planning evaluation and zoning enforcement in rapidly developing coastal cities.

items.title: Beyond barriers: perceived barriers and winter sport participation intentions in a predominantly Zhejiang-based Chinese sample
items.abstract: Background Following China's national strategy to promote winter sports, understanding the psychological mechanisms driving participation among residents in China's Yangtze River Delta region—a population with limited traditional exposure to ice and snow activities—has become increasingly important. This study integrated the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) with leisure constraint theory and self-efficacy theory to examine how perceived barriers were associated with winter sport participation intentions through attitudinal and behavioral control pathways, and whether self-efficacy moderates these relationships. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with 415 self-identified residents of southern China. Structural equation modeling was employed to test the hypothesized relationships among perceived barriers, attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioral control (PBC), self-efficacy, and participation intention. Bootstrap mediation analysis was used to assess indirect effects, and moderation analysis was performed to examine the conditional role of self-efficacy. Results Perceived barriers demonstrated significant positive associations with both attitude (β = 0.16, p = 0.001) and PBC (β = 0.32, p < 0.001), a pattern consistent with constraint negotiation theory. Among the TPB predictors, PBC (β = 0.23, p < 0.001) and subjective norm (β = 0.20, p = 0.007) both significantly predicted participation intention, while attitude did not reach statistical significance (β = 0.01, p = 0.792). Self-efficacy exhibited the numerically largest standardized coefficient for participation intention (β = 0.323, p < 0.001). However, its coefficient did not differ significantly from those of PBC or subjective norm. The indirect association through PBC was significant (β = 0.076, 95% CI [0.028, 0.141]), whereas the indirect association through attitude was not significant (β = 0.002, 95% CI [– 0.014, 0.025]). The hypothesized moderating role of self-efficacy between perceived barriers and PBC was not supported. Conclusions The positive associations of perceived barriers with attitude and PBC are inconsistent with a uniformly inhibitory interpretation of barriers, although the cross-sectional design and the absence of direct measures of constraint negotiation preclude conclusions about the underlying process. and underscore the importance of social influence and self-efficacy in shaping participation intentions. The independent predictive contribution of self-efficacy beyond PBC highlights the value of distinguishing these constructs in behavioral models. However, the cross-sectional design, convenience sampling, and geographic concentration of respondents limit causal inference and generalizability. These results offer theoretical and practical implications for promoting winter sport participation in non-traditional regions.

items.title: Integrated Assessment of Physicochemical, Microbiological and Heavy Metal Characteristics of a Tourist-Influenced Himalayan River in Sahastradhara, Dehradun, Uttarakhand
items.abstract: Freshwater ecosystems located in recreational landscapes are increasingly subjected to anthropogenic pressures that may alter their physicochemical and microbiological characteristics.The present study assessed the water quality of the Sahastradhara River, a popular tourist destination in the Shivalik foothills of Dehradun, Uttarakhand, India.Water samples were collected monthly during 2022 and 2023 from three sites representing upstream (S1), central tourist zone (S2) and downstream (S3) locations.Physicochemical parameters, heavy metals and microbial indicators were analyzed, and water quality was evaluated using the Water Quality Index (WQI) and Comprehensive Pollution Index (CPI).The river water remained slightly alkaline with pH ranging from 6.98 to 8.06.Electrical conductivity and total dissolved solids varied between 1055-2133 µS cm⁻¹ and 552-1116 mg L⁻¹, respectively, reflecting mineral-rich groundwater influence.Turbidity ranged from 7.4 to 55 NTU, with maximum values during the monsoon season.Dissolved oxygen and biochemical oxygen demand varied from 3.29-8.09mg L⁻¹ and 2.06-9.95mg L⁻¹, respectively, indicating moderate organic loading.Heavy metals remained within permissible limits, while microbial contamination was high, with total coliform counts reaching 2419 MPN 100 mL⁻¹.Seasonal WQI values ranged from 169.9 to 260.9, indicating poor to very poor water quality for drinking purposes, whereas CPI values ranged from 1.90 to 2.95, reflecting moderate pollution levels.Multivariate analysis indicated that water quality variations were primarily controlled by natural mineralization processes and tourism-related anthropogenic inputs.Continuous monitoring and improved management strategies are necessary to ensure sustainable use of this recreational river system.

items.title: Assessing and quantifying variations in the functioning of marine food webs across scales
items.abstract: The mismatch between the scale of ecological processes and management decisions represents a significant challenge in marine conservation. This misalignment can result in ineffective conservation measures and compromise the sustainability of marine ecosystems. The large spatial resolution commonly used to analyze food webs may obscure key ecological processes and their functioning, leading to inaccurate conclusions with important consequences for management and governance. To address this gap, we used a food web indicator, the survey-based mean trophic level (MTL), covering an entire bentho-demersal community across four subregions of the Northeast Atlantic. The indicator was developed at two spatial resolutions, subregional and local (0.2° × 0.2° cells), and we used a long-term dataset to assess food-web status. A set of 18 ecological scenarios, based on different trophic level (TL) thresholds and depth ranges, were established for each subregion, and linear models were applied to the historical series for each scenario. At the subregional scale, the results indicated potential recovery of top predators in the northern area; however, the stable patterns under various scenarios may have been attributable to ongoing fishing pressure rather than to true ecosystem stability or a genuinely balanced state. At the finer spatial resolution, local declining trends were revealed that had been masked in the broader-scale analysis. These contrasting patterns underscore the importance of spatial resolution when assessing the status of marine food webs and highlight the need to consider multiple ecological scenarios. We recommend aligning management strategies with the natural processes that govern marine ecosystems to enhance the resilience and long-term sustainability of ocean environments.

items.title: Research Progress on Structure, Pattern, Process Coupling Mechanisms in Desert Ecosystems of Arid China
items.abstract: Nearly two-fifths of the global land surface consists of arid-land ecosystems. Their impact on changes in terrestrial carbon sinks is uneven, and their function is difficult to estimate due to water limitation. This structured narrative review integrates the coupling of structure, pattern, and process of desert ecosystems in China’s arid regions. OpenAlex and Crossref were searched to identify candidate publications, supplemented by citation links, with the time span mainly covering January 2018 to July 2026, and earlier foundational research establishing relevant theoretical concepts was retained. 39 peer-reviewed publications were selected and coded. After comprehensive consideration, six recurring themes are summarized, including hierarchical organization. There is relatively strong evidence for the functional role of biological soil crusts, but there are many uncertainties regarding the transferability of idealized models. The problems that need to be addressed first involve causal relationships across scales. Solving such problems is necessary for evaluating restoration and carbon neutrality strategies, which cannot focus only on the extent of greening.

items.title: Searching for cosmic strings via black hole spin-down
items.abstract: Cosmic strings that are attached to rapidly spinning black holes can extract significant amounts of rotational energy and angular momentum. Here we study the effect on primordial black holes, which are expected to form with one or more cosmic strings attached. Although large primordial black holes are predicted to rapidly spin up due to accretion soon after forming, we argue that cosmic strings will spin them down again. We show that if there are cosmic strings with tension greater than $10^{-20}$, the spins of large primordial black holes of mass greater than $30 M_\odot$ should consequently be observed to be near zero. We also investigate the effect on a supermassive black hole of capturing a cosmic string and the possibility of observing the subsequent spin down by its effect on a pulsar orbiting the black hole.

items.title: Self-consistent Hubble expansion in exponential teleparallel gravity: confrontation with recent observations
items.abstract: We reconstruct the Hubble expansion history within an anisotropic exponential teleparallel gravity framework using recent cosmological observations, including Observational Hubble Data (OHD), the latest Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument Data Release 2 (DESI DR2) baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) measurements, gravitational-wave (GW) standard-siren data, and the Pantheon Plus and SH0ES Type Ia supernova compilations. The proposed anisotropic exponential f(T) model is investigated in both the absence and presence of shear, and is confronted with these independent observational probes through statistical analyses based on the reduced χ 2 , Akaike Information Criterion (AIC), and Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC), demonstrating its consistency with current cosmological observations. Furthermore, the cosmological viability of the model is investigated through a comprehensive study of the dynamical evolution, stability conditions, and linear matter perturbations, providing a unified assessment of its theoretical consistency and observational compatibility.

items.title: Quantum interferometric probe of neutron-hidden neutron oscillations
items.abstract: The nature of dark matter remains an outstanding problem in particle physics and cosmology. Hidden-sector extensions of the Standard Model predict a neutral partner of the neutron, whose weak mixing with ordinary neutrons induces oscillations between visible and dark baryonic states. We show that macroscopic quantum interferometry provides a direct and experimentally accessible probe of this phenomenon. In particular, a Mach--Zehnder interferometer with very cold neutrons converts neutron--hidden neutron oscillations into measurable phase-dependent intensity modulations. By combining controlled phase shifts with tunable magnetic fields and material potentials, the setup enables a resonant exploration of the hidden-sector parameter space. We find that existing cold-neutron facilities can probe mixing amplitudes down to $ε_{nn'} \sim 10^{-14}\,\mathrm{eV}$ for mass splittings $δm \sim 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{eV}$, accessing a previously unexplored region of parameter space relevant to baryonic dark matter scenarios. These results establish neutron interferometry as a precision laboratory tool for testing hidden-sector physics.

items.title: Robust continuous symmetry breaking and multiversality in the chiral Dicke model
items.abstract: The Dicke model (DM) serves as a paradigm for understanding collective light-matter interactions. We introduce the chiral Dicke model, a generalization where an atomic ensemble couples to a two-mode cavity via chiral interactions. Unlike the standard DM, the chiral DM is endowed with an inherent continuous $U(1)$ symmetry associated with angular momentum conservation. The ground-state phase diagram and the associated quantum phase transitions are charted out, revealing a $U(1)$-broken superradiant phase that spans a broad parameter space. We demonstrate that the spectrum of quantum fluctuations is highly tunable in both the symmetric and broken phases. Strikingly, our calculations reveal that the system exhibits `multiversality', where distinct universality classes govern the transition between the same two phases. In particular, along a special line in parameter space, the dynamical critical exponent for the normal-superradiant phase transition changes from $zν=1$ to $zν=1/2$. Our work establishes the chiral Dicke model as a powerful platform to realize novel quantum phases and multiversal critical phenomena in light-matter coupled systems.

items.title: Overview of X-ray Thomson scattering measurements of extreme states of matter
items.abstract: Since its first successful applications in the early 2000s, X-ray Thomson scattering (XRTS) has emerged as one of the most successful tools for the diagnostics of extreme states of matter in the laboratory. By sampling the dynamic structure factor of the electrons, XRTS is capable of giving detailed insights into the atomic-scale physics of the matter probed. Moreover, thermodynamic parameters, such as the mass density, temperature, and ionization state, are routinely inferred from XRTS measurements, providing a comprehensive characterization of the sample probed. In addition, the dynamic structure factor is of considerable interest in its own right, since it contains information on other effects such as the plasmon shift, miscibility between species, electronic states, and potential transitions between these states. In this work, we provide an extensive overview of previous XRTS experiments at both traditional laser and X-ray free-electron laser facilities, including information about the probed material (elements and conditions), scattering geometry, and analysis methods, as well as the corresponding references. In addition, we briefly discuss the advantages and shortcomings of widely used analysis methods for XRTS spectra and reflect on upcoming future developments in XRTS experiments and theory.

items.title: Ionization Structure and Metal Enrichment of the Galactic Center Minispiral Observed with JWST
items.abstract: Abstract Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*) is the nearest quiescent supermassive black hole, and its proximity offers a unique opportunity to study its surrounding fuel supply. We leverage extensive spatial and spectroscopic information provided by the JWST/MIRI Medium Resolution Spectrograph instrument to disentangle mid-infrared ionized gas structures in the central 0.1 pc of the Galaxy. The Galactic Minispiral’s Bar and Northern Arm are revealed by their distinct morphological and kinematic signatures. Several compact (<1″) gas structures including X7 also appear within ∼0.05 pc of Sgr A* in the plane of the sky, moving with blueshifted radial velocities ≳ 600 km s −1 . Fine-structure line measurements spanning ionization potentials ∼ 7–55 eV are used to constrain the incident radiation field, metal abundances (neon, argon, sulfur, nickel, and iron), and dust depletion or destruction for each identified gas structure. Overall, the Minispiral gas shows mildly supersolar abundances (∼1.8 × solar), a Wolf–Rayet-star-driven radiation field consistent with ionization parameters spanning − 1.6 ≲ log U ≲ − 0.6 , and significant nickel and iron dust destruction. In particular, the enhanced ionization state and strong dust processing in the high-velocity compact gas structures suggest that these features may experience localized fast shocks.

items.title: Microscopic origin of polytype-dependent melting in SiC revealed by machine-learning molecular dynamics
items.abstract: Predicting how crystal structure influences high-temperature stability remains a key challenge in materials modeling and design. Silicon carbide (SiC), one of the most thermally and chemically stable materials known, provides an ideal system for studying this problem because its many polytypes preserve similar local tetrahedral bonding while differing in long-range stacking geometry. To determine the impact of polytype structure on the high-temperature stability of SiC, we combine phase-coexistence machine-learning molecular dynamics with finite-temperature phonon analysis, enabled by a fine-tuned MACE interatomic potential that accurately describes crystalline, high-temperature, and disordered configurations across multiple SiC polytypes. We identify a clear stability ordering, 3C > 2H > 9R, reflected consistently in structural disordering, interlayer sliding, and finite-temperature phonon spectra. Across all polytypes, melting initiates through the formation of short C-C contacts and carbon-rich local regions, followed by a progressive loss of tetrahedral Si-C connectivity. The reduced stability of the long-period 9R polytype is associated with a denser manifold of low-frequency transverse-acoustic modes arising from its stacking periodicity and associated zone folding, which broaden and soften further at high temperature. These modes can provide additional low-energy channels for thermally activated lateral bilayer motion, consistent with the larger sliding amplitudes observed in 9R and their positive correlation with local structural disorder.

items.title: A MIGHTEE robust measurement of the star formation rate – radio correlation
items.abstract: Abstract Determining the relationship between star-formation rate (SFR) and the radio luminosity (L1.4) is critical if we are to trace the star-formation history of the Universe dust-agnostically using current and future radio facilities. However, until now, such work has relied on potentially biased binary classifications of sources to remove contaminating active galactic nuclei (AGN). We present a new, statistically-driven methodology for deriving the SFR – L1.4 relation, removing the need for problematic cuts. We use a Bayesian hierarchical mixture model fit to the radio-detected sources in the deep MIGHTEE COSMOS DR1 catalogue, incorporating the full SFR posterior probability distributions generated by state-of-the-art spectral energy distribution fitting code GRAHSP. This allows us to probabilistically determine a mean SFR – L1.4 relation for the SF dominated galaxies, whilst accounting for changing fractions of SF dominated sources across redshift, radio luminosity and stellar mass ranges. We find that the SFR – radio luminosity correlation exhibits a significant dependence on redshift, but a stellar mass dependence that is weaker than previous studies. Our resultant SFR-radio correlation is log10(SFR/M⊙ yr−1) = 0.790 × (log10(L1.4/W Hz−1) − 23) + 1.244 × (1 + z)0.122 − 0.033 × (log10(M*/M⊙) − 10), with an intrinsic scatter of 0.178 dex. We show that this redshift evolution could be explained by a moderate evolution in the radio spectral index of SF galaxies. We attribute the lack of observed strong dependence on stellar mass, compared to recent studies, to the novel statistical approach that does not rely on cuts to remove AGN.

items.title: Disentangling the dark and stellar mass through precise lens modelling of the JWST observation of lensed quasar WFI2033–4723
items.abstract: Abstract We use high-resolution JWST/NIRCam imaging and measured time delays to model the quadruply imaged quasar WFI2033–4723 with a composite stellar plus dark-matter mass model. We first construct an elliptical power-law baseline model and recover Fermat-potential differences (fpd) consistent with previous HST-based and JWST-based analyses, providing a reference scale for composite modelling. We then replace the total mass profile with a physically motivated decomposition in which the stellar mass follows a multi-Gaussian expansion of the lens light, with a free radial mass-to-light gradient, and the dark matter is described by a generalized Navarro–Frenk–White (gNFW) halo. Using two external cosmological priors, Planck+DESI and Pantheon+SH0ES, the measured time delays constrain the mass-sheet-transformation freedom that would otherwise damage the stellar–dark-matter decomposition. In both cosmological cases, the stellar normalization lies between the expectations for Chabrier and Salpeter initial mass functions, while the radial mass-to-light gradient is not strongly required by the data (mildly positive). The dark matter halo has an inner slope γin ≃ 1.3, steeper than a standard NFW cusp, and the main astrophysical conclusions are insensitive to the adopted cosmological prior. This work shows that composite time-delay lens modelling can effectively separate baryons from dark matter. As a qualitative check, we reverse the logic and use our composite lens model without kinematic information to infer the cosmology instead. However, the strong degeneracy between H0 and the halo scale radius Rs prevents a robust standalone constraint.

items.title: Design and Implementation of a Microservice-Architecture Master Control System for AIMS
items.abstract: Abstract The mid-infrared solar magnetic field telescope AIMS (An Infrared System for the Accurate Measurement of Solar Magnetic Field) is the first ground-based telescope designed to directly measure solar magnetic fields via Zeeman splitting in the 8–14 μm band, overcoming the century-long bottleneck of model-dependent indirect measurements. Its remote high-altitude site, heterogeneous multi-institute components, and complex observation modes comprising Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectropolarimetry and broadband imaging demand a highly autonomous Master Control System (MCS). We present the design and implementation of the AIMS MCS, featuring three key contributions: (1) a novel L0–L5 telescope automation classification inspired by the SAE J3016 autonomous driving standard, providing clear boundaries and a progressive evolution roadmap; (2) a three-layer system framework—device control, autonomy support, and central decision—implemented with a microservice software architecture that achieves loose coupling, high cohesion, and continuous integration of heterogeneous components; and (3) a suite of key enabling technologies including automatic pointing/tracking, autofocus via lucky-frame selection combined with power spectral ratio analysis, and environment-adaptive observation integrating auto-exposure, cloud detection, and power/thermal monitoring. The MCS has been validated across three telescopes at progressive automation levels: AIMS itself (L1, stable operation >2 years since April 2024), the WenQuan Solar Magnetic Field Telescope (L2, stable operation >3 years since February 2023), and the Solar Full-disk Multi-layer Magnetograph SFMM (L3, continuous autonomous operation >2.5 years since October 2023). Collectively, these deployments underscore the feasibility and stability of the proposed architecture, establishing a robust and scalable foundation for the next generation of embodied intelligent telescopes.

items.title: Infrasound Newtonian Noise Estimation at the Einstein Telescope Candidate Site Sos Enattos
items.abstract: Abstract We investigate the seasonal variability of atmospheric infrasound and its contribution to Newtonian noise (NN) at the Sos Enattos site, a leading candidate location for the Einstein Telescope (ET). Infrasound data recorded at three stations, SOE0 (surface), SOE1 (−84 m) and SOE3 (−160 m), are analysed over multiple seasons to characterise both the temporal variability and the depth dependence of the acoustic field. At the surface, the median amplitude spectral density (ASD) at 1 Hz shows no consistent seasonal modulation, and its variability is driven primarily by wind; the apparent dependence on sea state largely reflects its correlation with wind speed. Underground, where local wind noise is suppressed, a winter maximum of 4–7 dB above the quietest season is observed in both years of data. Using the measured sound-pressure spectra, we estimate the corresponding NN contribution for an underground cavern with the dimensions foreseen for ET, assuming an isotropic field of acoustic plane waves. The surface pressure field, acting through the atmosphere above a test mass at 200 m depth, exceeds the ET-D design sensitivity in median conditions between 1.6 and 7.1 Hz, by up to a factor of 4.7. Inside the cavern, the median NN remains a factor of 1.4 below ET-D with the pressure measured at SOE1, but exceeds it between 2.5 and 8.7 Hz, by up to a factor of 3.5, with the pressure measured at SOE3. The attenuation is not monotonic with depth: the deeper station SOE3 shows higher levels than SOE1 above a few hertz, pointing to local, anthropogenic sources in the underground infrastructure. These results show that underground placement is essential but not sufficient on its own, and that the acoustic emission of the underground infrastructure and future laboratory equipment will require careful evaluation and mitigation to keep atmospheric NN below the ET design sensitivity.

items.title: An ALMA study of hub-filament systemsII. Quiescent filaments converging towards highly dynamic hubs
items.abstract: Abstract Hub-filament systems are networks of converging interstellar filaments, often with active star formation at their centres, that may play an important role in high-mass star formation. In the first paper of this series, we found that the mass fraction that ends up in a clump’s most massive core is significantly higher in IR-dark hubs than IR-bright clumps, suggesting that the most-massive cores form early on. Such early massive core formation requires large inflow rates and dynamically active IR-dark clumps. We now present N2H+(J=1–0) observations of six IR-dark hub-filament systems mapped with ALMA 12m, 7m, and total power at ∼3″ resolution, to trace the kinematics of the dense gas. The data show intricate emission structures and complex spectra. To characterise their kinematics, we have developed mwydyn, a fully-automated, multiple velocity component, hyperfine line-fitting code. Our results reveal that the emission invariably consists of quiescent individual filaments in the outskirts that converge towards the hub centres where a systematic increase in velocity dispersion and number of components is observed. We also find that the distribution of centroid velocities is remarkably similar between clumps, despite spanning more than one order of magnitude in mass. We propose that our results are best explained by the mixing of gravitationally-driven multi-directional inflows, resulting in highly complex and dynamic hub centres. We also discuss the implications of the observed differentiated filament and hub gas kinematics in the context of the 3D morphology of hub-filament systems.

items.title: The FU Ori Outburst of PR Ori B
items.abstract: Abstract We report the discovery of a nearby FU Ori–type outburst (FUor), PR Ori B, in the L1641 cluster of the Orion star-forming region. The high-amplitude variability was first identified in the NEOWISE (3–5 μ m) photometry of the unresolved PR Ori binary system. Long-term, resolved optical photometric monitoring demonstrates that PR Ori B is the driver of a Δ G = 5 mag outburst, while PR Ori A has remained constant over the past 20 yr. The near-IR spectrum of PR Ori B changes from a late K-type spectral type during quiescence to a viscously heated disk during outburst, including deep absorption in 12 CO and H 2 O bands. The optical spectrum also exhibits features that are commonly associated with FUors, including P Cygni profiles in Na i D lines and absorption in the Ca ii infrared triplet. The luminosity of the outburst ( L acc ∼ 30–40 L ⊙ ) is similar to that commonly observed in FUors. The comparison of Spitzer/Infrared Spectrograph and Very Large Telescope/VISIR spectroscopy shows some evidence of silicate crystallization during the outburst. PR Ori B is one of the closest and brightest FUors discovered over the past few years, only one magnitude fainter than the archetype of the class FU Ori. The proximity and brightness will allow for future high angular resolution observations to probe the physics of the inner disk and to evaluate changes in the disk due to the increased luminosity.

items.title: Exploring the dynamics of the Coma galaxy cluster by mapping its X-ray emission line profiles with XRISM
items.abstract: Abstract The intracluster medium (ICM) in merging galaxy clusters exhibits turbulence and bulk flows. Unraveling these components is crucial not only for elucidating the geometry of the cluster mergers, but also for understanding the physics of magnetic field amplification and relativistic particle acceleration. XRISM/Resolve data for two $3^{\prime }\times 3^{\prime }$ fields in the core of the Coma cluster reveals that the ICM in the central field moves with $\Delta cz = -430$ km s$^{-1}$ relative to the cluster galaxy average, while that in the southern field moves with $\Delta cz = -730$ km s$^{-1}$ (see XRISM Collaboration et al. 2025, ApJ, 985, L20; hereinafter “Paper I”). In this paper, we perform a more detailed analysis of these data sets to search for non-Gaussian features in the Fe K line complex profiles. In the spectra from the north-west quadrant of the central field, in addition to the main and redshifted ICM components ($\Delta cz = -6$ km s$^{-1}$) reported in Paper I, we find evidence of another, blueshifted, component, moving with $\Delta cz = -1274$ km s$^{-1}$. For a systematic search for other significant velocity components, we perform a bias-free $3$ eV step multi-component fit to the Resolve full-array spectra from the central and southern fields. This search uncovers another redshifted component in the southern field, moving with $\Delta cz \sim +1250$ km s$^{-1}$. We estimate the energy densities of the ICM turbulence and bulk motion to be similar to each other and several times greater than the energy density of the cluster’s $B\sim 5\, \mu$G magnetic field.

items.title: Can Auroral Heating Explain Brown Dwarf Thermal Inversions?
items.abstract: Abstract Recent modeling of the JWST spectra of the Y dwarf CWISEPJ193518.59-154620.3 and the T dwarf SIMPJ013656.5+093347.3 indicates the presence of a thermal inversion in their atmospheres, implying an additional source of heating. Auroral energy deposition has been proposed as a potential mechanism. In this work, we model auroral energy deposition processes and the resulting atmospheric response to assess whether physically motivated auroral electron beam energy spectra can reproduce the inferred thermal inversions. We simulate the effects of several auroral electron beam energy spectra consistent with observations of the Jovian population of auroral electrons and scale them to the total electron flux expected for brown dwarfs. We find that auroral energy deposition alone cannot reproduce both the magnitude and pressure level of the inferred inversion in either object. While inversions are produced in our models, they occur at pressures that are too low compared to those required by the observations. These results suggest that the actual population of auroral electrons includes a stronger high-energy component than considered here, that additional heating mechanisms contribute to the observed thermal inversions, and/or that heterogeneous heating of the atmosphere is important for determining the observed emission.

items.title: Systematic Effects of Hydrogen and Helium Atmosphere Mismatch on Radius Inference in PSR J0740+6620–like Synthetic NICER Data
items.abstract: Abstract Constraints on neutron star radii provide insight into the properties of the cold, dense matter in their interiors. Previous studies using synthetic Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer (NICER) pulse waveform data have demonstrated that radius inferences derived therefrom are robust against several classes of modeling systematics. Here we explore the consequences of assuming the wrong atmospheric composition, using synthetic data based on the ∼2.1 M ⊙ pulsar PSR J0740+6620. We find that the assumption of a hydrogen atmosphere when the synthetic data assumed a helium atmosphere, or vice versa, produces little bias in the inferred radius at the spot-to-background ratio of the actual PSR J0740+6620 data. However, when we increase the spot-to-background ratio by a factor of ∼20 while keeping the total number of counts fixed at the observed ∼5.5 × 10 5 , we find that composition mismatch can produce significantly biased radius estimates while remaining hidden inside a fit with statistically acceptable residuals. Even in these cases, the Bayesian evidence consistently identifies the correct atmospheric model. Our findings reinforce the importance of using the Bayesian evidence for model comparison and goodness-of-fit tests.

items.title: Disk Truncation Triggers Relativistic Jet Launching of a Highly Accreting Supermassive Black Hole
items.abstract: Abstract Relativistic jets are among the most energetic phenomena in the Universe and influence galaxy evolution through energetic feedback, yet the physical connection between accretion flows and jet launching remains unresolved. Jet production is widely attributed to the Blandford–Znajek mechanism, which extracts black hole rotational energy via large-scale magnetic fields sustained by an accretion flow. Although this mechanism is observationally well supported for hot, geometrically thick accretion flows, highly accreting environments with strong jets present a paradox, as they are typically dominated by cold, geometrically thin disks incapable of sustaining large-scale magnetic fields. Here, we report coordinated X-ray microcalorimeter spectroscopy achieved by X-ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission (XRISM) and millimeter–radio interferometric observations by Global Millimeter Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) Array (GMVA), Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA), and East Asian VLBI Network (EAVN) of the broad-line radio galaxy 3C 120. High-resolution X-ray spectroscopy reveals a relativistically broadened Fe K α line, indicating that the cold, geometrically thin disk is truncated at ∼20 R g ( R g is the gravitational radius), with the inner region replaced by a hot, geometrically thick flow. Concurrently, radio imaging indicates that jet profile extrapolation toward the black hole horizon yields a radius comparable to or even narrower than the disk truncation radius. These results demonstrate that, even at high accretion rates, jet launching is linked to a hot inner flow, possibly via the Blandford–Znajek process, providing evidence for a universal disk–jet connection via geometric transition.

items.title: A Bayesian Inference Framework for Binary Lens Events Fully Incorporating Higher-order Effects
items.abstract: Abstract Higher-order effects, such as microlensing parallax and lens orbital motion, are essential for characterizing the physical properties of microlensing planetary systems, including their masses and distances. In practice, higher-order effects are often included in light-curve modeling only when their signals are strong, because their inclusion in weakly constrained cases tends to drive the inferred parameters toward regions of parameter space that are disfavored by standard Galactic models. This binary choice over physically continuous effects introduces an event-dependent selection function that complicates population-level interpretation and prevents strong and weak detections from being combined within a single uniform framework. In this work, we investigate the origin of instabilities associated with higher-order effects and show that such instabilities can arise from a mismatch between commonly adopted uninformative priors in the light-curve parameter space and the distributions predicted by Galactic models. Motivated by this, we develop a new Bayesian framework that enables higher-order effects to be incorporated in a stable and uniform manner. As part of this framework, we introduce the Galactic Prior Modeling Engine ( gapmoe ), a dedicated tool that enables efficient evaluation of the Galactic prior density and allows it to be incorporated directly into the light-curve inference. Using simulated events, we demonstrate that our framework robustly recovers the true physical parameters while fully accounting for microlensing parallax and lens orbital motion. This framework eliminates the need for ad hoc model selection and provides a scalable and statistically consistent pathway for analyzing the large samples expected from next-generation surveys such as the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

items.title: Accreting Neutron Stars in Low-Mass X-ray Binaries
items.abstract: Abstract Neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries (NS LMXBs) are systems in which a neutron star accretes matter from a Roche-lobe-filling companion via an accretion disc, releasing gravitational energy with an efficiency of order 10–20% of the rest-mass energy. Unlike black holes, neutron stars possess a solid surface and a magnetic field, making NS LMXBs uniquely rich laboratories for high-energy astrophysics and dense-matter physics. In this article we review the current understanding of accretion onto neutron stars in LMXBs, tracing matter from the outer disc radii to the stellar surface across five decades of observational discovery. We survey the principal classes of accreting neutron star systems — canonical atoll and Z-sources, ultracompact X-ray binaries, accreting millisecond pulsars, and transitional millisecond pulsars — and discuss how their spectral states, timing properties, and multiwavelength behaviour encode the physics of the inner accretion flow. We examine thermonuclear Type-I X-ray bursts as probes of nuclear burning and neutron star structure, and review the boundary and spreading layers where accreted matter decelerates onto the stellar surface. We discuss relativistic jets and ionised disc winds as regulators of the accretion–ejection cycle. Finally, we present X-ray polarimetric results from the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer ( IXPE ), which for the first time provide new, though model-dependent, constraints on the geometry of the emission regions — disc, corona, spreading layer, and jets — that spectroscopy alone cannot resolve, alongside complementary optical and infrared polarimetric observations.

items.title: High-Resolution Astronomical Imaging: Resolving Close Binaries and Stellar Surfaces via Optical Coherence
items.abstract: Due to the diffraction limit of conventional telescopes, the angular resolution of single-aperture instruments in the visible band is typically restricted to ~0.02 arcseconds, which hampers the effective resolution and imaging of close binary systems and stellar surface features. To overcome this limitation, optical interferometry has emerged as a powerful technique for high-resolution astronomical imaging, grounded in optical coherence theory and the van Cittert–Zernike theorem. By employing key technologies such as telescope arrays, baseline synthesis, closure phase calibration, and u−v plane sampling, milli-arcsecond angular resolution can be achieved, enabling precise determination of orbital parameters in close binaries, as well as accurate measurements of stellar masses and radii, while allowing direct imaging of stellar magnetic activity features such as starspots and faculae. Observational approaches are generally divided into model-fitting and image-reconstruction methods, each with distinct advantages and limitations. Nevertheless, ground-based interferometry remains constrained by atmospheric turbulence, sparse u−v plane coverage, limited sensitivity, and high computational complexity. Looking ahead, future developments are expected to focus on space-based interferometers, large-scale interferometric arrays, and artificial intelligence-assisted image reconstruction. These advancements not only enrich the fundamental database of stellar physics but also provide high-precision observational support for studies of stellar evolution, binary dynamics, and exoplanetary systems.

items.title: Thermospheric response to solar EUV variability probed with orbital-energy decay from NinjaSat CubeSat GNSS telemetry
items.abstract: Solar extreme ultraviolet (EUV) radiation heats and expands the thermosphere, modulating atmospheric density at altitudes in low Earth orbit and thereby increasing satellite drag and accelerating orbital decay. Previous studies have relied on empirical solar proxies, such as the F10.7 cm radio flux and Two-Line Element (TLE)-derived orbit solutions, which lack sufficient spectral resolution and temporal cadence to resolve wavelength-dependent thermospheric responses, and on orbital-decay metrics—most commonly the satellite altitude itself—that are not conserved quantities along the orbit and have rarely been validated against independent-density measurements. Here, we combine spectrally resolved EUV irradiance from the GOES-18 Extreme Ultraviolet and X-ray Irradiance Sensors at seven wavelengths (25.6–140.5 nm) with high-cadence GNSS position and velocity data from NinjaSat, an X-ray-astronomy 6U CubeSat orbiting at approximately 500–530 km altitude, over an 8-month period (April–November 2024). We derive the orbital-decay signal from the $$J_2$$ -corrected specific mechanical energy computed directly from the GNSS position and speed telemetry—a conserved quantity whose within-orbit scatter is about 50 times smaller than that of an altitude-based (point-mass energy) decay metric and which, unlike TLE/SGP4-based approaches, requires no propagated reference orbit. This energy-based decay rate correlates with independent thermospheric-density retrievals from the Swarm and GRACE-FO missions with Spearman coefficients of 0.85–0.92 (daily means), and its systematic-error budget (radiation pressure, unmodeled gravitational perturbations) remains below the statistical uncertainty of the daily decay rate. Cross-correlation analysis shows that the decay rate is strongly related to EUV and far-ultraviolet (FUV) irradiance (Spearman coefficients up to $$\sim$$ 0.8), with a positive lag of order 1–3 days. Using a block-bootstrap procedure that accounts for the strong autocorrelation of both series, we find that the 95% confidence intervals of the estimated lag overlap across all seven wavelengths, extending from the 6-h search floor to approximately 100 h, while the central lag estimates lie at roughly 30–70 h depending on wavelength and analysis choice; a wavelength-dependent separation of the response times is not statistically resolved with the present dataset and remains a plausible but unconfirmed hypothesis pending independent constraints from physics-based thermosphere models. These results demonstrate that standard GNSS telemetry from a CubeSat, combined with a conserved orbital-energy metric and independent-mission validation, can quantitatively characterize the thermospheric drag response to solar EUV forcing, offering a scalable observational approach for space-weather monitoring and satellite drag modeling.

items.title: Evaluating Magnetic Reconnection Through the Nanoflare Heating Model: Evidence from Modern Solar Observations
items.abstract: The solar corona reaches temperatures exceeding one million Kelvin, far higher than the approximately 5,800 K temperature of the photosphere, giving rise to the long-standing coronal heating problem. This paper reviews modern observational evidence related to the nanoflare heating model and discusses the extent to which it supports magnetic reconnection as a mechanism for coronal heating. A qualitative literature review was conducted using three representative studies that provide complementary perspectives: theoretical predictions of nanoflare heating, observational evidence from solar active regions, and the thermal evolution of individual coronal loops. The studies were compared in terms of observed heating signatures, consistency with theoretical predictions, and their main limitations. The reviewed evidence shows several behaviors consistent with impulsive nanoflare heating, including temperature-dependent emission sequences, heating and cooling patterns in coronal loops, and signatures associated with small-scale episodic energy release. These characteristics are observed across different spatial scales and generally agree with predictions of nanoflare-based models. However, the evidence remains indirect because individual nanoflares and their associated magnetic reconnection events cannot yet be directly resolved by current instruments. In addition, observational uncertainties and differences between modeled and observed loop behavior limit the strength of the conclusions. Overall, modern solar observations support nanoflares as an important potential contributor to coronal heating, but they do not establish magnetic reconnection through nanoflares as the sole primary heating mechanism. Further improvements in observational resolution and theoretical modeling are required to better determine the role of nanoflares in coronal heating.

items.title: Inspiring the Next Generation of Students through Active Participation in Radio Astronomy Research via International Partnerships
items.abstract: The growing demand for specialists in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) across Europe highlights the need for innovative educational approaches capable of attracting and preparing the next generation of researchers. In this context, radio astronomy represents a particularly effective multidisciplinary platform, combining physics, astronomy, electronics, telecommunications, software development, signal processing, and data science within a single scientific domain. The Erasmus+ project Radio Astronomy Collaboration between European Universities: Developing Scientific and Technological Skills Through Astronomy (RACOBEU) was established to leverage these characteristics and create an international framework for engaging secondary-school and university students in authentic scientific research. RACOBEU brings together the Public University of Navarre, Spain, Ventspils University of Applied Sciences, Latvia and Adam Mickiewicz University, Poland, together with associated secondary schools in all three countries. The project integrates research, education, and international mobility through a combination of student projects, practical workshops, remote observing activities, scientific conferences, and collaborative research placements. Students participate in activities ranging from solar and radio astronomy observations to satellite tracking, radio signal analysis, software-defined radio applications, and astronomical data processing. An important role within the project is played by the research infrastructure of the Ventspils International Radio Astronomy Centre (VIRAC), including the RT-32 and RT-16 radio telescopes and the LOFAR-Latvia station. These facilities provide students with direct access to professional astronomical instrumentation and datasets, enabling participation in studies of solar activity, space weather, radio-frequency interference, astronomical signal processing, spectropolarimetric observations, and radio source investigations. Additional educational opportunities are provided through the remotely accessible Jocelyn Bell Burnell radio telescope at UPNA, allowing students to perform real radio astronomy observations through a web-based interface. During the project, students and staff participated in international conferences held in Latvia, Poland, and Spain, completed multiple collaborative research projects, developed educational resources in four languages, established a new university-level radio astronomy course, and produced nine bachelor’s theses linked to radio astronomy and related STEM fields. Several of these activities resulted in peer-reviewed scientific publications and the development of new instrumentation and software tools for radio astronomy applications. The RACOBEU experience demonstrates that active participation in real scientific research, supported by international partnerships and access to modern astronomical infrastructure, significantly strengthens student engagement with STEM disciplines while fostering technical skills, scientific communication, and cross-border collaboration. The project provides a sustainable model for integrating research infrastructures into education and for developing future generations of scientists and engineers in Europe. Keywords: Radio astronomy; STEM education; Research-based learning; Astronomy education; Science outreach; Remote observations; Radio telescopes.
